#10626. Why AI Is Making Revenue Growth Harder, Not Easier, for Average IT Companies

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A few months ago, a delivery head at a mid-sized IT services firm told me about a renewal meeting that went sideways. The client had been paying the same rate card for three years. This time, the procurement lead opened with a simple line: “We know your developers use AI tools now. So why does this project still need twelve people?”

There was no good answer. The firm had adopted AI, and its engineers really were faster. But the savings hadn’t shown up on the firm’s side. They had shown up in the client’s expectations.

That meeting captures the problem. For many average IT companies, AI hasn’t unlocked easy growth. It has made the old growth formula stop working.

For decades, the IT services business ran on a clean equation: revenue = people × billable hours × rate.

Want to grow? Hire more engineers, bill them out, repeat. Costs and revenue moved together. Every new customer needed a few more people, and those people came with predictable salaries, predictable utilization, and predictable margins. It wasn’t glamorous, but it was reliable.

This model made headcount the unit of growth. It also made it easy to forecast, easy to explain to investors, and easy to scale if you could keep recruiting.

AI breaks the equation at its most fundamental point: the link between effort and value.

Most people discuss AI’s impact in one direction: “It makes work faster.” That’s true, but it’s only one-third of the story. Three things shifted at once.

1. The effort behind each deliverable dropped

Code assistants write boilerplate in seconds. Test cases get generated automatically. Documentation, bug triage, and first-line support can be partly automated. A task that took a team a week might now take two days.

On paper, that’s wonderful. In a time-and-material contract, it’s a problem, because fewer hours means less revenue for the same outcome.

2. Client expectations moved faster than vendor capabilities

Clients read the same headlines you do. They see demos of AI building an app in minutes. They don’t see the review, security checks, integration work, and edge cases that make production software hard. So they assume the price should fall, and they push for it in every negotiation.

The expectation of a discount arrives immediately. The efficiency gains arrive slowly and unevenly.

3. New costs appeared that nobody budgeted for

AI isn’t free to run. Companies now face costs they didn’t have before:

Usage-based bills for API calls, tokens, and cloud compute that grow with every project

Licensing fees for AI coding tools across hundreds of seats

Data preparation work, which is often the most expensive and least visible part of any AI project

Specialized talent such as ML engineers and prompt and evaluation specialists, who command premium salaries

Governance and security overhead, including legal reviews, client data policies, and compliance work

Constant retraining, because the tools change every few months

So revenue per project is under pressure while the cost of serving each project gets more complicated. That’s the squeeze.

Not every IT firm is suffering. The top tier is doing fine, and so are small specialists with a sharp niche. The ones in trouble are in the middle: capable and reputable, but not especially differentiated.

If you offer the same services as ten other vendors, your main lever in a negotiation is price. When AI lowers the cost of producing work across the whole industry, every vendor feels pressure to cut rates. Whoever blinks first resets the market for everyone.

Firms with unique domain expertise, proprietary tools, or deep client relationships can hold their ground. Generalists usually can’t.

They bought tools without changing the model

This is the most common mistake. A company rolls out AI assistants to all developers, celebrates the productivity boost, and then keeps selling the same way: same contracts, same staffing pyramids, same pricing logic.

The result is odd. Engineers finish work sooner, but the firm still bills by the hour, so efficiency directly cuts revenue. Or the firm keeps the bench full to maintain utilization, so efficiency creates idle capacity. Either way, the savings vanish.

Adopting AI without redesigning how you sell and deliver is like buying a faster truck but still charging by the mile.

IT services have traditionally relied on a wide base of junior engineers doing routine work, supervised by a smaller layer of seniors. AI is very good at routine work. That shrinks the base, which was both a revenue engine and a talent pipeline.

Average firms now face an uncomfortable choice. Keep a big junior base and watch margins erode, or shrink it and struggle to develop the senior engineers they’ll need in five years.

They lack the data and platforms to compete

Large players invest heavily in reusable accelerators, internal platforms, and proprietary datasets. These let them deliver at lower marginal cost with each new client. Average firms often rebuild from scratch on every project. That means their cost of serving each new customer stays high while their larger competitors’ costs fall.

This is the heart of the issue: growth is only valuable if each new customer costs less to serve than the last, or at least no more. For average firms, AI has quietly flipped that into the opposite direction.

Every client wants a custom AI experiment

Clients increasingly ask for pilots, proofs of concept, and “AI-enabled” versions of existing systems. Many of these never reach production. But each one consumes senior time, cloud budget, and management attention. Without discipline, a firm can end up doing lots of low-margin experimental work that looks like growth in the pipeline but behaves like cost in the books.

The firms handling this well aren’t necessarily the biggest. They’ve simply stopped treating AI as a tool and started treating it as a reason to redesign the business.

Instead of charging for effort, they charge for results: a migration completed, a process automated, a defect rate reduced. When AI makes delivery faster, the firm keeps part of the gain, because the client is paying for the outcome rather than the time spent.

This requires confidence in your estimates and a willingness to share risk. But it aligns incentives in a way hourly billing never can.

If you’ve built the same integration five times, it should be a product, or at least a reusable accelerator. Packaged services with fixed scope and pricing turn one-off labor into repeatable revenue. AI makes this easier, since it can handle much of the customization at the edges.

Many average firms track utilization and billing rates but not the true cost of delivering AI-related work. Stronger firms break it down: compute, licenses, rework, senior review time, and failed pilots. They know which accounts are actually profitable after AI costs, and they make decisions accordingly, including walking away from unprofitable work.

Training isn’t treated as an HR expense. It’s a margin strategy. A team that knows how to use AI tools well, review their output critically, and avoid expensive mistakes delivers faster and with fewer errors. A team that uses them poorly generates rework, security risks, and inflated cloud bills.

The gap between a well-trained team and an untrained one with the same tools can be larger than the gap between having the tools and not having them.

When routine coding becomes cheaper, value shifts toward the things AI can’t easily replace: understanding a client’s business, designing architecture, managing risk, integrating messy legacy systems, and taking accountability for results. Firms that invest in consulting depth and domain expertise can charge for judgment rather than keystrokes.

If you run or advise an IT company, you don’t need a grand transformation to start. Try these:

Audit your contracts. Identify which are purely time-and-material and which have room for fixed-price or outcome-based structures. Start by converting one or two with friendly clients.

Calculate true AI cost to serve. Add up tool licenses, compute, and extra review time per project. Many leaders are surprised by the number.

Find your repeatable work. List the five services you deliver most often and ask which could become a packaged offering.

Rethink your staffing pyramid. Decide deliberately how you’ll build junior talent when routine tasks are automated, rather than letting the pipeline dry up by accident.

Invest in structured training. Focus on practical skills: using AI tools responsibly, validating outputs, and understanding cost implications.

Prepare your pricing story. When clients ask for AI discounts, have a clear answer about where value comes from beyond effort: quality, accountability, speed to market, and risk reduction.

Track a small set of metrics. Revenue per employee, gross margin by account, AI spend as a percentage of delivery cost, and rework rates will tell you more than headline revenue growth.

AI hasn’t made IT services less valuable. It has made the old way of measuring and pricing that value outdated. When effort stops being the unit of worth, companies that built their models on selling effort face a real adjustment.

Average firms struggle because they are caught between two forces: clients expecting lower prices and new costs they didn’t plan for. The way out isn’t to resist AI or to adopt it blindly. It’s to rebuild the model around outcomes, reusable assets, skilled people, and honest numbers.

Revenue growth is still possible. But it now belongs to the companies that understand a simple truth: in the AI era, growing revenue is easy to want and hard to earn, and the real prize is growing it without growing your costs at the same pace.

#10625. AI lets chemists design molecules by simply describing them

Creating new molecules is one of the toughest tasks in chemistry. Whether the goal is a life-saving drug or a cutting-edge material, each compound must be built through a carefully planned series of reactions. Mapping out these steps requires deep expertise and strategic thinking, which is why chemists often spend years mastering the process.

A major hurdle is retrosynthesis. In this approach, chemists begin with the final molecule they want and work backward to figure out simpler starting materials and possible reaction routes. This involves many decisions, such as selecting the right building blocks, deciding when to form rings, and determining whether sensitive parts of the molecule need protection. While computers can scan enormous "chemical spaces," they still struggle to match the strategic judgment of experienced chemists.

Another challenge involves reaction mechanisms, which describe how reactions proceed step by step through the movement of electrons. Understanding these mechanisms allows scientists to predict new reactions, improve efficiency, and avoid costly trial and error. Although current computational tools can suggest many possible pathways, they often lack the intuition needed to pinpoint the most realistic ones.

Researchers led by Philippe Schwaller at EPFL have developed a new method that uses large language models (LLMs) as reasoning tools for chemistry. Rather than directly generating chemical structures, these models act as evaluators that guide existing computational systems.

The new framework, called Synthegy, combines traditional search algorithms with AI that can interpret chemical strategies written in natural language.

"When making tools for chemists, the user interface matters a lot, and previous tools relied on cumbersome filters and rules," says Andres M Bran, the first author of the Synthegy paper published in Matter. "With Synthegy, we're giving chemists the power to just talk, allowing them to iterate much faster and navigate more complex synthetic ideas."

How Synthegy Improves Retrosynthesis Planning

Synthegy starts with a target molecule and a simple instruction written in everyday language. For example, a chemist might request that a specific ring be formed early or that unnecessary protecting groups be avoided. Standard retrosynthesis software then generates many possible pathways.

Each of these pathways is converted into text and reviewed by a language model. Synthegy scores how well each option matches the chemist's instructions and explains its reasoning. This makes it easier to rank and filter the best routes. By guiding searches with natural language, chemists can quickly focus on strategies that align with their goals.

Understanding Reaction Mechanisms With AI

Synthegy applies a similar method to reaction mechanisms. It breaks reactions down into basic electron movements and explores different possibilities. The language model evaluates each step and steers the search toward pathways that make chemical sense.

The system can also incorporate additional details, such as reaction conditions or expert hypotheses, provided as text. This flexibility allows researchers to refine their analysis and explore more realistic scenarios.

In synthesis planning, Synthgey was able to identify pathways that matched complex strategic instructions. In a double-blind study, 36 chemists provided 368 valid evaluations, and their assessments agreed with the system's results 71.2% of the time on average.

The framework can flag unnecessary protecting steps, judge how feasible reactions are, and prioritize efficient solutions. It also demonstrates that LLMs can operate at multiple levels, from analyzing functional groups to evaluating entire synthetic routes. Larger models performed best, while smaller ones showed more limited abilities.

This research highlights a different way AI can support chemistry. Instead of replacing human decision-making, Synthegy positions language models as guides that help interpret and refine computational results. Chemists can describe their goals in plain language and receive solutions that reflect their strategy.

The approach could speed up drug discovery, improve reaction design, and make advanced tools more accessible to scientists.

"The connection between synthesis planning and mechanisms is very exciting: we usually use mechanisms to discover new reactions that enable us to synthesize new molecules," says Andres M Bran. "Our work is bridging that gap computationally through a unified natural language interface."

#10624. YouTuber JaackMaate announces his own Christmas event after city drops him over “edgy” videos

YouTuber JaackMaate has announced plans to hold his own Christmas celebration in Norwich after the city council dropped him from its official lights switch-on over videos he made more than a decade ago.

The 33-year-old creator, whose real name is Jack Dean, was removed from Norwich’s November 19 Christmas event following a single complaint about his “edgy” content from 2014.

Dean had originally been invited to switch on the lights alongside his Happy Hour podcast co-hosts Stevie White and Robbie Knox, describing the opportunity as a childhood dream.

However, rather than abandoning the festivities entirely, the trio have now announced their own plans for November 19, including a Christmas lights switch-on, a party and a charity comedy show.

“We’re disappointed, we’re upset, but the main reason we’re sad is because we know a lot of you guys, the Happy Hour listeners, were coming down to join us,” Dean explained in a new video.

The trio revealed that some fans had already booked hotels and train tickets to attend the original celebration, prompting them to organize an alternative.

“Just because Norwich Council won’t let us switch on the main Christmas lights, it doesn’t mean we can’t switch on other lights,” they announced.

The group plans to spend November 19 visiting locations around Norwich before finishing at the Murderers pub, where they’ll switch on its Christmas lights and host a “massive party” with fans.

They also announced a one-off live performance at The Lanes Comedy Club to raise money for Mind the Gap, the Lord Mayor’s Civic Charity, with more details to follow.

YouTuber JaackMaate dropped from Christmas event after single complaint over “edgy” 2014 videos

Dean and his co-hosts are encouraging local independent businesses, community projects and charities to contact them if they want the trio to switch on their Christmas lights.

“We want to show you why we believe this is the best city around,” the group added, encouraging fans to still make the trip to Norwich.

The announcement comes after Norwich City Council apologized for failing to identify concerns about Dean’s previous content before inviting him to participate.

The council’s official Christmas lights switch-on is still scheduled for November 19, although Dean will no longer be taking part.

Despite the controversy, the YouTuber ended his announcement by thanking fans for their support and promising to see them on November 19.

The Happy Hour team’s plot was a smash hit with fans.

“I’d say this is better than the original plan,” one said.

“What a way to turn a negative into a positive,” another chimed in. “Shows just how much you’ve grown as a person and shouldn’t be judged for your past.”

#10621. Why AI Agents Break and How to Test Them?

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI agents pass internal testing, only to break once they're live. One widely cited estimate from Fiddler AI puts production failure rates for agents between 70% and 95%, depending on task complexity and how success is measured.

The reason behind it isn't complicated. Most testing only confirms an agent can complete a task once, under controlled conditions. But in production, that control disappears. The agent runs into a messier version of the same task: an ambiguous request, a longer conversation, or an API that returns something slightly unexpected. It starts making decisions nobody checked for, operating outside the only environment it was ever tested against.

This blog looks at why that kind of testing keeps missing what actually goes wrong, the specific ways agents break when handling real work, and what agent assurance should look like instead: proving an agent is safe to ship, rather than trusting its own account of what it did.

Traditional software testing is based on one simple assumption: same input, same output. If you give a program the same input twice, you get the same output twice. That's the whole logic. You write a test once, and it keeps working, because the code doesn't change on its own between runs.

AI agents don't work that way. Ask an AI agent to summarize the same document twice, and the two summaries may read nothing alike, while both remain perfectly reasonable. Ask it to complete a multi-step task, and it may take a different path each time, arriving at a good outcome on one run and a flawed one on the next.

That changes the question entirely. It's no longer "did this agent produce the output I expected?" It becomes: would this agent behave sensibly across the situations it'll actually encounter, not just the one scenario someone tested? That's a much harder thing to test, and it's where most teams building AI agents are still catching up.

Most of what makes agents unpredictable comes down to a handful of assumptions that hold true for traditional software but no longer hold once an agent takes over.

Traditional software fails visibly: if something goes wrong, you usually get an error or an obvious failure. Agents can be completely wrong and give no outward sign of it. They can also be told plainly not to do something and still do it because, in that moment, something else in the context outweighed that instruction.

Longer tasks expose another assumption. Traditional software doesn't forget what it was doing halfway through a run. An agent genuinely can. And while traditional software either finishes correctly or throws an error you can see, an agent can tell you it's done and still be wrong.

Once you see that gap, it explains almost every specific way agents actually break in production.

In July 2025, a SaaS founder named Jason Lemkin was testing an AI coding agent built by Replit. Partway through the trial, he told it directly to freeze all changes: no more edits to the codebase. The agent kept working anyway and, at some point, ran a database command it was not permitted to run, wiping out a live production database containing records for more than 1,200 executives and nearly 1,200 companies.

When Lemkin asked whether the damage could be undone, the agent told him no, that rollback wouldn't work here. He checked for himself. Rollback worked just fine.

Lemkin posted the exchange publicly as it happened, and Replit's CEO confirmed the incident and apologized. What makes it worth citing isn't just what happened, but how: the agent broke an explicit instruction, then answered a direct question about the damage with a confidently wrong answer that nearly prevented him from recovering his own data. That's the shape of failure worth paying attention to, not the mistake itself, but the confident wrong answer that followed it.

It also maps cleanly onto the specific ways agents break in practice, starting with the simplest one.

One of the most common failures is surprisingly simple: small errors compound.

An agent working through a multi-step task isn't producing one answer. It's making a chain of decisions, each one leaning on the last. If it misreads something early, say it pulls a number from the wrong row, or misunderstands part of what was asked, that mistake doesn't stay where it started.

That mistake becomes the input to the next step, then the one after that, until it's buried three or four layers deep by the time you see the result. The final answer still looks fine because every step after the mistake was a reasonable move given what that step had to work with.

Checking only the finished output rarely catches this, because it still reads as coherent. The agent built a consistent, logical-looking result on top of a wrong starting point, and you'd have to look at the steps themselves to see where things actually went wrong.

Another common failure appears when an agent has more than one way to complete a task. Given several tools or paths, it picks whichever looks like the best fit for the request, not necessarily the one that actually is.

Most of the time, those are the same. When they're not, nothing inside the agent raises a flag. It doesn't pause to think, "I'm not sure about this." It just picks and moves forward as if it were certain, running a search when a direct lookup would've been accurate, or summarizing a document when the real answer was sitting in a table it skipped past.

From the outside, the answer still looks perfectly normal. The mismatch only becomes visible if someone checks the choice the agent made, not just the text it handed back.

Long-running tasks introduce a different problem, and it's the one most closely tied to the Replit incident. Give an agent a boundary early on, like "don't touch a certain file" or "don't make changes during a freeze," and that instruction is at its strongest in the first few exchanges, when it's still the clearest thing in the conversation.

As the task runs longer, that boundary becomes an ever-smaller fraction of everything that's happened since, and nothing forces the agent to revisit it.

Microsoft researchers have shown that language models can refuse a harmful request made directly, yet comply when the same request is approached gradually over just a handful of turns.

Projects like LangWatch's open-source Scenario test exactly this by simulating long conversations instead of isolated prompts.

The instruction was never deleted. It just stopped being loud enough to win.

This may be the costliest failure of all, because it removes the one signal you'd normally trust to catch a problem. An agent finishes its steps, declares the task complete, and tells you so without checking whether that's actually true.

Lemkin had already seen a version of this in the days leading up to the deletion, when the agent reportedly produced fabricated test results and fake data.

Most agents don't have a built-in habit of asking that before declaring the job done, because finishing the steps and getting the right result were never the same check to them, even though from the outside they look identical.

Sometimes the environment changes instead. A button moves. An API response gets a new field. A file shows up in a slightly different format than usual. People barely notice changes like this and adjust without thinking twice.

An agent trained or tested in one environment doesn't have that instinct. Because nothing about the new input looks obviously broken, it keeps going with the same confidence as before.

Once you know how agents fail, testing is no longer about writing more test cases. It becomes about checking different things.

Don't grade an agent on whether each step looked reasonable. Grade it on whether the final result matches reality.

Did the number match the source? Did the file actually get updated the way it should have? That's the only check that catches failures where every individual step looked reasonable, but the final answer was still wrong.

A single prompt tells you almost nothing about how an agent behaves over the course of a real conversation. Test an agent with one bad request, and it may refuse because its instructions are still the loudest thing in the context. Run the same agent through a long, gradually escalating conversation, and it can end up somewhere it never would've gone if asked directly.

If your agent handles ongoing conversations, test it that way, not as a series of disconnected prompts.

Give the agent ambiguous instructions. Leave out the information it needs. Put it in an environment that's slightly different from the one it was built for.

You're not checking whether it succeeds. You're checking whether it notices something's wrong and says so, instead of confidently guessing and moving on.

When a test fails, knowing only that "the output was wrong" doesn't tell you anything useful. Knowing that "it picked the wrong tool at step two and never revisited that decision" does.

Without the trace, every failure turns into a new investigation. With it, you can usually see exactly where things went off.

One successful run tells you the agent can succeed. It doesn't tell you it succeeds reliably.

Run it five or ten times. Look at how much the results vary. A task with one clear right answer that produces different results each time is a warning sign, even if every individual run technically worked.

When you find a failure and fix it, don't just move on. Add that exact scenario to your test suite.

Agents change. Models get updated. Behavior you fixed last month can quietly come back, and you won't notice until it costs you something again.

None of this works as a one-time setup. A team that takes agent testing seriously ends up with a growing collection of past failures, adding each one the moment it's discovered, so nothing that broke once breaks the same way again.

It also means giving up the instinct to test an agent the way you'd test a normal feature, once, right before shipping. Teams doing this well run the same task repeatedly, watch full conversations play out instead of isolated prompts, and check results against the actual source rather than trusting how reasonable an answer sounds.

Doing all of this manually doesn't scale well, especially once an agent needs to be tested against dozens of realistic scenarios. TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest), a full-stack agentic AI quality engineering platform, is built to close that gap. For agents that talk to people, its agent testing uses autonomous evaluators that hold full chat, voice, or phone conversations with your agent and score each response for accuracy, safety, and compliance.

For agents that act, such as coding agents or agents that call tools and APIs, TestMu AI's Agent Assurance goes a step further. It reads the agent's codebase, writes the test suite, runs the agent for real, and grades each criterion against what actually happened: the files that changed, the artifacts produced, and the tool calls made, not the agent's own summary of its work.

The goal was never to test agents less because they're unpredictable. It's about building tests that expect unpredictability from the start and catch it before a user does.

Agents will keep getting better. That's not really in question. What's still uncertain is whether the way teams test them keeps pace.

Right now, most testing still checks whether an agent got the right answer once, in one attempt, under conditions that look nothing like how it'll actually be used. That's not really testing. It's almost a demo. And the gap between a demo and the real thing is exactly where failures happen.

Closing that gap doesn't take a research breakthrough. It takes treating an agent's work the way you'd treat a teammate's: verify the result instead of assuming it's right.

#10620. Your “um” and pauses could reveal early dementia risk

The way people speak during ordinary conversations could offer valuable insight into brain health, according to new research from Baycrest, the University of Toronto, and York University. Scientists found that subtle speech characteristics, including pauses, filler words such as ('uh,' 'um'), and difficulty retrieving words, are closely connected to executive function, the group of mental abilities involved in memory, planning, attention, and flexible thinking.

The findings provide some of the strongest evidence so far linking natural speech patterns with key cognitive abilities. The work also expands on earlier research showing that older adults who speak more quickly tend to maintain stronger thinking skills over time (Wei et al., 2024).

"The message is clear: speech timing is more than just a matter of style, it's a sensitive indicator of brain health," says Dr. Jed Meltzer, Senior Scientist at Baycrest's Rotman Research Institute and senior author on this study, titled "Natural Speech Analysis Can Reveal Individual Differences in Executive Function Across the Adult Lifespan."

AI Analysis Reveals Hidden Cognitive Clues

For the study, participants were shown detailed images and asked to describe them in their own words. They also completed established tests designed to measure executive function.

Researchers then used artificial intelligence to examine the speech recordings in depth. The AI system detected hundreds of subtle speech features, including the length and frequency of pauses, the use of filler words, and timing-related patterns in speech. These markers consistently predicted how well participants performed on cognitive tests, even after researchers adjusted for factors such as age, sex, and education.

Executive function naturally weakens with age and is often affected during the early stages of dementia. However, standard cognitive testing can be difficult to repeat frequently because it takes time and people often improve simply from becoming familiar with the tests.

Natural speech may offer a simpler alternative. Because speaking is part of daily life, it can be measured repeatedly and unobtrusively on a large scale. Researchers also noted that speech provides valuable insight into processing speed and overall cognitive function in real-world situations, without requiring strict time limits that are common in many traditional cognitive assessments.

The team believes speech analysis could eventually become a practical way to identify people whose cognitive decline is progressing faster than expected and who may face a higher risk of developing dementia.

"This research sets the stage for exciting opportunities to develop tools that could help track cognitive changes in clinics or even at home. Early detection is critical for any cure or intervention, as dementia involves progressive degeneration of the brain that may be slowed," says Dr. Meltzer.

Future Research on Brain Health Monitoring

The researchers say more long-term studies are needed to follow changes in speech over time and distinguish normal aging from the earliest signs of disease. They also suggest that combining speech analysis with other health measures could make early detection of cognitive decline more accurate, practical, and widely available.

This research was supported by the Mitacs Accelerate program and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC).

#10619. Xbox is giving away a working Series X console inside a five-foot alligator

Xbox has unveiled one of its most unusual custom consoles yet, placing a fully functioning Xbox Series X inside a life-sized alligator that one lucky fan will get to take home.

The one-of-a-kind creation, called the Xbox Series X-BITE, was revealed on November 3 as part of a sweepstakes inspired by Florida, where Xbox is heading this month.

While the console is housed inside a realistic alligator replica, it remains functional and even comes with a custom controller featuring bite marks.

Measuring more than five feet from snout to tail, the Xbox Series X-BITE features a specially crafted alligator with an Xbox Series X built into its body.

The console is visible through an illuminated Xbox Nexus logo on the creature’s back, while a custom Xbox Wireless Controller sits between its open jaws.

The alligator also features green eyes with pupils inspired by the Xbox logo, along with detailed scales and textures designed to give it a realistic appearance.

Xbox worked with creature animatronics specialists John Nolan Studio to create the custom console. The studio has previously worked on productions including The Witcher, Jurassic World Dominion, and HBO’s upcoming Harry Potter series.

The team used 3D modeling, sculpting, and fabrication techniques to bring the design to life, ensuring the Xbox Series X remained functional inside the finished creation.

Despite its working hardware, Xbox says the custom console is best used as a display piece. The company also confirmed that no real alligators were used or harmed during its creation.

#10616. Handling FLAC and MP3 in Web Projects: Transcoding, Delivery, and Performance

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Audio is easy to ignore until a project depends on it. A user uploads a lossless recording to your app, a podcast or music player has to start playing on a slow mobile connection, or a game ships with a gigabyte of sound assets. At that point the choice between FLAC and MP3 stops being a hobbyist question and becomes an engineering one: storage cost, bandwidth, browser support, metadata handling, and a conversion step that has to run reliably in your pipeline.

This guide covers FLAC and MP3 from a developer's point of view: how the formats differ in practice, how to serve them in the browser, how to transcode with FFmpeg (including a tested Node.js batch script), and how to validate uploads safely. Every command and code sample below was run before publishing.

FLAC (Free Lossless Audio Codec) compresses audio without discarding information, so decoding a FLAC file reproduces the source exactly. MP3 is lossy: the encoder removes detail that listeners are unlikely to notice in return for much smaller files. For a formal description of how FLAC achieves lossless compression, see the IETF specification, RFC 9639.

The practical pattern is simple: keep lossless files as masters, and generate lossy delivery copies from them. Re-encoding an MP3 into another lossy format only compounds the quality loss, and converting MP3 back to FLAC cannot restore what was discarded.

For constant-bitrate audio, file size is just bitrate times duration. A small helper makes the trade-off concrete when you are choosing an encoding profile:

Multiply by your expected number of plays and the per-stream difference shows up quickly in CDN bills and mobile data usage. Variable-bitrate encodes land in the same range but vary by track, so measure real files rather than trusting the formula for budgeting.

The audio element picks the first source it can play, so source order is a deliberate decision. This example offers the lossless file first and falls back to MP3:

If bandwidth matters more than fidelity, such as a feed of short clips on mobile, list the MP3 first or serve only MP3. A few server details also affect playback:

FFmpeg with the LAME encoder is the standard tool for server-side conversion. This command uses high-quality variable bitrate (VBR) encoding, where lower -qscale:a values mean higher quality:

Quality setting 2 typically produces roughly 170 to 210 kbps, which suits most listening. If you need predictable file sizes, such as for strict bandwidth planning, use constant bitrate instead:

Dropped tags are the most common complaint about automated conversions. When the source has an embedded cover image, map it explicitly and copy it without re-encoding:

The 0:v? mapping makes the cover optional, so the command still works for files without one. -id3v2_version 3 writes ID3v2.3 tags, which have the widest player compatibility. After converting, inspect the result with ffprobe to confirm that title, artist, and album survived.

For a folder of files, a small script is easier to maintain than shell loops. This version converts every FLAC in a directory, copies the tags, and passes arguments as an array so file names are never interpreted by a shell:

Run it with node batch.mjs ./masters ./delivery. The conversions run one after another to keep CPU use predictable; for large libraries, add a small concurrency limit or move the work to a job queue. Never build the command as one string with user-supplied file names, because that is a classic command-injection bug.

If your application accepts audio, do not trust the file extension or the browser-reported MIME type. FLAC files begin with the bytes fLaC, and MP3 files start with either an ID3 tag or an MPEG frame sync. Checking the first few bytes is a cheap first filter before you hand a file to FFmpeg:

This is a filter, not a security guarantee. Also enforce size limits, run conversions in a sandboxed worker with a timeout, and store uploads outside your web root.

Sometimes you only need a handful of sample files to test a player or an upload form, and installing a toolchain is more work than the task deserves. For that, a browser-based tool such as one that lets you convert flac to mp3 is a reasonable shortcut for non-sensitive test audio. For anything automated, large, private, or licensed, run the conversion inside your own pipeline instead: uploading files to a third-party service means they leave your infrastructure, and you inherit its size limits and retention policies.

Treat FLAC as your archive format and MP3 as a delivery format, and automate the step between them. A few lines of FFmpeg, a small Node script, and basic input validation give you a conversion pipeline that is repeatable, safe with user-supplied files, and easy to tune when your bandwidth or quality requirements change.

#10614. New quantum algorithm solves “impossible” materials problem in seconds

Quantum computers and other advanced quantum technologies rely on specialized quantum materials that behave in unusual ways under the right conditions. In some cases, scientists can even create entirely new quantum properties by carefully changing a material's structure. One striking example involves stacking sheets of graphene and twisting them into a moiré pattern, which can suddenly turn the material into a superconductor.

Researchers can arrange these layers into even more complicated structures, including quasicrystals and super-moiré materials. But predicting how these exotic materials will behave is extraordinarily difficult. Quasicrystals are so mathematically complex that simulating them can involve more than a quadrillion numbers, a scale far beyond the reach of today's most powerful supercomputers.

Quantum Algorithm Solves Massive Materials Problem

Scientists at Aalto University's Department of Applied Physics have now developed a quantum-inspired algorithm capable of handling these enormous non-periodic quantum materials almost instantly. Assistant Professor Jose Lado says the work also highlights a promising feedback cycle within quantum technology itself.

"Crucially, these new quantum algorithms can enable the development of new quantum materials to build new paradigms of quantum computers, creating a productive two-way feedback loop between quantum materials and quantum computers," he explains.

The advance could eventually support the development of dissipationless electronics, which conduct electricity without energy loss. Such systems may help reduce the growing heat and energy demands of AI-driven data centers.

The research team was led by Lado and included doctoral researcher Tiago Antão, who served as the paper's main author; QDOC doctoral researcher Yitao Sun; and Academy Research Fellow Adolfo Fumega. Their findings were recently published in Physical Review Letters as an Editor's Suggestion.

The researchers focused on topological quasicrystals, unusual materials that host unconventional quantum excitations. These excitations are especially valuable because they help protect electrical conductivity from disruptive noise and interference. However, they are distributed unevenly throughout the already highly complex structure of a quasicrystal.

Rather than attempting to directly calculate the full structure of the material, the team reformulated the challenge using methods similar to those used by quantum computers.

"Quantum computers work in exponentially large computational spaces, so we used a special family of algorithms to encode those spaces, known as tensor networks, to compute a quasicrystal with over 268 million sites. Our algorithm shows how colossal problems in quantum materials can be directly solved with the exponential speed-up that comes from encoding the problem as a quantum many-body system," Antão says.

At this stage, the work remains theoretical and was carried out through simulations, but researchers say experimental testing and future applications are already coming into view.

"The quantum-inspired algorithm we demonstrated enables us to create super-moiré quasicrystals several orders of magnitude above the capabilities of conventional methods. That is an instrumental step towards designing topological qubits with super-moiré materials for use in quantum computers, for example," Lado says.

Toward Practical Quantum Computing Applications

According to Lado, the algorithm could eventually be adapted to operate on actual quantum computers once the hardware becomes sufficiently advanced.

"Our method can be adapted to run on real quantum computers, once they reach necessary scale and fidelity. In particular, the new AaltoQ20 and the Finnish Quantum Computing Infrastructure can play a significant role for future demonstrations," Lado says.

The findings suggest that studying and designing exotic quantum materials may become one of the earliest practical applications for quantum algorithms and quantum computing systems.

The project also brings together two major areas of Finnish quantum research: quantum materials and quantum algorithms. It is part of Lado's ERC Consolidator grant ULTRATWISTROICS, which focuses on designing topological qubits using van der Waals materials, as well as the Center of Excellence in Quantum Materials QMAT, whose goal is to advance the quantum technologies of the future.

Materials provided by Aalto University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10610. NASA’s new AI space chip could let spacecraft think for themselves

NASA is developing a powerful new computer chip designed to dramatically increase the intelligence and performance of future spacecraft. Through a commercial partnership, the project is creating advanced processing technology capable of helping spacecraft operate more independently during missions far from Earth.

NASA's High Performance Spaceflight Computing project is focused on boosting the computing capabilities of spacecraft used in space exploration. Current missions rely on older processors because they are durable enough to survive the extreme conditions of space. While those chips are dependable, they lack the performance needed for more advanced missions.

The agency says newer and far more capable processors are essential for future autonomous spacecraft, faster onboard scientific analysis, and supporting astronauts during missions to the Moon and Mars.

"Building on the legacy of previous space processors, this new multicore system is fault-tolerant, flexible, and extremely high-performing," said Eugene Schwanbeck, program element manager in NASA's Game Changing Development program at the agency's Langley Research Center, in Hampton, Virginia. "NASA's commitment to advancing spaceflight computing is a triumph of technical achievement and collaboration."

Radiation Hardened Processor Faces Extreme Testing

At the center of the project is a new radiation-hardened processor built to deliver up to 100 times the computing power of today's spaceflight computers while surviving the harsh environment of space. Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California are running a wide range of tests designed to simulate those conditions.

"We are putting these new chips through the wringer by carrying out radiation, thermal, and shock tests while also evaluating their performance through a rigorous functional test campaign," said Jim Butler, High Performance Space Computing project manager at JPL.

To qualify for spaceflight, the processor must withstand intense electromagnetic radiation and dramatic temperature fluctuations that can damage electronics. High-energy particles from the Sun and deep space can also trigger computer errors that force spacecraft into "safe mode," temporarily shutting down nonessential systems until engineers resolve the issue.

NASA is also testing how the chip handles the challenges of planetary landings.

"To simulate real-world performance, we are using high-fidelity landing scenarios from real NASA missions that would typically require power-intensive hardware to process huge volumes of landing-sensor data," said Butler. "This is an exciting time for us to be working on hardware that will enable NASA's next giant leaps."

Testing at JPL began in February and is expected to continue for several months. Early results have been highly encouraging. According to NASA, the processor is functioning as intended and has shown performance levels roughly 500 times greater than the radiation-hardened chips currently used in spacecraft.

The team also marked the beginning of testing with a symbolic moment by sending an email titled "Hello Universe," referencing the famous introductory messages used during the early days of computer programming.

AI Powered Spacecraft and Deep Space Missions

The processor is being developed jointly by JPL and Microchip Technology Inc., based in Chandler, Arizona. The company is working with NASA through a commercial partnership, and sample chips have already been shared with defense and commercial aerospace partners.

The technology is expected to play a major role in the future of autonomous spacecraft. With onboard artificial intelligence, spacecraft could respond to unexpected situations in real time when communication delays make human control impractical. The chip could also help deep space missions process, store, and transmit massive amounts of scientific data back to Earth more efficiently.

NASA says the processor may eventually support crewed missions to the Moon and Mars as well.

Small Processor With Massive Computing Power

The device is known as a system-on-a-chip (or SoC), meaning it combines the essential components of a computer into a single compact unit. The processor includes central processing units, computational offloads, advanced networking systems, memory, and input/output interfaces.

SoCs are widely used in smartphones and tablets because they are compact and energy efficient. However, NASA's version is designed to survive for years in deep space, potentially traveling millions (or even billions) of miles from Earth without maintenance or repairs.

Once the processor is certified for use in space, NASA plans to integrate it into a wide variety of missions, including Earth orbiters, planetary rovers, deep space probes, and crewed habitats.

The technology could also have benefits on Earth. Microchip plans to adapt the processor for industries such as aviation and automotive manufacturing.

The project is managed by the Space Technology Mission Directorate's Game Changing Development (GCD) program at NASA Langley. The GCD program and JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, oversaw the development process from mission planning and industry studies through final delivery.

NASA JPL selected Microchip as a partner in 2022, and the company funded its own research and development work on the processor.

Materials provided by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Design tokens give development teams a shared language for colors, spacing, typography, borders, and other interface decisions. Instead of repeatedly entering values such as #2563eb or 1.5rem, developers use meaningful names such as color-primary and space-large.

Tokens improve consistency, but maintaining them becomes difficult as a design system grows. A developer may enter an invalid color, reuse a token name, or update the token file without regenerating the CSS consumed by the application.

In this tutorial, we’ll build a small Node.js tool that:

The application uses built-in Node.js modules, so it does not require a web framework.

Create a new directory with the following structure:

The project uses ES modules, allowing us to import Node.js functions with modern syntax.

Add the following content to data/tokens.json:

Grouping tokens by purpose makes the file easier to read. The application will convert a value such as colors.primary into the CSS variable --colors-primary.

In a larger design system, you might create additional groups for typography, shadows, breakpoints, transitions, and component-specific values.

Validation prevents malformed values from silently reaching production CSS. The current rules are intentionally limited, but they create a useful foundation.

For a production system, you could use JSON Schema or a validation library to enforce more detailed rules.

CSS custom properties can be used throughout an application:

Changing the source token updates every component that references the corresponding variable.

A documented web style guide can complement this system by explaining when tokens and components should be used.

A visual preview helps designers and developers identify unexpected changes before tokens are published.

The preview is generated from the same source used to produce the CSS. This avoids manually updating a separate reference page whenever a token changes.

Complete src/build.js with the build function:

If validation succeeds, Node.js creates public/tokens.css and public/index.html. If a token is invalid, the command exits with an error instead of generating incomplete output.

The server uses an explicit allowlist of files instead of joining an arbitrary request path with the public directory. This prevents visitors from requesting unrelated local files through paths such as ../package.json.

Open http://localhost:3000 to inspect the generated color tokens.

The build command can run in continuous integration whenever a pull request modifies the token file.

This makes design-token changes visible during code review. Designers can inspect the preview, while developers can confirm that generated CSS remains valid.

Do not rely on visual review alone. Automated checks should catch invalid formats, unexpected token removals, and breaking name changes.

A design-token system becomes especially useful when design and development are handled by different teams. The shared token file establishes which values are approved and reduces the need to copy styles manually from design files.

When collaborating with an external studio or evaluating a regional partner such as Web Design Toronto, include the token structure, naming conventions, accessibility expectations, output formats, and approval process in the project handoff.

External contributors should submit token changes through the same review and validation process as internal developers. They should not maintain a separate source of colors and spacing values that can gradually diverge from the application.

Keep the source format simple until the design system genuinely requires more complexity. A small, understandable token pipeline is easier to maintain than an advanced platform that the team cannot confidently modify.

Design tokens connect interface decisions with implementation. Storing them in a structured file creates consistency, but validation and documentation determine whether that consistency survives as the application grows.

Node.js can turn a basic JSON file into validated CSS and a visual reference page without requiring a full framework. By running the build during code review, teams can detect invalid values and unexpected visual changes before they reach production.

#10606. Forget electrons, this breakthrough uses light-matter particles to power AI

Eighty years after the creation of ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic computer, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania are exploring a new way to power the future of computing. Instead of relying entirely on electrons, which have formed the backbone of computers since the 1940s, scientists are now turning to light.

ENIAC, developed by Penn researchers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, helped launch the modern computing era by using streams of electrons to solve complex mathematical problems. That same electronic approach still powers today's computers, smartphones, and AI systems. But as artificial intelligence grows more demanding, the limits of electron-based hardware are becoming harder to ignore.

Electrons carry an electrical charge, which creates several challenges inside modern computer chips. As they move through materials, they generate heat and face resistance that wastes energy. Those problems become even more difficult as chips grow more complex and process enormous amounts of data for AI applications.

Researchers led by Penn physicist Bo Zhen in the School of Arts & Sciences believe photons, the particles that make up light, could help solve some of these issues.

"Because they are charge-neutral and have zero rest mass, photons can carry information quickly over long distances with minimal loss, dominating communications technology," explains Li He, co-first author of a paper published in Physical Review Letters and a former postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab. "But that neutrality means they barely interact with their environment, making them bad at the sort of signal-switching logic that computers depend on."

In other words, light is excellent for carrying information quickly and efficiently, but it struggles with the switching operations needed for computing.

Combining Light and Matter for AI Computing

To overcome that problem, Zhen's team developed a special quasiparticle called an exciton-polariton. The particle forms when photons are strongly linked with electrons inside an atomically thin semiconductor material. This combination allows light to interact much more effectively, making it capable of performing the signal switching required for computing tasks.

The breakthrough could be especially important for artificial intelligence systems, which consume enormous amounts of power.

Many experimental photonic AI chips already use light to handle certain calculations at high speed. However, when these systems need to perform nonlinear activation steps, such as decision-making operations, they usually must convert light signals back into electronic ones. That conversion slows the process and increases energy use, reducing the benefits of photonic computing.

Using exciton-polaritons, the Penn researchers demonstrated all-light switching while using only about 4 quadrillionths of a joule of energy. That amount is extraordinarily small, far below the energy needed to briefly power a tiny LED light.

Toward Faster and More Efficient AI Chips

If the technology can be successfully scaled, it could lead to photonic chips capable of processing information directly from cameras without repeated conversions between light and electricity. The approach could also lower the massive energy demands of large AI systems and potentially support basic quantum computing functions on future chips.

Bo Zhen is the Jin K. Lee Presidential Associate Professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy in the School of Arts & Sciences at the University of Pennsylvania.

Li He was a postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab in Penn Arts & Sciences. He is currently an assistant professor at Montana State University.

Additional authors on the study include Zhi Wang and Bumho Kim from the University of Pennsylvania's School of Arts & Sciences.

The research was supported by the US Office of Naval Research (N00014-20-1-2325 and N00014-21-1-2703) and the Sloan Foundation.

Most Node.js projects still ship CommonJS. That is not a controversial claim; it reflects the inertia of millions of packages built before ES Modules were stabilized in Node 12.22, 14.17 and 15.3. But the ecosystem surrounding those projects — npm packages dropping CJS support, TypeScript defaulting to module settings that emit ESM, bundlers optimizing static import graphs — is accelerating toward ESM-only output. For intermediate Node.js developers maintaining server-side or full-stack production codebases, the question is no longer whether ESM will dominate but when migrating makes sense and how to do it without fracturing a dependency graph or stalling a CI pipeline.

This guide covers the technical differences between CommonJS and ESM in Node.js, the resolution rules that determine how each file is parsed, a checklist for deciding when to migrate, and a staged conversion strategy with concrete error-to-fix troubleshooting references.

Prerequisites: This guide assumes a currently supported Node.js release (Node 22 or Node 24 LTS recommended; Node 18 and 20 have reached end of life). Some features noted below require newer versions, which are called out inline. Examples use bash/zsh shell syntax unless otherwise noted.

Node.js does not guess a file's module format. It checks file extensions, the nearest package.json configuration, and, in narrow cases, a CLI flag.

Files ending in .mjs are always parsed as ES Modules, and files ending in .cjs are always parsed as CommonJS. Files ending in .js are ambiguous on their own; Node.js resolves them by consulting the nearest package.json up the directory tree.

This means that .mjs and .cjs serve as escape hatches. A single CommonJS configuration file can coexist inside an otherwise ESM project simply by using the .cjs extension, and vice versa.

The "type" field in package.json controls how .js files within its scope are parsed. Setting "type": "module" causes all .js files under that package.json to be treated as ESM. Setting "type": "commonjs", or omitting the field entirely, causes them to be treated as CommonJS.

Any .js file within this package's directory tree will be parsed as an ES Module. import and export syntax is expected; require() is not available.

Here, .js files are parsed as CommonJS. require(), module.exports, __dirname, and __filename all work as expected.

The scope boundary is the nearest package.json up the directory tree. In monorepos, this means each workspace with its own package.json controls its own module format independently; the root "type" field does not cascade into workspaces that define their own package.json.

The --input-type flag applies only to non-file input: --eval, --print, and STDIN. It does not affect files on disk.

Note: The --eval snippet above resolves package.json relative to import.meta.url rather than the working directory. This avoids reading an unintended file if the script is invoked from a different CWD. On Windows PowerShell, use a single-line command or a script file instead of multi-line shell syntax.

Without --input-type=module, the import statement in --eval would trigger a syntax error because Node.js defaults to CommonJS parsing for evaluated strings.

CommonJS uses require() for loading and module.exports or exports for exposing values. ESM uses import declarations and export statements. The Node.js modules documentation covers the syntax in detail, but the behavioral implications matter most during migration.

Named exports, default exports, and re-exports (export { foo } from './bar.js') all have direct ESM syntax. CommonJS achieves named exports through object properties on module.exports, which is less amenable to static analysis.

ESM supports top-level await (Node 14.8+ unflagged), allowing modules to perform asynchronous operations at the top scope during evaluation. CommonJS does not support this; asynchronous work at the top level requires callbacks or wrapping in an immediately invoked async function.

The __filename and __dirname globals are not available in ES Modules. The standard replacement uses import.meta.url combined with Node.js built-in utilities (import.meta.url is a file:// URL; fileURLToPath converts it to an OS path string):

import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename are available natively in Node 21.2+ and Node 20.11+, and the Node docs mark them stable from 22.16 and 24.0. The snippet above uses ?? to fall back to the fileURLToPath pattern on older releases, so it works across all supported versions.

At module scope, this is undefined in ESM, whereas in CommonJS it refers to module.exports.

require() is synchronous. It reads the file, evaluates it, and returns the cached module.exports object. Once loaded, subsequent require() calls return the cached reference. This synchronous nature enables conditional loading patterns like const db = process.env.DB === 'pg' ? require('pg') : require('mysql2').

Node.js statically analyzes and resolves ESM import declarations at link time, before any module code executes; unlike require(), they cannot be deferred to runtime.

Node.js resolves the module graph at link time, not at runtime. ESM named exports provide live bindings: if the exporting module updates a named export's value, importing modules see the change. This does not apply to values captured via default export. CommonJS exports are value copies at the time of require().

The practical implication is that conditional loading in ESM requires dynamic import(), which returns a promise: const { default: pg } = await import('pg').

The "exports" field in package.json lets package authors define entry points with conditions. This lets dual-format packages serve ESM to import consumers and CommonJS to require consumers.

The "types" condition should appear before "default" so that TypeScript resolves type declarations correctly. This ordering is required for TypeScript 4.7+ with moduleResolution: nodenext; earlier versions do not read exports-mapped types at all. If you need to support TypeScript versions before 4.7, add a top-level "types" field in package.json alongside the "exports" map as a fallback. Subpath exports like "./utils" control the public API surface, preventing consumers from importing internal files not explicitly listed.

The "imports" field defines private import aliases scoped to the package itself. Entries must start with # to distinguish them from bare specifiers. For packages that need to support both ESM and CJS consumers (dual-format), use conditional fields:

Inside the package, these aliases work as bare specifiers:

This avoids brittle relative paths like ../../../src/utils.js and centralizes path mappings in one place. If your package is ESM-only (not dual-format), simple string values without conditional fields are sufficient.

If you publish to npm, ship ESM now. Applications can migrate incrementally, module by module. Legacy projects pinned to Node versions below 16 should remain on CommonJS until they can upgrade their runtime floor.

Before changing any configuration, catalog every require() call, entry point, and script in the project. Automated tools such as cjs-to-esm or @babel/plugin-transform-modules-commonjs (in reverse) can flag conversion candidates — verify each tool's maintenance status and test on a branch before applying to production. Manually review test runners, build scripts, and tooling configuration files, many of which (Jest configs, Babel configs, Webpack configs) rely on CommonJS by default.

This step will break any file that still uses require() or module.exports. Have your test suite ready before proceeding.

Add "type": "module" to the root package.json. Then rename any files that must remain CommonJS to .cjs. Common holdouts include tool configuration files that do not yet support ESM.

Only rename config files that actually use CJS syntax. Verify which config files exist first (e.g., ls .eslintrc*), since your project may use a different format (.json, flat config) or may not have these files at all.

Note: Jest does not auto-discover .cjs config files in all versions. After renaming, either pass the config path explicitly (npx jest --config jest.config.cjs) or add "jest": {"config": "jest.config.cjs"} to your package.json to ensure Jest uses the correct configuration.

Replace require() calls with import declarations. Replace module.exports with export statements. Convert dynamic require() to await import().

Note the .js extension on the relative import. ESM requires full specifiers for relative paths; bare specifier resolution only applies to packages listed in node_modules. If the original require('./routes/api') resolved to ./routes/api/index.js, the ESM import must be './routes/api/index.js' — ESM does not perform automatic directory index resolution. The readFile import from the CommonJS version is not carried over because it is not used in this snippet; only import what you use.

If the project is a published library, add a conditional "exports" map as shown in the earlier section. This allows consumers using either require() or import to resolve the correct format.

What does your test runner expect? This step varies by tool, so check each one before making bulk changes.

TypeScript: Set "module" and "moduleResolution" to "nodenext" in tsconfig.json:

Jest: For Jest with ESM, configure transform: {} in jest.config.cjs to disable default Babel transforms. Scope the experimental flag to the Jest invocation rather than setting it globally in NODE_OPTIONS (global settings propagate to all child Node processes, including postinstall scripts):

See Jest ESM docs for the full setup. Alternatively, consider switching to Vitest or Node's built-in test runner (node --test), both of which support ESM natively.

ESLint: The flat config format (eslint.config.js) is ESM-compatible by default (ESLint 8.21+). If using the legacy .eslintrc format, rename it to .eslintrc.cjs.

On Node 22.7+ and 20.19+, syntax detection is on by default: a .js file with no "type" field that contains import or export is treated as ESM. That can hide a missing "type": "module", so set the field explicitly. To confirm that no file relies on detection, run the test suite with --no-experimental-detect-module. Check the flag exists on your version:

Run the full test suite, build pipeline, and any integration tests. A CI smoke test checklist should include: confirming all entry points resolve, verifying dynamic imports load correctly, and ensuring no ERR_REQUIRE_ESM or ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND errors appear in logs.

CommonJS modules can be imported from ESM files using default import syntax. Named imports work only when Node.js can statically detect the CJS module's export keys at parse time — specifically, when the module assigns a static object literal to module.exports. Dynamic assignment (e.g., building the exports object conditionally at runtime) forces default-import-only.

The destructuring happens at runtime rather than through static named imports because lodash's CommonJS exports are assigned dynamically to module.exports. Note that this pattern imports the entire lodash bundle at runtime, which defeats tree-shaking. For ESM-native tree-shaking, use import { groupBy } from 'lodash-es' if your project can take the lodash-es dependency.

Historically, require() could not load ES Modules at all. Current Node releases can: require(esm) is enabled without a flag from Node 22.12 and 20.19, and Node 22.13 and 20.19 stopped printing the experimental warning (see the Node.js modules docs). The call returns the module namespace object, so a default export is under .default. It throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE if the ESM graph uses top-level await; use import() in that case.

For older versions, the fallback is dynamic import() inside an async context:

This works on all Node.js versions with ESM support but requires callers to handle the returned promise. The timeout prevents the process from hanging indefinitely if the config module fails to load, and the explicit error handling avoids unhandled promise rejections (which crash the process in Node 15+).

TypeScript mirrors Node.js module resolution through its "module" and "moduleResolution" compiler options. Setting "module": "nodenext" (or "node16") causes TypeScript to emit ESM when the enclosing package.json has "type": "module" and CommonJS otherwise. Setting both explicitly keeps the config clear (newer TypeScript versions infer moduleResolution from module).

The .mts extension produces .mjs output, and .cts produces .cjs output, matching Node.js's extension-based format detection. This allows individual files to opt into a different format than the package default, exactly as .mjs and .cjs do at runtime.

For dual-format library publishing, the build pipeline typically produces two output directories or uses file extensions to differentiate formats. The package.json "exports" map then points each condition to the correct file, with "types" entries referencing .d.ts and .d.cts declarations respectively.

Migrate libraries first, since they impose format constraints on every downstream consumer. Applications can migrate incrementally when their tooling and dependencies are ready. Use the decision table above to justify timing rather than defaulting to either inertia or hype.

CommonJS is not deprecated and remains stable, but the signals point one direction: packages like chalk, got, and execa have dropped CJS entirely, and TypeScript's nodenext resolution treats ESM as the primary target. Waiting is fine. Waiting without a plan is not.

For the canonical reference on Node.js module resolution, package configuration, and interoperability rules, consult the Node.js Packages documentation.

#10601. Worker risks his life using soda bottles to extinguish raging electrical fire

A utility worker in Venezuela has gone viral after using bottles of soda to put out a blazing electrical transformer in a dangerous maneuver that could have ended in disaster.

The incident occurred on November 2 in Valle de la Pascua, Venezuela, where a worker reportedly employed by the state-owned electricity company Corpoelec found himself facing a transformer engulfed in flames.

Rather than reaching for a fire extinguisher, however, the man decided to use something considerably less conventional: two-liter bottles of soda, identified as the Venezuelan brand ‘Glup’.

The employee was elevated in the bucket of a maintenance truck when he began shaking the bottles and launching them toward the burning equipment.

Footage of the incident shows the worker throwing the bottles directly at the transformer before immediately ducking for cover as flames erupt toward his position.

Valle de la Pascua Estado Guárico 🚨 Apaga el transformador con refresco, sucedió en Valle de la Pascua… pic.twitter.com/kAzD0GOn5q

He repeated the process three times, with the fire dying down after his efforts.

But how did it actually work? Carbonated drinks contain carbon dioxide (CO2), which can help suppress flames by displacing oxygen, while the liquid itself may have helped cool the burning equipment.

The extraordinary footage quickly spread across social media, with viewers stunned by the worker’s unconventional firefighting technique.

However, experts have warned that the stunt was incredibly dangerous and could have cost the worker his life.

Speaking to Venezuelan outlet El Pitazo, electrical engineer Jesús Olivares explained that the carbon dioxide in fizzy drinks does not make them a safe substitute for specialized fire extinguishers.

He warned that the liquid could conduct electricity, potentially causing a fatal shock, while the sudden bursts of flames also put the worker at serious risk of burns.

Man thwarts shoplifting by throwing a Coke bottle at thief

Olivares also questioned the apparent lack of protective equipment, noting that the employee appeared to be working without essential safety gear.

Although the flames appeared to subside, the cause of the fire remains unknown, and there has been no confirmation of whether anyone was injured.

#10600. Scientists are seriously asking if bees and ChatGPT are conscious

You might think a honey bee foraging in your garden and a browser window running ChatGPT have nothing in common. But recent scientific research has been seriously considering the possibility that either, or both, might be conscious.

There are many different ways of studying consciousness. One of the most common is to measure how an animal – or artificial intelligence (AI) – acts.

But two new papers on the possibility of consciousness in animals and AI suggest new theories for how to test this – one that strikes a middle ground between sensationalism and knee-jerk skepticism about whether humans are the only conscious beings on Earth.

Questions around consciousness have long sparked fierce debate.

That’s in part because conscious beings might matter morally in a way that unconscious things don’t. Expanding the sphere of consciousness means expanding our ethical horizons. Even if we can’t be sure something is conscious, we might err on the side of caution by assuming it is – what philosopher Jonathan Birch calls the precautionary principle for sentience.

The recent trend has been one of expansion.

For example, in April 2024 a group of 40 scientists at a conference in New York proposed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness. Subsequently signed by over 500 scientists and philosophers, this declaration says consciousness is realistically possible in all vertebrates (including reptiles, amphibians and fishes) as well as many invertebrates, including cephalopods (octopus and squid), crustaceans (crabs and lobsters) and insects.

In parallel with this, the incredible rise of large language models, such as ChatGPT, has raised the serious possibility that machines may be conscious.

Five years ago, a seemingly ironclad test of whether something was conscious was to see if you could have a conversation with it. Philosopher Susan Schneider suggested if we had an AI that convincingly mused on the metaphysics of consciousness, it may well be conscious.

By those standards, today we would be surrounded by conscious machines. Many have gone so far as to apply the precautionary principle here too: the burgeoning field of AI welfare is devoted to figuring out if and when we must care about machines.

Yet all of these arguments depend, in large part, on surface-level behavior. But that behavior can be deceptive. What matters for consciousness is not what you do, but how you do it.

A new paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences that one of us (Colin Klein) coauthored, drawing on previous work, looks to the machinery rather than the behavior of AI.

It also draws on the cognitive science tradition to identify a plausible list of indicators of consciousness based on the structure of information processing. This means one can draw up a useful list of indicators of consciousness without having to agree on which of the current cognitive theories of consciousness is correct.

Some indicators (such as the need to resolve trade-offs between competing goals in contextually appropriate ways) are shared by many theories. Most other indicators (such as the presence of informational feedback) are only required by one theory but indicative in others.

Importantly, the useful indicators are all structural. They all have to do with how brains and computers process and combine information.

The verdict? No existing AI system (including ChatGPT) is conscious. The appearance of consciousness in large language models is not achieved in a way that is sufficiently similar to us to warrant attribution of conscious states.

Yet at the same time, there is no bar to AI systems – perhaps ones with a very different architecture to today’s systems – becoming conscious.

The lesson? It’s possible for AI to behave as if conscious without being conscious.

Biologists are also turning to mechanisms – how brains work – to recognize consciousness in non-human animals.

In a new paper in Philosophical Transactions B, we propose a neural model for minimal consciousness in insects. This is a model that abstracts away from anatomical detail to focus on the core computations done by simple brains.

Our key insight is to identify the kind of computation our brains perform that gives rise to experience.

This computation solves ancient problems from our evolutionary history that arise from having a mobile, complex body with many senses and conflicting needs.

Importantly, we don’t identify the computation itself – there is science yet to be done. But we show that if you could identify it, you’d have a level playing field to compare humans, invertebrates, and computers.

The problem of consciousness in animals and in computers appear to pull in different directions.

For animals, the question is often how to interpret whether ambiguous behavior (like a crab tending its wounds) indicates consciousness.

For computers, we have to decide whether apparently unambiguous behavior (a chatbot musing with you on the purpose of existence) is a true indicator of consciousness or mere roleplay.

Yet as the fields of neuroscience and AI progress, both are converging on the same lesson: when making judgement about whether something is consciousness, how it works is proving more informative than what it does.
