#10597. WWE star Danhausen hits back after fans think his facepaint trademark targets Magic: The Gathering

WWE superstar Danhausen has responded to backlash after an old interview about his trademarked facepaint resurfaced online, with some fans believing he was preparing to take legal action against Magic: The Gathering.

Danhausen, whose real name is Donovan Danhausen, is known for his black-and-white facepaint, comedic curses, jars of teeth, and “Very Nice, Very Evil” persona. He joined WWE earlier this year after previously wrestling for AEW and Ring of Honor.

The resurfaced clip came from a 2025 appearance on Insight with Chris Van Vliet. During the interview, Danhausen explained that he had already been wearing his signature makeup when he saw a Magic: The Gathering card with a strikingly similar design. The card was identified in the repost as Juri, Master of the Revue.

The clip prompted some fans to accuse Danhausen of claiming that Wizards of the Coast copied his character. He pushed back against that interpretation on X.

“If you’re mad about this, you’re stupid,” Danhausen wrote. “This isn’t so Danhausen can Willy nilly try to sue people. It’s literally so no one can yell at Danhausen.”

He later replied to another fan, writing, “Bingo. Danhausen loves Magic.”

Danhausen’s facepaint trademark predates his WWE career. The USPTO filing was submitted under his real name in 2020 and describes the mark as a stylized face used across merchandise and wrestling entertainment.

If you’re mad about this, you’re stupid. This isn’t so Danhausen can Willy nilly try to sue people. It’s literally so no one can yell at Danhausen. https://t.co/l7TsobDBiB

During the original interview, Danhausen also said he was the first wrestler to trademark his facepaint. He claimed Sting later worked with the same attorney to protect his own signature look. Danhausen’s makeup is inspired by the demon Pazuzu from The Exorcist.

The clarification arrived during a major week for Danhausen, who hosted a WWE YouTube special, appeared in a Danhausen-themed SmackDown episode, and hosted NXT Halloween Havoc.

#10596. React Form Validation Using Shared Zod Schemas and Server Actions

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Duplicated validation logic is one of the most persistent sources of bugs in React applications. A client-side rule changes, the server-side copy stays the same, and invalid data slips through the gap. React form validation that relies on a single Zod schema, shared between React Hook Form on the client and a Next.js Server Action on the server, eliminates that drift entirely. This tutorial walks through building that pattern from scratch: a contact form with client-side validation via zodResolver, server-side re-validation with safeParse, accessible error rendering following ARIA authoring practices, and a Vitest test suite that locks down the schema's correctness.

The result is a Next.js App Router contact form where every validation rule lives in one file. When the server rejects a submission, field-level errors map back to individual inputs using setError, and screen readers announce them through aria-describedby associations.

Prerequisites: you should know React, TypeScript, and the Next.js App Router. You will also need Node 20.9 or later, which is the minimum for current Next.js releases. The code below was type-checked with TypeScript 5.9.3 and 7.0.2 and the tests were run with Vitest 5.0.5, React Hook Form 7.90.0, @hookform/resolvers 5.9.1 and Zod 4.6.7.

Start with the standard create-next-app scaffolding. The flags below suppress all interactive prompts and ensure the resulting directory structure matches the file paths used throughout this tutorial:

Each flag matters: --no-src-dir places the app/ directory at the project root (rather than inside src/), and --import-alias '@/*' configures the @/ path alias in tsconfig.json so that imports like @/lib/schemas/contact resolve correctly.

The form layer requires three packages: react-hook-form for state management, @hookform/resolvers for connecting external schema libraries, and zod for schema definition. Testing relies on vitest.

Add @testing-library/react if you plan to write component-level tests beyond the schema tests shown in this tutorial.

After installation, the relevant portion of package.json should look similar to:

The devDependencies block shown is abridged. Your actual file will also contain @types/react, @types/react-dom, @types/node, and ESLint-related packages installed by create-next-app. Those are omitted here for brevity.

The schema lives in its own file so both the client component and the Server Action can import it without pulling in unnecessary dependencies.

Each field carries a custom error message. This tutorial uses Zod 4, where z.email() replaces the deprecated z.string().email(); on Zod 3 keep the older form. The ContactFormData type is inferred directly from the schema with z.infer, so the TypeScript type and the runtime validation rules can never diverge.

Both the client component and the Server Action import contactSchema from this one module. On the client, zodResolver wraps the schema so React Hook Form can evaluate it during its validation cycle. On the server, safeParse() runs the same rules against raw input and returns structured errors without throwing. You author the schema once, but it executes in two runtimes. Any change to a validation rule propagates to both sides immediately.

You author the schema once, but it executes in two runtimes. Any change to a validation rule propagates to both sides immediately.

The complete component is shown below as a single file. It combines the hook setup, the onSubmit handler, and the JSX return in the order they appear in the source.

The useForm hook accepts a resolver option that delegates validation to Zod. Setting mode to 'onTouched' means fields validate on blur and re-validate on subsequent changes, giving users immediate feedback without triggering errors before they interact with a field.

The register function connects inputs to React Hook Form's internal state. errors provides per-field error objects, and isSubmitting tracks whether an async submission is in flight.

Every input receives aria-invalid when its corresponding error exists and aria-describedby pointing to a that holds the error message. The aria-describedby attribute is always present (pointing to a consistently rendered ) so that screen readers maintain the association even when errors are cleared. This follows the ARIA authoring practices for inline error messages: aria-describedby links the error to its input, and aria-invalid signals the error state, so screen readers announce the error when the user focuses the field.

The noValidate attribute on the

element turns off built-in browser validation so Zod's rules run instead. The submit button disables itself during submission to prevent duplicate requests. The aria-busy attribute on the form communicates the loading state to assistive technology.

When React Hook Form's client-side validation passes, onSubmit fires. It calls the Server Action, inspects the response for field errors, and maps any server-returned errors back to individual inputs using the applyServerErrors helper (defined in the "Mapping Server Errors" section below). A try/catch block wraps the handler so that network failures or unexpected Server Action crashes surface as a root-level form error instead of leaving the form stuck in a submitting state.

The type: 'server' string used inside applyServerErrors is a convention, not a React Hook Form requirement. It makes it possible to distinguish server-originated errors from client-originated ones when logging, styling, or routing analytics events.

The Server Action imports the same contactSchema and runs safeParse against the incoming data. If parsing fails, the flattened field errors return to the client. If it succeeds, business logic executes inside a try/catch block to ensure unexpected errors come back as structured responses rather than crashing the action. In a real application, the success branch would perform a concrete operation like inserting a row into a contacts table via Prisma or dispatching a transactional email.

The parameter is typed unknown deliberately. Typing it ContactFormData would let TypeScript accept the data without re-parsing, defeating server-side re-validation.

The z.flattenError() helper turns a ZodError into a flat { formErrors: string[], fieldErrors: { name: string[], email: string[] } } shape, which maps directly to the setError loop on the client. (Zod 3 and 4 also have an error.flatten() method, deprecated in Zod 4.) Zod types each field value as optional via a partial record, so the filtering step above narrows out undefined entries and the returned fieldErrors object is a safe Record.

Client-side validation runs in the browser. A user can bypass it entirely by disabling JavaScript, manipulating form data through DevTools, or submitting requests directly via cURL or an automated bot. Server re-validation using the same schema guarantees that identical rules apply regardless of how the request arrives.

Server re-validation using the same schema guarantees that identical rules apply regardless of how the request arrives.

Implement rate limiting and CSRF token verification alongside schema validation. These complementary measures address different threat vectors, though they fall outside the scope of this tutorial.

The applyServerErrors helper (used in the onSubmit handler above) takes each key from the server's fieldErrors object and injects it into React Hook Form's error state. Because the error spans in the JSX read from formState.errors.fieldName, the correct re-renders automatically and aria-invalid toggles to true on the corresponding input. The accessible error contract stays intact without adding manual DOM queries or event listeners.

For unexpected errors that do not map to a specific field, React Hook Form supports root-level errors via setError('root.serverError', { message: '...' }) (requires react-hook-form >=7.34.0; alternatively use setError('root', ...) on earlier versions). This is useful for handling cases like network failures or internal server errors where no individual field is at fault.

To keep this pattern DRY across multiple forms, the mapping logic lives in a reusable helper. The helper accepts an explicit list of valid field paths and routes any unrecognized keys to a root-level error, preventing server-supplied keys from silently corrupting form state:

This helper is generic over the form's field values type, so it works with any Zod schema and any form that uses React Hook Form. The validFields parameter ensures that only known form field paths are passed to setError, while any unexpected keys from the server response are safely routed to a root-level error. The ContactForm component imports it directly, replacing the inline loop shown in earlier drafts.

Create vitest.config.ts at the project root. This configures the @/ path alias so Vitest can resolve the same imports used in the application code:

Because the schema is a standalone module with no UI dependencies, it can be tested in isolation with fast unit tests. Each test calls safeParse and asserts on the structured result.

These tests assert exact error messages, which catches regressions in user-facing copy as well as validation logic.

Run the full suite with npx vitest run. For continuous feedback during development, npx vitest starts watch mode. Adding either command to a CI pipeline ensures that schema changes are verified on every push.

A single Zod schema, shared between React Hook Form's zodResolver and a Next.js Server Action, eliminates validation drift. The setError mapping closes the feedback loop between server and client. ARIA attributes ensure that error states are perceivable by assistive technology. Vitest locks down the schema's correctness independent of the UI.

A single Zod schema, shared between React Hook Form's zodResolver and a Next.js Server Action, eliminates validation drift.

From here, add file upload validation on the client with z.instanceof(File). Note that server-side file validation requires inspecting FormData entries directly, since uploaded files arrive in the server's FormData rather than in a typed object. You can also integrate useFormStatus from React DOM for streaming submission indicators; this hook must live in a child component of the element, not in the component that renders the form itself. For multi-step forms, split a larger schema across wizard steps using z.pick() or z.omit() so each step validates only its own subset.

#10595. A classic brain test exposed AI's biggest weakness

Artificial intelligence systems can write essays, answer questions, and solve complex problems. But new research suggests they may struggle with something humans do every day: staying focused on the task at hand when distractions get in the way.

Researchers led by Suketu Patel put several leading AI models through a well-known psychology experiment called the Stroop task. The results revealed a significant difference between how AI systems process information and how the human brain manages attention.

The Stroop task is a classic psychological test that has been used for decades to study attention, concentration, and self-control.

In the test, color words such as "red," "blue," or "green" are displayed in colored ink. Sometimes the word and the ink color match. For example, the word "red" might appear in red ink. Other times they conflict, such as the word "red" printed in blue ink.

Participants are asked to name the color of the ink rather than read the word itself.

That sounds simple, but it creates a challenge because reading words is an automatic habit for most people. The brain must suppress the urge to read the word and instead focus on identifying the ink color.

Psychologists often use the task to measure what is known as executive control, a set of mental processes that helps people regulate attention, resist distractions, and stay focused on goals.

The researchers wanted to see whether modern large language models (LLMs) handle this challenge in the same way humans do.

LLMs are the AI systems behind tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. They are trained on enormous amounts of text and learn patterns in language, allowing them to generate responses that often appear remarkably human.

When given short lists containing five color words, the AI systems generally performed well, even when the words and colors did not match.

However, the picture changed dramatically as the lists became longer.

GPT-4o achieved 91% accuracy when working with five words. At ten words, its accuracy fell to 57%. When the list expanded to forty words, accuracy dropped to just 15%.

Claude 3.5 Sonnet maintained stable performance through lists of twenty words but then experienced a sharp decline, falling to 24% accuracy with forty-word lists.

The researchers observed similar patterns in GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1, and Gemini 2.5.

The challenge became even more difficult when matching and mismatched color words appeared together in the same list.

Under those conditions, performance deteriorated further. Accuracy for the mismatched items dropped to nearly zero in some cases.

According to the researchers, the AI models had trouble maintaining the instruction to identify ink colors. Instead, they increasingly defaulted to reading the words themselves.

In other words, the systems appeared unable to consistently suppress the response they had been most heavily trained to produce.

This finding is particularly interesting because humans face a similar conflict. People are generally much better at reading words than naming ink colors. Yet despite this bias, most individuals can maintain high accuracy and stable performance even when confronted with long lists of conflicting words and colors.

The study highlights an important distinction between human and artificial intelligence.

Although modern AI systems can produce impressive language and reasoning capabilities, their underlying mechanisms differ from the attention processes found in biological brains.

Humans can often sustain focus on a specific goal while filtering out competing information. The results suggest that current AI models may struggle with this type of cognitive control when tasks become increasingly demanding.

The researchers argue that the performance collapse seen in these experiments points to fundamental limitations in today's large language models. While AI can sometimes mimic human behavior, its ability to maintain attention appears to operate very differently from the way people do.

The findings offer a reminder that even the most advanced AI systems still have weaknesses, particularly when tasks require them to resist distractions and stay focused over extended sequences of information.

#10592. Reddit testing new feature that puts ads in search results

Reddit has announced that it’s testing new advertisements in its search results, meaning users could start seeing sponsored products related to whatever they’re looking for.

In a November 3 announcement, Reddit confirmed that it has started experimenting with additional advertising placements on its search pages.

Rather than showing the same promotions to everyone, the company says the ads can be influenced by what individual users are searching for.

“Ads in search may appear based on a range of factors, including contextual relevance to a user’s search query,” the statement reads.

They used the example that someone looking for advice on building a home office could encounter advertisements for desks, monitors, or office chairs. Likewise, searching for ways to set up a coffee station might bring up promotions for coffee machines, beans, and mugs.

Reddit explained that the idea is to reach users who are already researching particular products or considering purchases. However, the company isn’t rolling out the new placements to every advertiser immediately.

“This is an initial test with a select group of eligible advertisers,” Reddit confirmed. “During this test, we will evaluate and understand how users respond to these ads so we can refine the experience for users and advertisers over time.”

It’s worth noting that Reddit already features advertising across its platform, so this isn’t the introduction of ads to the site for the first time.

Instead, the experiment focuses on additional ads while searching, potentially making sponsored products more prominent when users are looking for posts or communities.

#10591. Brain-inspired chip runs near absolute zero and could transform quantum computing

Researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) have unveiled a significant advance in cryogenic electronics that could help overcome key challenges in quantum computing and support future deep space missions. The team, from HKU's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering and the Centre for Advanced Semiconductors and Integrated Circuits (CASIC), developed a programmable neuromorphic hardware platform capable of operating at temperatures near absolute zero.

The research was led by Professor Yuhao Zhang and PhD student Xin Yang. Their work introduces a new method for generating and controlling negative differential resistance (NDR) in industry standard Silicon Carbide (SiC) MOSFETs. Using this approach, the researchers demonstrated for the first time that a single transistor can reproduce the energy efficient "spiking" activity of biological neurons at temperatures as low as 10mK.

Brain-Inspired Hardware for Quantum Computing

Quantum computers depend on sophisticated control electronics to manage qubits, which are highly sensitive and must be kept at millikelvin temperatures. Existing silicon based control systems consume considerable power and produce unwanted heat, making it necessary to position them away from the qubits themselves. That distance creates extensive wiring requirements that can hinder performance and make large scale quantum computers more difficult to build.

"Our work introduces a hardware platform that can be integrated alongside quantum processors," said Professor Zhang. "By using the unique carrier dynamics in silicon carbide, we can create circuits that are thousands of times more energy-efficient than conventional electronics, significantly reducing the thermal load on cryogenic systems."

Silicon Carbide Reveals Unique Cryogenic Behavior

The team found that SiC MOSFETs display a strong "S-shape" NDR effect when cooled below 2K. This behavior is driven by electron-donor impact ionization (EDII). Unlike other technologies that depend on heat generated within a device, the newly observed mechanism arises directly from the material's atomic properties. As a result, it remains highly stable and can be reproduced consistently across different manufacturing batches.

"This is a robust and scalable approach," said Mr. Yang. "Because SiC is already used globally in electric vehicles and power grids, we can leverage existing industrial foundries to manufacture these cryogenic chips on 300-mm wafers."

From Artificial Neurons to Deep Space Missions

The study also demonstrated that these artificial neurons can be linked together, or "cascaded," into larger networks. This capability could enable advanced local data processing at cryogenic temperatures and improve important quantum computing functions such as quantum error correction and real time quantum control.

The potential applications extend well beyond quantum computing. Because the circuits are designed to operate reliably in extremely cold environments, they could also be valuable for deep space exploration. Future systems may be able to function in the harsh conditions found on the Moon's surface or in the distant regions of our solar system.

The findings were published in Nature Communications in a paper titled "Cryogenic neuromorphic circuits using gate-controlled negative differential resistance in silicon carbide."

As web applications grow, JavaScript code can quickly become difficult to manage. What begins as a few functions in a single file may eventually include API requests, user interface logic, validation, data processing, and reusable utilities. Keeping all this functionality in one place makes code harder to understand, test, and maintain.

JavaScript modules provide a structured way to divide an application into smaller, independent files. Each module can expose specific functionality while keeping its internal implementation separate from the rest of the application.

Modern JavaScript supports native modules through import and export, allowing developers to organize code without relying on global variables or manually combining scripts.

This guide explains how JavaScript modules work, how to structure them effectively, and how to avoid common problems when building maintainable web applications.

A JavaScript module is a file that can import functionality from other modules and export its own functions, objects, or values.

Consider a utility function that calculates the total price of a shopping cart. Without a modular structure, this logic might be placed directly inside a large application file.

Instead, create a separate file named cart.js:

The export keyword makes the function available to other modules.

The calculation now exists in one dedicated location. If another part of the application needs the same functionality, it can import the function rather than duplicate the implementation.

This separation also makes the calculation easier to test independently.

JavaScript supports two common export styles: named exports and default exports.

Named exports allow a module to expose multiple explicitly named values.

Another module can import one or both functions:

Named exports are useful for utility files that contain related functions.

A default export represents the module's primary exported value:

It can be imported using a locally chosen name:

Neither export style is universally better. Named exports can make dependencies explicit, while default exports can be convenient when a module has one clear primary purpose.

For a consistent codebase, teams should establish conventions and apply them throughout the project.

Splitting a large file into many smaller files does not automatically improve maintainability. A useful module should have a clear responsibility and a reasonably understandable interface.

For example, an online store might use the following structure:

products.js handles communication with the product API.

cart.js contains shopping-cart operations.

renderProducts.js updates the product interface.

formatCurrency.js formats monetary values.

This structure makes it easier to locate functionality and understand how different parts of the application interact.

The exact organization depends on the project's size. A small website may need only a few modules, while a larger application may benefit from grouping files by feature rather than creating a separate directory for every technical category.

The objective is clarity, not the maximum possible number of files.

A common source of complexity is mixing network requests, data transformation, and DOM updates in a single function.

A more maintainable approach is to place API communication in its own module.

The function checks the HTTP response before attempting to use its data. This matters because fetch() does not automatically reject its promise for HTTP error responses such as 404 or 500.

The interface module can then use the API function:

This example keeps the network request separate from the application entry point.

In a production application, developers would typically add suitable loading states, user-facing error messages, response validation, and any required authentication or caching logic.

It is also important to remember that a separate API module does not replace server-side authorization or input validation.

Static imports are appropriate for dependencies that an application needs as part of its normal execution. However, some functionality is only required after a user performs a particular action.

Dynamic imports allow modules to be loaded when needed.

The report module is requested when the button is clicked rather than being loaded through a static import at the beginning of the application.

This can be useful for analytics dashboards, advanced editors, charts, and other features that are not immediately necessary.

Dynamic imports return promises, so the application should account for loading failures and the delay before the feature becomes available.

For larger applications, bundlers can also use dynamic imports as code-splitting boundaries. This may reduce the amount of JavaScript required for the initial page, although the actual benefit depends on the application's dependency graph and build configuration.

Circular dependencies occur when modules depend on each other, directly or indirectly.

For example, user.js might import a function from permissions.js, while permissions.js also imports something from user.js.

Some circular dependencies can work, but they can make initialization order and module behavior harder to understand. Problems are especially likely when modules access imported bindings before the relevant values have been initialized.

A better design is often to extract shared functionality into a third module.

Instead of importing from each other, the two modules depend on a common utility module.

This approach can reduce coupling and make the dependency structure easier to follow. It is not necessary to eliminate every cycle blindly, but unexpected circular dependencies deserve investigation.

Native JavaScript modules have different loading behavior from traditional classic scripts.

For example, an HTML page can load an application entry point with:

Browsers treat this as a JavaScript module. Module scripts are deferred by default, meaning they are evaluated after HTML parsing rather than blocking parsing in the same way as ordinary synchronous classic scripts.

Modules also have their own scope, so top-level declarations are not automatically added to the global object.

During development, avoid testing module-based pages by simply opening the HTML file through a file:// URL. Browser security restrictions can prevent module imports from working correctly in that environment.

Use a local development server instead. Also verify the correct MIME types and paths when deploying modules to a production server.

One of the main advantages of modular code is that individual functions can be tested without loading the entire application.

For example, the calculateTotal() function can be tested using simple assertions:

This example uses Node.js's built-in assertion module and assumes the project is configured to support ECMAScript modules.

Additional tests should cover edge cases, such as empty arrays, invalid data, and unexpected values, according to the function's intended contract.

API modules can be tested separately from rendering code, while interface modules can be tested for the expected DOM behavior.

Small modules do not automatically guarantee good tests, but clearly defined responsibilities generally make it easier to identify what needs to be tested.

When adopting JavaScript modules, developers should watch for several recurring problems.

Creating modules without clear responsibilities: A file that contains unrelated functions can become difficult to maintain even if it is technically modular.

Duplicating shared logic: If multiple modules implement the same business rule, changes can become inconsistent. Extract genuinely reusable behavior into a shared module.

Using dynamic imports everywhere: Loading every dependency dynamically can introduce unnecessary complexity and delays. Use dynamic imports when deferred loading provides a meaningful benefit.

Ignoring error handling: Network requests and dynamic imports can fail. Applications should handle failures appropriately instead of assuming every operation succeeds.

Overusing shared mutable state: Modules can export objects that multiple parts of an application modify. Uncontrolled shared state can create difficult-to-trace bugs.

Confusing development and production behavior: Module paths, server configuration, and bundler settings should be verified in the actual deployment environment.

JavaScript modules provide a straightforward foundation for organizing modern web applications. Named and default exports make dependencies explicit, separate files clarify responsibilities, and dynamic imports provide opportunities to load optional functionality when required.

The most effective modular architecture is not necessarily the most elaborate. It is one that makes code easy to locate, test, understand, and change without introducing unnecessary dependencies.

By separating API communication from interface logic, keeping module responsibilities focused, and testing individual functions, developers can create JavaScript applications that remain maintainable as their complexity grows.

#10588. SpaceX wants to build AI data centers in space. Will it work?

Imagine if one company could become the railroad, electric utility and cloud-computing provider of the emerging space economy. That potential fueled excitement around the long-anticipated initial public offering of SpaceX. Investors are not simply betting on rockets anymore. They are betting on an entire orbital ecosystem.

Among the most ambitious and challenging ideas riding this wave of enthusiasm is something that sounds almost like science fiction: orbital data centers. SpaceX may be one of the most well-known companies seeking to build them, but it is not the only one.

The logic is seductive: Launch the data centers into orbit, where solar energy is abundant and land, water and local power grids are no longer constraints. As artificial intelligence drives an explosion in computing demand, companies are pitching orbital data centers as a way to escape the growing environmental and infrastructure pressures of Earth-based computing. Data centers often also face backlash from the public at having these centers located in their communities.

But there is a vast difference between launching satellites and operating an industrial-scale computing infrastructure in orbit. Space is unforgiving. Radiation damages electronics. The electronics generate enormous amounts of heat, and getting rid of that heat is surprisingly difficult in space. Repairs are extraordinarily expensive, and every pound launched into orbit still carries a significant cost.

We are engineering professors who study data center design and space systems engineering. Building a space-based data center will involve considerations from both sides.

First off, consider what goes into an Earth-based data center, like those that you’ve probably begun to see pop up everywhere. These facilities power cloud computing, video streaming, online banking, scientific computing and, increasingly, artificial intelligence. But a data center is much more than a room full of servers.

A data center needs several things to operate reliably. The first is electric power. Servers, networking equipment and storage devices consume large amounts of electricity, and that power demand is growing rapidly with AI.

The second is cooling. Almost all the electricity consumed by servers eventually becomes heat. If that heat is not removed quickly and reliably, equipment performance drops, failures increase and the data center can shut down. Cooling systems often include air handling units, chillers, cooling towers, pumps and, increasingly, liquid-cooling equipment. In many facilities, cooling is the largest energy consumer after the computing equipment itself.

The third is physical infrastructure, including the necessary land, buildings, structural support, backup power, water systems, communication networks and maintenance access. Data centers also need to be close enough to users and network backbones to provide fast digital services.

In short, Earth-based data centers are large electrical and thermal infrastructure systems built around computing hardware.

So what would it take to build these data centers in space, and why are companies finding this possibility such an interesting business proposition?

As on Earth, these data centers would require massive amounts of power. In space, this power would come from solar panels. The Sun always shines in space and can’t be blocked by clouds. However, depending on the orbit the solar panels are put in, the Earth may shadow them for some portion of the orbit.

And even the best solar cells available today can convert only about half the sunlight that hits them to electricity.

Another potential advantage found in space is cooling. The cold background of space (near minus 455 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 270 degrees Celsius) creates an opportunity: waste heat from the data center could escape into space through radiators, keeping the electronics cool.

In principle, that design could eliminate some of the bulky and water-intensive cooling infrastructure used on Earth. However, those thermal radiators would require a large amount of surface area, and that would be in addition to the area required by the solar panels.

In space, there is no air to blow across hot equipment and help heat escape. The heat has to leave as infrared radiation, which is a relatively slow process. As a result, removing 10 megawatts of waste heat can require radiator surfaces comparable to the size of two football fields.

Space-based data centers could also avoid some of the local conflicts that come with building large data centers on the ground. Many communities resist new data center developments because of their land use, energy and water demand, and noise and environmental impact.

A space-based system would avoid competing for local land and water resources, and it would not generate neighborhood noise or require local zoning approval in the same way.

However, space is already getting crowded, and launching thousands of large orbital data centers would accelerate this issue. Orbital debris and micrometeorites are hazards because they can puncture the space data center, and a worst-case collision could destroy it and create even more space debris.

The frequency of space launches necessary to send all the equipment to orbit may also become a concern for some communities. SpaceX has had protests at its launch complex in Boca Chica, Texas, from local activists who argue that its rocket testing and launches damage the surrounding environment.

All that data would need to be sent between Earth and these data centers – and between the data centers themselves – using radio waves or laser communications systems. Although satellite constellations such as Starlink and Amazon Leo have demonstrated that doing this is possible, the amount of data sent to and from space would balloon.

These data centers, along with their solar panels and radiators, cannot be launched in one piece and would need to be assembled in space. This process would require new equipment for in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing.

Another key challenge is the refresh cycle of computing hardware. Data center servers are not built to last forever. Operators on Earth usually replace or upgrade hardware every three to five years as chips improve, workloads change and equipment ages.

And equipment failures can require replacing components. The refresh and repair processes are relatively straightforward on Earth, where workers can physically remove and replace servers.

In space, refresh and repair becomes much harder. Hardware sent to orbit may be difficult or too expensive to upgrade. If the computing platform cannot be updated, or too many components fail, it may become obsolete long before the surrounding infrastructure reaches the end of its useful life.

In a field where performance improves so rapidly and demand from computing continues to increase, this hurdle could prove a major economic and operational challenge.

Then there is the harshness of space. These data centers would be in a near vacuum, with constant radiation hitting them. And depending on their orbit, they would go from hot when in the sunlight to cold in Earth’s shadow many times a day. All of these challenges, and more, are issues that will need to be addressed.

Despite these challenges, companies are moving forward with designing space-based data centers. SpaceX just announced the design for its AI1 Compute Satellite, which it hopes to use as an orbital data center spacecraft. However, this satellite is 100 to 1,000 times less capable than current Earth-based data centers.

Not every computing task makes sense to do in space. Many data center applications depend on fast response times and close connections to users on Earth. Financial transactions, interactive AI services and most cloud applications are extremely sensitive to delay.

More feasible early applications may be those that are less latency-sensitive and more tightly connected to space operations. Examples could include processing Earth observation data from satellites, military or intelligence data processing, scientific computing related to space missions, or specialized computing for satellites and other space assets.

In other words, the first viable space data centers may serve space-based customers before they compete with mainstream cloud data centers on Earth.

#10584. Building Accessible Web Interfaces With Modern HTML and CSS

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Accessibility is an essential part of modern web development. A website may look polished and function correctly with a mouse, yet remain difficult to use for people who rely on keyboards, screen readers, magnification, or other assistive technologies.

Building accessible interfaces does not necessarily require complicated frameworks or extensive JavaScript. Many improvements begin with choosing the right HTML elements, providing clear labels, maintaining visible focus indicators, and using CSS that accommodates different user needs.

For developers, the goal is to create interfaces that remain understandable and usable across different devices, input methods, and accessibility requirements.

This article explores practical HTML and CSS techniques that can help make web interfaces more inclusive without adding unnecessary complexity.

Semantic HTML gives elements a meaningful purpose. Browsers and assistive technologies can use this information to communicate the structure of a page to users.

For example, a clickable div might appear to be a button, but it does not automatically provide the keyboard behavior and accessibility semantics of a native button.

It may look like a button after styling, but keyboard support and button semantics must be implemented separately.

A native button is generally a better choice:

Native buttons support keyboard interaction and communicate their role to assistive technologies without requiring custom ARIA attributes.

The same principle applies to navigation links, headings, lists, and form controls. Use elements according to their intended meaning rather than choosing them solely for their default appearance.

Not everyone uses a mouse or touchscreen to navigate a website. Some users rely entirely on a keyboard or an alternative input device that simulates keyboard interactions.

Interactive elements should therefore have a logical focus order and a visible focus indicator.

A simple CSS rule can improve focus visibility:

The :focus-visible pseudo-class allows browsers to display focus indicators when they determine that the indication is appropriate, commonly during keyboard navigation.

Developers should avoid removing outlines without providing an effective alternative. A link or button that receives focus but gives no visual indication can make navigation confusing.

For larger applications, keyboard testing should cover menus, dialogs, dropdowns, forms, and any custom interactive components.

A useful test is to navigate the page using only the Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and arrow keys where appropriate. Users should be able to identify their current position and operate the interface without becoming trapped in an unexpected focus sequence.

Forms are a common source of accessibility problems. Placeholder text alone is not a reliable replacement for a persistent label because it disappears or becomes less visible when users enter information.

An explicitly associated label provides a more dependable structure:

The for attribute on the label matches the input's id, creating an explicit association.

The autocomplete attribute can help browsers recognize the type of information being requested. The required attribute also communicates that the field must be completed.

However, browser validation alone does not guarantee accessible error handling. When validation fails, applications should explain the problem clearly and help users identify the field that needs attention.

For more complex forms, developers can associate additional instructions with controls using aria-describedby and provide appropriate error messages.

Accessible interfaces should accommodate different viewport sizes, text preferences, and reading needs.

Fixed dimensions can cause problems when text becomes larger or content changes length. A card with a fixed height, for example, may clip a heading when users zoom in.

Instead of forcing content into a rigid box, allow the layout to grow:

The clamp() function allows the heading size to scale within a defined range. The line-height gives body text room to breathe, while overflow-wrap helps prevent unusually long strings from overflowing their container.

These settings are starting points rather than universal requirements. Developers should test the actual content, fonts, languages, and supported zoom levels.

Text needs sufficient contrast against its background to remain readable for users with low vision or reduced contrast sensitivity.

A color combination that looks attractive in a design mockup may be difficult to read when displayed on a real device.

For example, consider a secondary label on a white background:

This darker gray generally provides stronger contrast than a very pale gray on white.

Developers should measure actual color combinations rather than relying on visual judgment alone. Under WCAG 2.2, the usual minimum contrast ratio is 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text at Level AA.

Contrast requirements also apply to relevant graphical elements and user interface components. A contrast checker can help identify combinations that need improvement.

Color should not be the only way information is communicated. For example, an invalid field should have a clear error message or another suitable indicator rather than relying solely on a red border.

Animations can improve feedback and communicate changes, but excessive motion may cause discomfort for some users.

CSS media queries allow developers to respect a user's reduced-motion preference:

This example removes the transition and hover movement when reduced motion is requested.

The appropriate response depends on the interface. Some animations communicate important information, so developers should ensure that removing decorative movement does not remove essential feedback or functionality.

Reduced-motion support should be part of the initial design process rather than an afterthought.

Images often communicate information that is not available in surrounding text. Users who cannot see an image need an appropriate text alternative when that information matters.

The alternative text describes the image's relevant purpose rather than listing every visual detail.

Decorative images should generally use an empty alternative:

This allows assistive technologies to skip an image that does not contribute meaningful information.

Complex images, such as detailed charts, may require a longer explanation elsewhere on the page. The alternative text should be based on what users need to understand, not simply on the image filename.

Automated accessibility tools can identify many common problems, including missing labels, some contrast failures, and certain structural issues. However, automated checks cannot determine whether every interaction makes sense to a real user.

A practical testing process should include:

Navigating the interface with a keyboard.

Checking focus order and focus visibility.

Testing forms with missing or invalid information.

Zooming in and checking for clipped content.

Testing meaningful content with a screen reader.

Running an automated accessibility audit and investigating its findings.

The W3C Web Accessibility Initiative provides standards and educational resources for understanding accessibility requirements. WCAG is a useful reference for evaluating web content, but meeting individual technical checks does not automatically guarantee a usable experience.

For important applications, testing with people who use assistive technologies can reveal problems that automated tools and developer assumptions may miss.

Accessible web development begins with thoughtful implementation choices. Semantic HTML, clear form labels, visible keyboard focus, readable typography, sufficient contrast, and reduced-motion support can significantly improve how people interact with a website.

These practices also help create more consistent and maintainable code. Native browser behavior often eliminates the need for custom interaction logic, while clear markup makes interfaces easier to understand and test.

Accessibility should not be treated as a final checklist applied after development. By considering different user needs from the beginning, developers can build web interfaces that are more inclusive, robust, and practical for everyone.

#10581. Millions of exploding stars could soon reveal dark energy's secrets

Researchers led by the Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona (ICCUB) have developed a new technique that could greatly improve how scientists study the expansion of the Universe and investigate the mysterious force known as dark energy.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the research introduces a framework called CIGaRS that can extract far more information from Type Ia supernovae, the powerful stellar explosions used to measure vast cosmic distances. Unlike many current approaches, the method relies mainly on imaging data rather than expensive spectroscopic observations. The advance is expected to help astronomers take full advantage of the enormous datasets that will soon arrive from next generation sky surveys, particularly those conducted by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Type Ia supernovae occur when white dwarf stars explode. Because these explosions reach nearly the same intrinsic brightness, astronomers use them as "standard candles": by comparing their actual brightness with how bright they appear from Earth, researchers can calculate their distance.

These measurements played a crucial role in the discovery that the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Scientists attribute that acceleration to dark energy, one of the most significant unsolved questions in modern physics.

However, there is an important complication. Type Ia supernovae are not perfectly identical.

How Host Galaxies Affect Supernova Measurements

Over the past 20 years, astronomers have found that a supernova's observed brightness is influenced by the galaxy where it occurs. Supernovae found in older or more massive galaxies can appear slightly different from those occurring in younger or less massive galaxies.

Researchers have typically accounted for these differences using relatively simple correction methods. While useful, these approximations can limit the accuracy of distance measurements and, in turn, the precision of cosmological studies.

A Unified Model of Supernovae and the Universe

The new framework addresses this challenge by modeling multiple factors simultaneously. Rather than treating each component independently, the researchers built a single, integrated model that includes the supernova explosions themselves, their host galaxies, the dust that alters their light, changes in supernova rates throughout cosmic history, and even the expansion of the Universe.

By connecting all of these ingredients within one statistical and physical framework, the team can capture relationships that are often overlooked when the pieces are analyzed separately.

"A powerful way of modelling the Universe is to simulate it ab initio in the computer using Bayesian inference," says Raúl Jiménez (ICREA-ICCUB), co-author of the study. "This provides a way to vary all possible parameters at the same time to predict what Universe we live in. Furthermore, by having this capacity, one can look into possible 'unknown unknown' systematics to understand their effect. The impact of these systematics in our inference is arguably the most important missing ingredient in current approaches to model the Universe."

Using Artificial Intelligence To Analyze the Cosmos

Building such a comprehensive model would normally require enormous computing power. To make the approach practical, the researchers turned to a modern technique called simulation-based inference.

The process begins with scientists generating large numbers of simulated universes based on physical models. A neural network (a type of artificial intelligence) then learns how the simulated observations relate to the physical properties that produced them. Once trained, the system can compare real astronomical observations with its simulations and determine the most likely underlying parameters.

This strategy makes it possible to analyze tens of thousands of supernovae simultaneously, a task that would be impractical using traditional techniques.

Accurate Galaxy Distances From Images Alone

One of the study's most significant findings is that the framework can determine galaxy distances (redshifts) with high accuracy using only imaging data.

Redshift measures how much a galaxy's light has been stretched as the Universe expands. It provides information about both the galaxy's distance and how far back in time we are observing it.

According to the researchers, the new method delivers redshift estimates with precision comparable to spectroscopic measurements, but without requiring spectra. This capability is especially important because upcoming surveys are expected to identify millions of supernova candidates, while only a small percentage can realistically receive spectroscopic follow-up observations.

Ready for the Rubin Observatory Data Deluge

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, currently being built in Chile, is expected to begin a decade long survey of the sky in the near future. During that mission, it will discover an unprecedented number of supernovae. Roughly 99% of those objects will be observed only photometrically, meaning through images taken in different colors rather than detailed spectra.

The CIGaRS framework was specifically developed with this challenge in mind.

"Unlike other frameworks, which require analytic simplifications, our no-compromise end-to-end simulation-based inference approach is uniquely capable of extracting the full cosmological and astrophysical information from the Rubin Observatory's hard-earned data, while avoiding the pitfalls of selection and modelling biases," says Konstantin Karchev (ICCUB-SISSA Trieste), lead author of the study.

The benefits extend beyond measuring dark energy. The framework also provides new information about the origins of Type Ia supernovae themselves.

By reconstructing how supernova occurrence rates vary with the ages of stars in different galaxies, the model helps scientists investigate long standing questions about the systems that eventually produce these explosions.

The researchers found that combining physics based simulations with artificial intelligence can overcome several limitations of current cosmological methods. They estimate that the approach could improve cosmological constraints by as much as a factor of four compared with traditional techniques that depend only on a relatively small sample of spectroscopically observed supernovae.

As the Rubin Observatory prepares to usher in a new era of astronomical discovery, tools such as CIGaRS could help scientists extract the maximum amount of information from its observations and gain a deeper understanding of the Universe.

#10580. Modern CSS Grid: Build Responsive Layouts With Less Complexity

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Creating responsive website layouts is a fundamental part of modern front-end development. Developers need interfaces that work across mobile phones, tablets, laptops, and large desktop displays without requiring separate markup for every screen size.

CSS Grid provides a powerful way to organize content into rows and columns. Unlike older layout techniques that often require additional wrappers or complicated positioning, Grid allows developers to define two-dimensional layouts directly in CSS.

When combined with flexible sizing functions, intrinsic layout techniques, and a small number of carefully chosen media queries, CSS Grid can make responsive interfaces easier to build and maintain.

This article explores practical CSS Grid techniques for creating flexible layouts, avoiding common mistakes, and writing cleaner responsive stylesheets.

CSS Grid begins by defining a grid container. Its direct children become grid items, which can be positioned within the resulting layout.

The layout can be defined with a few CSS declarations:

The display: grid declaration establishes the grid formatting context. The grid-template-columns property creates three equal-width columns, while gap controls the spacing between grid items.

This works well when the available space can accommodate three columns. On a narrow screen, however, the columns may become too small. Responsive sizing can solve this without requiring a separate rule for every device.

One useful CSS Grid technique is combining repeat(), auto-fit, and minmax().

This declaration allows the browser to create as many columns as comfortably fit within the available space.

The expression has three important parts:

auto-fit fits available tracks into the grid and collapses empty repeated tracks when appropriate.

minmax() establishes a flexible range for each column.

The nested min(100%, 16rem) also helps prevent the minimum column size from exceeding the container's available width on narrow screens.

As the container grows, more columns can fit. As it shrinks, items naturally move onto additional rows.

This technique is especially useful for product listings, article cards, image galleries, and resource directories.

It does not eliminate the need for testing. Content length, available space, and the desired visual hierarchy may still require additional layout rules.

The auto-fit and auto-fill keywords look similar, but they handle empty repeated grid tracks differently.

With auto-fill, the browser preserves the space for tracks that can fit within the grid, even when there are not enough items to occupy them.

With auto-fit, empty repeated tracks collapse after placement, allowing occupied tracks to expand into the available space.

This can be a good choice for a gallery where a small number of images should expand to fill the available row.

If the design needs to preserve the expected track arrangement even when some positions are empty, auto-fill may be more appropriate.

Neither option is universally better. The choice depends on whether the layout should expand existing items or preserve space for potential additional items.

CSS Grid is also useful for larger page layouts that contain a header, navigation, main content, a sidebar, and a footer.

Grid template areas allow developers to describe this arrangement using named regions.

The corresponding CSS might look like this:

The named areas make the intended layout easier to understand than a collection of unexplained numeric positions.

The minmax(0, 2fr) declaration also helps the main column shrink below its intrinsic content size when necessary, rather than allowing long content to force the entire layout wider.

On smaller screens, the areas can be rearranged:

The same HTML now supports a single-column layout on narrow screens.

One common CSS Grid problem occurs when content forces a column to become wider than expected.

Grid items can have automatic minimum sizes influenced by their content. Long URLs, unbroken strings, wide images, and large code examples may therefore cause overflow.

A practical solution is to allow grid items to shrink:

The zero minimum in minmax(0, ...) gives the tracks more flexibility, while min-width: 0 helps individual grid items shrink when their content would otherwise create an unwanted minimum width.

For code blocks, horizontal scrolling may be preferable to forcing long lines to wrap and changing their formatting.

These techniques address common overflow problems, but the best solution depends on the type of content and how users are expected to interact with it.

Responsive layouts do not always need explicit breakpoints. CSS Grid can often determine a suitable arrangement from the available space and the intrinsic dimensions of its content.

This creates flexible columns with a preferred minimum size of approximately 20rem, unless the container is narrower.

For a card collection, this may be enough to provide a responsive layout without a collection of device-specific media queries.

However, some designs require more deliberate changes. A navigation bar might need to become a menu button, or a sidebar may need to move below the primary content. These are behavioral or structural decisions that intrinsic sizing alone cannot make.

A useful approach is to let Grid handle flexible dimensions and use media queries when the design genuinely needs a different arrangement.

CSS Grid is powerful, but it is not always the simplest tool for the job.

Flexbox is often a better fit for a one-dimensional layout, such as aligning a group of buttons in a row or arranging an icon beside a label.

Grid is generally useful when relationships between rows and columns matter, while Flexbox is particularly effective when content flows primarily along one axis.

Both systems can work together. A page can use Grid for its overall structure and Flexbox for individual components.

The best layout method is the one that expresses the design clearly without introducing unnecessary rules.

A grid that works with three short placeholder headings may behave differently when real content is introduced.

Before shipping a responsive layout, developers should test:

Empty or partially populated card collections.

Intermediate widths where columns begin to feel cramped.

Browser developer tools make it easy to inspect grid tracks and experiment with container dimensions.

It is also useful to test the actual content rather than relying exclusively on idealized examples. Realistic content exposes sizing problems that placeholder text often hides.

CSS Grid provides a flexible foundation for responsive web layouts. Features such as minmax(), auto-fit, named grid areas, and intrinsic sizing allow developers to create adaptable interfaces with relatively little CSS.

The most effective layouts combine these features thoughtfully. Let Grid manage two-dimensional structure, use Flexbox for simpler one-dimensional arrangements, and introduce media queries when the design requires a meaningful change.

By accounting for intrinsic content sizes, preventing overflow, and testing realistic scenarios, developers can build responsive interfaces that are easier to understand and maintain.

#10578. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake review – A masterpiece made better

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is the most critically acclaimed game ever released, and Nintendo has worked its magic once again, pairing a smorgasbord of improvements with breathtakingly beautiful visuals to make an extraordinary adventure even better.

It’s been nearly three decades since Ocarina of Time was released on the Nintendo 64, and while the 1998 epic famously returned with a remake for the 3DS, Link’s time-travelling quest has never truly received the overhaul it deserves.

While Ocarina of Time famously helped revolutionize gaming with its Z-targeting system and 3D interconnected world, the legendary title feels pretty dated when compared to new adventures like Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

Enter the Switch 2 remake, an enhanced version of Nintendo’s masterpiece boasting completely new visuals and game-changing quality-of-life improvements that make Ocarina of Time look and play better than ever before.

Ocarina of Time follows Link, a young boy tasked with saving the kingdom of Hyrule from Ganondorf. He teams up with Hyrule’s Princess Zelda, who tells him that Ganondorf is seeking the Triforce, an ancient relic capable of granting a wish to whoever secures all three pieces.

To stop Ganondorf from plunging Hyrule into darkness, the green-clad hero must claim the legendary Master Sword and embark on a time-hopping quest to awaken the Seven Sages, whose power is needed to defeat him and save the kingdom.

Ocarina of Time remake packs plenty of improvements that elevate the 27-year-old adventure, with many plucked from Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. The biggest, and most welcome, is the addition of a jump and a run button, which gives you greater control and freedom when exploring Hyrule and its dungeons.

Zelda fans obsessed with Dark Link’s “aura farming” in Ocarina of Time remake trailer

Ocarina of Time remake launches November 5 with major gameplay changes

Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake sparks endless memes about Link’s new look

That’s provided 90s muscle memory doesn’t kick in, and you actually remember there’s no auto jump and you don’t plummet off a ledge into the ground with a pained yelp from Link.

Being able to run indefinitely is also a fantastic feature, especially given how time-consuming traversal can be as Young Link in early sections when you don’t have access to Epona or location-warping Ocarina songs. It also avoids your ears from being bombarded with the shrill ‘Hyuuuuup! Hyaaaaa!’ rolling sound effects of the original, always a bonus for anyone who wants to speed things up without losing their sanity.

Threads of Time also helps you keep track of every quest you pick up during your journey, which proved extremely useful when working through all the Happy Mask Salesman requests and trying to remember the steps in the comically long-winded Biggoron’s Sword quest.

One of the most wholesome additions is the ability to play Link’s ocarina by humming, singing, or playing a real ocarina using the Switch 2’s microphone to activate the songs in-game. While not necessary, being rewarded for memorizing Zelda’s Lullaby or Epona’s Song is pretty cute stuff, even if your neighbors may not share the same enthusiasm.

Then there’s the ability to use gyro controls to aim Link’s bow and ranged gadgets like the Hookshot, which really helps with catching Poes on horseback, hitting hidden switches to open secret doors, and whacking bosses where it hurts when chasing the best clear times in the new Hall of Fallen Foes boss rush mode.

Nintendo has also improved combat, with the Master Sword now having a real sense of heft behind it. Striking enemies comes with satisfying feedback from the Switch 2 controller’s improved HD rumble, giving your slashes a weighty feel. This is especially true when using the Megaton Hammer to flatten foes like a pancake or slicing an enemy with the two-handed Biggorn Sword.

While Wolfos and Skulltulas still rely on you waiting for that perfect opportunity to hit their weak points, tougher enemies like Lizalfos and Gerudo Warriors are more reactive, flitting in and out of combat and dashing in for some cheeky damage when you let your guard down.

Ocarina of Time’s bosses are also more of a spectacle now, with upgraded arenas, attacks, and flashier animations. Remake’s Ganon is bigger and badder than his older, blockier brother. In fact, he makes his 1998 counterpart look positively tame. From raining down blood-red lightning strikes from the sky to charging on all fours, his demonic beast form is even more badass than ever before.

While none of these improvements drastically change the adventure you know and love, they do make an already great game even better.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake isn’t just the best-looking Nintendo Switch 2 game, it’s also the most detailed Zelda ever. Kokiri Forest is filled with lush green foliage, moss-covered rocks, and beautiful babbling brooks.

Hyrule Field is also blanketed with swaying grass and pretty wildflowers, while rugged terrain near Gerudo Valley and rocky formations near Zora’s River give these areas a more distinct look compared to the flatter landscape of the original. Environmental details like Kakariko Village’s signature windmill and houses nestled on the hills beneath Hyrule Castle also help make this smaller-scale adventure feel more lived-in than ever.

Ocarina of Time’s newly added signs of life were especially apparent in populated locations like the sleepy mountainside dwellings of Kakariko Village and the cobbled streets of Hyrule Castle Town. Ducking into alleyways of the latter and having a right good nosy proved particularly good fun, especially now that you can freely explore and interact with the colorful townsfolk.

Nintendo has carried this same level of detail into the remake’s dungeons, where atmospheric fog carpets the stone floors and reacts to Link’s footsteps and sword swings. Dust particles also now hang in the air and glisten as they catch the light, while deeper shadows and improved lighting heighten iconic areas like Kakariko’s nightmarish well and Ganondorf’s Castle.

Even the Hero of Time and his companions have received a graphical glow-up, with hyper-realistic hair and outfits. The most eye-catching is Link’s iconic tunic, which now features woven green straw fibers, intricately designed belts, and enough tassels to have cosplayers curse Nintendo for the level of intricacy in his new, highly detailed drip.

For veteran Zelda players, exploring these well-trodden environments feels like returning to your favorite childhood haunts as an adult. Although each setting has had a significant upgrade, navigating Hyrule and its dungeons feels familiar but fresh. Nintendo has taken so much care recreating its beloved world that it’s hard not to get pulled back into another 20+ hour adventure, gallivanting around Hyrule atop Epona searching for Heart Containers like it’s 1998 all over again.

Just like Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, everyone barring Link and minor NPC characters is now fully voiced. While this may be a controversial addition for purists hoping to go back to Zelda’s silent era, the new cutscenes help add more life to the Seven Sages and provide more details that will have lore lovers happy to revisit Hyrule’s history.

Characters like the Goron patriarch Darunia are now way more expressive, while Nintendo has done more for Princess Ruto and Link’s one-sided romance than even the most die-hard fanfiction writer. There’s also a greater sense of emotion behind certain events, like when Link leaves Kokiri Forest thanks to some heartfelt voiced lines from Saria. Then there’s Ganondorf himself, whose grand entrance and signature organ playing are elevated further by some particularly infectious evil laughter that I may or may not have tried to imitate.

Whether you’re a returning player or a newcomer, Ocarina of Time remake is the definitive way to play Link’s legendary adventure. Nintendo has successfully breathed new life into its decades-old world of Hyrule, giving it a loving lick of paint that not only elevates it over the original, but also makes it the best-looking Switch 2 game.

Just like Link’s time-travelling epic, Ocarina of Time remake honors its past and carefully combines new improvements borrowed from the series’ present to give this timeless classic the treatment it deserves. Ocarina of Time remake isn’t just a masterpiece, it’s a timeless adventure everyone needs to play.

#10577. Quantum mechanics once baffled scientists. Now it's changing the world

For much of the early 20th century, quantum mechanics was one of the most puzzling ideas in science. The theory challenged conventional thinking and left even leading physicists struggling to make sense of its implications. A century later, it has become the foundation of technologies that influence daily life, including lasers, microchips, secure communications, and emerging quantum computers.

In a new perspective article published in Science, Dr. Marlan Scully of Texas A&M University reflects on the remarkable evolution of quantum mechanics, from an abstract theory about tiny particles to a powerful framework helping researchers tackle some of the most difficult questions in science.

"Quantum mechanics started as a way to explain the behavior of tiny particles," said Scully, who is also affiliated with Princeton University. "Now it's driving innovations that were unimaginable just a generation ago."

Scully has played a major role in advancing the field. He co-authored the influential textbook Quantum Optics, a resource that has educated generations of physicists. His research in coherent nanoscale laser spectroscopy helped make it possible to study molecules with atomic-scale precision. He has also developed groundbreaking concepts involving quantum heat engines, which challenge traditional assumptions about thermodynamic efficiency and may one day lead to new energy technologies.

From Schrödinger's Cat to Quantum Technology

One of the most famous illustrations of quantum mechanics came in 1935, when Erwin Schrödinger proposed his cat paradox. The thought experiment suggested that a cat could exist in a state that is both alive and dead until it is observed. Schrödinger introduced the idea to highlight how strange quantum theory appeared.

Today, those once-bizarre concepts have moved far beyond philosophical debates.

"That 'quantum weirdness' is no longer just a philosophical puzzle," said Scully. "It's the foundation of quantum computing, quantum cryptography and even gravitational wave detection."

The foundations of quantum mechanics were built by pioneers including Schrödinger and Werner Heisenberg. They developed two different mathematical approaches, wave mechanics and matrix mechanics, to describe quantum systems. Over time, these approaches were unified and contributed to the development of quantum field theory, which explains how particles interact through electromagnetic and nuclear forces.

Their work expanded on Niels Bohr's early atomic model, which pictured electrons orbiting the nucleus much like planets orbit the sun. While later discoveries refined that picture, Bohr's model helped pave the way for modern quantum theory.

Among the most important concepts in quantum mechanics is quantum coherence. This phenomenon allows particles such as atoms and photons to remain linked in a coordinated state, even across significant distances.

Quantum coherence led directly to the development of the laser, a technology that many once believed could never work. Today, lasers are used throughout modern society, from supermarket barcode scanners to vision correction procedures and advanced scientific instruments.

Coherence is also closely tied to quantum entanglement, the phenomenon that prompted Albert Einstein to describe it as "spooky action at a distance."

Entanglement enables particles to share information through uniquely quantum properties. These effects form the basis of quantum encryption systems and improve the sensitivity of sophisticated instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which detects tiny ripples in spacetime.

Quantum Heat Engines Challenge Classical Limits

One of the more surprising applications of quantum physics involves quantum heat engines.

Traditional engines are constrained by the Carnot Limit, which defines the maximum efficiency allowed by classical thermodynamics. Researchers have found that by exploiting quantum coherence, it may be possible to create engines that exceed those classical limits.

"It's a striking example of how quantum principles can rewrite the rules of classical physics," Scully said.

The influence of quantum mechanics now extends far beyond physics.

In biology, techniques such as coherent Raman spectroscopy allow researchers to examine viruses and other structures at the nanoscale, providing valuable insights into the microscopic world.

Quantum ideas are also shaping efforts to understand the universe itself. Scientists working on concepts such as string theory and quantum gravity are attempting to reconcile quantum mechanics with Einstein's theory of relativity, one of the biggest unsolved problems in modern physics.

Researchers are even applying quantum concepts to the long-standing challenge of understanding turbulence. The chaotic motion of air and fluids affects weather patterns, climate systems, and aircraft performance. By studying superfluid helium, a substance that displays unusual quantum behavior, scientists are uncovering patterns that could improve climate modeling, storm prediction, and aviation safety.

Despite a century of success, quantum mechanics continues to raise profound questions.

Can gravity be quantized (i.e., does gravity behave like other forces at the quantum level)? Could quantum computers transform medicine and materials science? What new insights about the universe might emerge from future quantum technologies?

Scully believes the search for answers is only beginning.

"At the start of the 20th century, many thought physics was complete," he said. "Now, in the 21st century, we know the adventure is just beginning."

Five Ways Quantum Mechanics Affects Everyday Life
