#10574. How AI Search Is Changing Property and Local Discovery: What Developers Should Build

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Property searches used to be a list of filters: price, bedrooms, postcode. Increasingly they start as a question typed or spoken in plain language, such as which neighborhoods near good schools have easy transit and a quiet park. AI search tools answer those questions by pulling facts from many pages and combining them. If you build listing sites, local directories, or any location-based product, that changes what "good data" means: your pages are now inputs to someone else's answer.

This article looks at the shift from a developer's point of view. It covers how to model location data so machines can read it, how to generate structured data safely, how to expose neighborhood facts, and how to keep your content crawlable and trustworthy. The code samples are small and meant to be adapted.

A keyword search such as "3 bed house Springfield" maps neatly onto a database filter. A conversational query does not: "somewhere walkable with a library nearby and a short commute" mixes several attributes, some of which your listing form never captured. AI systems work best with pages that state concrete, attributable facts in a consistent structure.

In practice that means three engineering habits:

Structured data in JSON-LD lets search engines and AI systems read a listing without guessing. This function builds the markup from the same record that renders the page, so the two cannot drift apart, and it escapes the output so listing text can never close the script tag early:

Validate the output with the Schema Markup Validator or Google's Rich Results Test during review, and add the check to your test suite so a template change cannot silently break it. Markup must match what visitors can see on the page, otherwise it can be ignored or treated as misleading.

Questions about schools, transport, and local facilities are really questions about distance. If your data lives in PostgreSQL with the PostGIS extension, a radius query on geography types returns distances in meters and is easy to expose as page content or an API field:

Add a spatial index on both geometry columns for production workloads. Then render the results as plain HTML (a short list or table with the source and date) rather than only inside a client-side map widget. A map that needs JavaScript to draw hides the very facts crawlers and AI systems are looking for.

People increasingly ask AI tools to compare properties and to look beyond the asking price, including taxes, utilities, and commute costs. If you publish such figures, publish where they come from. A small convention goes a long way:

This is good engineering hygiene as well as good SEO: it makes stale data easy to find and easy to fix.

Not all discovery starts with a listing. Many people first get a feel for an area from videos and posts by local creators, and AI search surfaces that material too. Vivien Garnès, Co-CEO at Upfluence, puts it this way: "Buyers rarely start with a spreadsheet anymore. Many first learn about a neighborhood from creators filming their commute, their local coffee shop, or a weekend at the park. That kind of content answers the lifestyle questions listings ignore. The smart move is to treat it as inspiration and then check the facts, because a great video can't tell you about school boundaries or property taxes."

The engineering takeaway is to make your own factual pages the place where that inspiration gets verified. If you embed neighborhood videos, give each one a transcript and descriptive surrounding text, and pair it with the structured facts above so the lifestyle story and the checkable details live on the same URL.

Buyers also ask for local professionals and services. For businesses and directories, the basics matter most:

None of the work above helps if crawlers cannot read your pages. Server-render the key facts, make sure important content is not hidden behind interactions that only run in the browser, and decide deliberately which crawlers may access your site. That decision lives in robots.txt:

Check each crawler's documentation for its current user-agent name before adding rules for it, since these change. Also keep an accurate XML sitemap with real modification dates, so updated listings are discovered quickly.

AI search is changing how people ask about places, but the underlying engineering advice is familiar: model your data carefully, say where it came from, and make it readable by machines as well as people. The sites that answer real, specific questions with checkable facts are the ones most likely to be quoted.

As per Gamer’s Voice, the new proposal would “require all gamers to prove their age in order to access communication features,” similar to how some nations deal with in-game gambling features.

“Gaming isn’t simply another form of social media. When young people join a gaming guild, work together in a team or make friends through a shared hobby, they are participating in a social activity that can be enormously positive,” Tom Shannon, spokesperson for Gamer’s Voice, said.

#10571. Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence. Their findings suggest that decision making begins much earlier in the brain than traditional theories propose, offering fresh ideas for designing future AI systems that are more capable and far more energy efficient.

Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS). The study points to an unexpected role for early sensory brain regions in decision making, challenging the long accepted view that decisions emerge only after information moves through a strict hierarchy of brain regions.

The human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe. Scientists still do not fully understand how it works, which is why reverse engineering the brain was identified by the National Academy of Engineering in 2008 as one of the 14 grand challenges for engineering in the 21st century.

For decades, many artificial intelligence systems, including convolutional neural networks, have been inspired by the idea that the brain processes information in a one way sequence. According to this traditional model, sensory information travels upward through increasingly complex brain regions until it reaches the frontal cortex, where decisions are made.

Vlasov and other researchers have increasingly questioned whether that picture is complete.

Instead, they are exploring a model based on natural intelligence, which has been refined through evolution over hundreds of millions of years. In this framework, the brain does not rely only on a step by step flow of information. Decision making also depends on interconnected feedback loops that allow information to move in both directions between brain regions.

Because biological intelligence performs remarkably complex tasks while using far less energy than today's AI systems, understanding this architecture could help guide the development of future artificial intelligence.

"We want to learn from a billion years of evolution," Vlasov said. "How is that biological intelligence organized architecturally? Can we learn from the architectural side of the brain and emulate that to make AI more effective, less power hungry, and more intelligent than it currently is? In the level of decision-making, that's where current AI is lacking."

Early Brain Regions Show Decision Making Activity

To investigate how these processes work, the research team focused on the brain's earliest stages of sensing and perception.

The scientists recorded neural activity in mice as they navigated a virtual reality corridor and made perceptual decisions. They found evidence of decision related activity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), one of the brain's earliest sensory processing areas.

Rather than simply passing information forward, S1 appeared to be influenced by higher brain regions through feedback loops. This top down regulation suggests that decision making involves continuous communication across multiple brain areas instead of a simple one direction flow of information.

"The neural code of the brain is still mostly an unknown language," Vlasov said. "But this systems-level understanding can be viewed as a potential impact on how more efficient artificial neural networks can be built -- how the next generation of AI can be thought through. Maybe with these analogies that we learn from real brains, we can improve AI further."

What the Findings Could Mean for Future AI

The researchers emphasize that the study does not provide a blueprint for building better artificial intelligence. Instead, it offers new insights into how the brain organizes decision making that could eventually inspire future AI architectures.

Next, Vlasov and his team plan to investigate the timing of these brain signals in greater detail. They also intend to develop new technologies for measuring neural activity to better understand how feedback loops emerge and coordinate different levels of brain processing.

"By looking at the fast temporal dynamics of neural activity, maybe we can understand better how these feedback loops are engaged in making decisions," Vlasov said. "Maybe that's the approach that potentially uncovers these currently unknown mechanisms -- how these feedback loops are organized dynamically and how they form and shape different levels of processing. Maybe that can be implemented in new architectures for AI."

Materials provided by University of Illinois Grainger College of Engineering. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10569. How to prepare for a meta engineer interview

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Two LeetCode mediums in about 40 minutes. That is still the core of a Meta coding round, and most candidates who fail it run out of time rather than not knowing the pattern.

But since October 2025 the loop has picked up a second kind of coding round, one where you get an AI assistant and a multi-file project. A lot of the prep advice online hasn't caught up, so here's how I'd prepare in 2026, round by round.

The process usually runs four to eight weeks from the first recruiter call to a decision. Roughly:

It replaced one of the two traditional onsite coding interviews. You get 60 minutes in CoderPad with a chat panel, and instead of two unrelated puzzles you work through one extended problem with several stages, often starting with getting an existing codebase to run.

You can switch models mid-interview. Candidates have reported GPT-5, Claude Sonnet and Haiku, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Meta's own Llama 4 Maverick.

E3 and E4 candidates often get no design round at all. From E5 up, design carries as much weight as coding, and the behavioral round gets harder because it's partly deciding your level.

Meta's classic coding round is the most predictable interview in big tech, which makes it the most trainable. The question pool leans on a familiar set of topics:

Dynamic programming shows up less than at Google. Don't ignore it, but don't spend a week on it either.

Work through Meta-tagged problems on LeetCode. Premium is worth paying for a month or two, purely for the company tag and frequency sort.

Aim for under 20 minutes per medium, including talking. Many candidates report they couldn't run their code, so practice in a plain editor with no autocomplete, and dry-run your solution on a small input before you say you're done. Interviewers notice when you catch your own bug.

An opinion you can ignore: doing the top 150 Meta-tagged mediums twice beats grinding 300 problems that include hards. Meta rarely asks them, and the second pass is what builds speed.

This is where strong candidates get burned. They assume the round is easier because they have help, then spend 15 minutes reading generated code they don't trust.

What's being measured is still engineering. Can you read unfamiliar code, break the task into pieces, check output, and catch edge cases? Meta has said fairly directly that it's testing classic coding skills, with AI there to make the setting realistic.

The bar is also higher than in a normal coding round. Because you have an assistant, interviewers expect you to get further through the stages than you would alone.

Meta gives you a practice environment before the interview with a sample problem called "the puzzle." Do it. Then practice the shape of the round elsewhere: take a small open-source project, set a 60-minute timer, and add a feature with Cursor or Claude Code while narrating out loud. Hello Interview has a sandbox built around this format too.

Choose your model before the day. Some candidates found GPT-5 too slow under interview pressure and switched to Claude. Whatever you pick, know how it behaves before the clock starts.

Many candidates get to choose between system design and product architecture. Product architecture is about APIs, data models and client-server interaction; system design is about scale, storage and distribution. Backend and infra people should take system design. Product and full-stack engineers usually do better in product architecture.

Alex Xu's System Design Interview (both volumes) is still the standard starting point. After that, Hello Interview's write-ups of common questions like news feed, chat, Instagram and top-K.

Meta likes questions that look like its own products, so practicing "design the Facebook News Feed" is homework, not cheating.

Candidates who burn 20 minutes on requirements never reach that last step, and it's the part that separates E5 from E6.

It's easy to treat this round as a chat. It isn't. Meta scores it on specific signals, including handling conflict, driving work through ambiguity, learning from failure and the size of your impact, and at senior levels it feeds directly into leveling.

Write six to eight stories from the last three years. Each one should contain a number: latency cut from 800ms to 200ms, a launch that reached 2 million users, five engineers across two teams you got aligned. Map every story to two or three signals so you can reuse them.

Use STAR loosely. Interviewers interrupt with follow-ups, so know the details cold: who disagreed with you, what you'd do differently, what actually happened afterwards.

It's the most common mistake in this round. They want to know what you did.

Solo practice gets you to knowing the material. Mock interviews get you to performing it while someone watches, and that gap is where most people fail. You probably want a mix of AI, human and peer mocks.

These are the cheapest way to get volume:

The upside is that you can do one at 11pm on a Tuesday, and they're good at drilling the habit most people neglect, which is thinking out loud. The downside is that quality varies a lot and AI interviewers tend to be generous with hints and praise. Take their scores with a grain of salt. Also helps if you follow an interview guide for a Meta Engineer

A general assistant works surprisingly well. Give Claude or ChatGPT (voice mode is good for this) a prompt like:

You're a Meta E5 interviewer. Ask me one medium problem from Meta's usual topics, give no hints unless I ask, interrupt with follow-ups, and at the end grade me harshly on communication, correctness and time.

It's especially useful for behavioral practice if you tell it to dig into your stories the way a skeptical engineering manager would.

interviewing.io runs anonymous mocks with engineers from Meta and other large companies, and it's the closest you'll get to the real loop. Paid coaching usually costs $100 to $200 an hour.

Peer mocks through Discord groups, Reddit or a friend at another company are free and much better than nothing.

AI mocks for the first few weeks to build the narrating habit, then two or three human mocks in the last two weeks, at least one of them for design.

If you're working full time, give yourself six to eight weeks.

Ask your recruiter for more time if you need it. Meta recruiters push dates by a few weeks all the time, while a rejection usually means waiting six months to a year before you can reapply (one recent candidate was told a full year). Taking the interview before you're ready is the most expensive mistake in the whole process.

#10568. Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

Alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J. Denning.

In his new book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today. The first is that intelligence can exist independently of a physical body and therefore be recreated in computer software. The second is that a machine can demonstrate intelligence by successfully imitating a human in conversation, an idea that later became known as the Turing test.

"These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes. "My premise is that our acquiescence to these claims has led to the AI mess in which we find ourselves today."

Denning argues that pursuing artificial general intelligence (AGI), or machines with human level intelligence, is unlikely to succeed. Instead, he warns, the technologies society is building could introduce significant new risks.

At the heart of Denning's argument is the idea of tacit knowledge, the vast amount of human understanding that cannot easily be put into words or represented in a form that computers can process.

He says machine learning cannot capture five major categories of tacit knowledge: common sense, everyday interactions with people and the environment, emotions and perception, practical performance skills, and the social and historical knowledge embedded in culture.

Researchers have long attempted to organize common sense into databases. One of the best known efforts was Douglas Lenat's Cyc project, which began in the 1980s with the goal of creating an extensive collection of common sense facts. After four decades of work, the project contained roughly 25 million entries.

"Yet even this treasury could not add up to a background of common sense sufficient to make expert systems smart enough to be experts," Denning notes. "Cyc validated that much of the knowledge that makes people experts cannot be articulated as propositions."

Denning believes practical skills present an even greater challenge.

"Our performance skills in thousands of domains cannot be communicated to machines," he explains. "Whereas descriptions of skillful outcomes ('know what') can often be represented as bits and stored in a machine, we do not know how to encode the embodied knowledge for skillful performance ('know how')."

He points to accomplished musicians as an example.

"A virtuoso violinist can play beautiful music yet cannot describe to an acolyte how to produce it.

"Even if a robot could observe and imitate skilled humans, having no biological body, a robot cannot grasp how the musician feels when playing beautiful music or how an audience feels when hearing it."

Denning also includes intuition, gut feelings, imagination, and spontaneous creativity among the forms of tacit knowledge that remain beyond the reach of machines.

Denning argues that all of these limitations stem from what he calls the "representation problem."

Computers can only perform calculations using data and instructions that have been encoded into physical forms they can recognize and process. Tacit knowledge, however, does not naturally fit into that framework.

"Behind every word is a deep well of tacit knowledge that gives it meaning," Denning says. "Words are but symbolic representations of meanings, not the meanings themselves. Commonly used Large Language Models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini only manipulate words, they cannot know or understand the meaning of what they are saying."

According to Denning, this creates a fundamental divide. Because scientists still cannot fully explain how tacit knowledge works in humans, they also cannot translate it into a form machines can use.

"How we host tacit knowledge is largely a mystery," Denning admits. "All we know is that it is embodied. We have no idea what we might observe and measure in our bodies to reveal it."

Denning also argues that intelligence depends heavily on context, the surrounding circumstances that give words, actions, and decisions their meaning.

Context allows people to recognize sarcasm, humor, sincerity, and emotion. It helps determine when to be diplomatic, when to joke, and how to interpret countless social cues.

"When you inquire into where an assumption of the current context came from, you discover it rests on previous conversations from previous contexts. Each of those in turn rests on further previous conversations and their contexts. This pattern is endless and fractal," Denning explains.

Culture presents another major obstacle for AI.

Denning describes culture as encompassing values, norms, judgments, history, communities, moods, and even relationships involving power and care.

"Human conversations are imbued with background assumptions that give meaning and relevance to the words being used," Denning explains.

"Scaling up LLMs with ever larger neural networks will not enable them to acquire the embodied human knowledge we call culture. LLMs will not attain the objective of the Turing test: to demonstrate machine thought indistinguishable from human thought."

AI Safety and the Limits of Human Understanding

Denning concludes that humans and AI systems may ultimately develop different forms of tacit knowledge that neither can fully understand.

"Machines cannot read our tacit knowledge and we cannot read theirs," he writes. "We are aliens across an uncrossable divide."

He argues this gap raises serious concerns about AI safety. If machines cannot interpret the unspoken context behind human intentions, reliably aligning advanced AI systems with human goals may prove impossible.

"Through AI automation, agentic networks of machines are likely to develop their own machine intelligence that does not reach the level of human general intelligence but is still quite capable of creating severe problems for humans. This threat is a greater than a take-over by superintelligent machines," he explains.

"Machine intelligence has different concerns from us and does not appear to care about us. Its ways of thinking and problem-solving look alien to us. We do not yet know how to live safely with these machines.

"Pulling back from an AI automation singularity will demand much from us. We start by accepting that the familiar culture is fading away as intelligent machines appear in our society and we do not know what is coming. We decline to think like machines or be subservient to machines. We refuse to submit to a yoke imposed by low-intelligence machines. Most importantly, we reassert our humanity, declare once again what makes us different from machines, and celebrate those differences."

Materials provided by Taylor & Francis Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

He then reclined and activated the chair’s massage functions before continuing to preach about those who are only faithful when it’s easy.

“I’m only doing it if it’s comfortable,” he said. “I’m only doing it if it does not require me to move out of my spot.”

He then used the chair to explain how prioritizing comfort could prevent people from helping others.

“How good could I fight from this position?” he asked. “How good could I protect myself? How good could I actually help somebody who was in need right there?”

#10562. New programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.

The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.

Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck

The rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how quickly they can transmit data.

These challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.

However, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.

To address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.

The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.

Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait

Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information quickly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.

Systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.

One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.

CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.

Traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.

For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely new photonic device.

That lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever new capabilities are needed.

The problem is especially important for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.

A Programmable Design for Controlling Light

The research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.

Together, these changes created a new design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.

Using the new CRIT structure, the researchers showed that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.

This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.

Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape

The researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.

This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.

Numerical simulations also showed that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.

The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.

Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical

The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.

They also evaluated a range of real-world issues that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.

The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.

One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions

The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.

The design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several important capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.

These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.

The same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.

Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers

If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.

In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.

This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.

Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.

Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.

Researchers Plan Larger Programmable Photonic Systems

Professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a new design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We plan to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies."

Co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We plan to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation."

Dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is currently conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.

Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.

The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

Dr. Seungkyun Park also participated in the study with support from the InnoCORE program (PICORE Center).

#10561. Top Accessibility Errors in Production and How to Avoid Them

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most accessibility problems on a website aren't hard to fix. Low-contrast text. An image with no alt text. A button that doesn't tell a screen reader what it does. None of these need a rebuild or a specialist.

Every year, WebAIM scans the home pages of the top million websites and checks them against basic accessibility standards. The 2026 report found that almost 96% of the pages scanned had at least one automatically detectable accessibility failure.

What stands out even more is what the errors actually are. The same problems have topped this report for seven years in a row. These aren't new, complex edge cases; they are the same simple, repeating mistakes.

In this guide, we'll look at what those top errors actually are, why they keep making it to production, and the simple workflow habits you can use to catch them before your users do. We'll also cover where tools like TestMu AI's Accessibility Testing Suite fit into that workflow.

It's easy to assume teams just don't care. But that's rarely the reason. Most developers know what alt text is for. Most designers know low contrast is a problem. The real issue is simpler; a few patterns explain most of it:

None of these come from not knowing accessibility rules. They come from how software is actually built: fast, in multiple moving pieces, with much of the page assembled from components and third-party code that nobody on the team wrote from scratch.

WebAIM's report found that a small number of accessibility issues account for most detectable WCAG failures across the top one million websites. The sections below explain what each issue is, why it matters, and how to fix it.

This is the single most common accessibility error, appearing on nearly 84% of homepages, according to WebAIM.

Poor contrast means the text color is too close to the background color, making it hard to read. For instance, light gray text (#999) on a white background (#FFF) yields a contrast ratio of 2.85:1, which is well below the standard requirement. For anyone with low vision or color blindness, that text becomes unreadable.

The Fix: WCAG asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text. Running a quick check with tools like the WebAIM Contrast Checker or a Lighthouse audit will give you the exact ratio before your page ships. Because the tools lay it out so clearly, this is easily one of the quickest errors on this list to catch and fix.

This is the second most common accessibility error, appearing on more than half of the homepages scanned by WebAIM.

Alt text is the written description a screen reader reads out loud in place of an image. Without it, a screen reader either skips the image entirely or announces the file name, which tells a user nothing about the image.

For example, if it's a product photo, a chart, or an icon that functions as a button, missing alt text means a screen reader user has no idea what they're looking at, what it does, or what happens when they click it.

The Fix: Describe what the image actually shows instead of just saying it's an image. If it's purely decorative and adds nothing a screen reader user needs, use an empty alt attribute (alt="") instead of leaving it off. That tells the screen reader to skip it cleanly.

Missing form labels appeared on 51% of home pages. This one is easy to miss because the form inputs often still look labeled. A form field looks perfectly labeled on screen when the label is simply placed next to the input box. A sighted user sees "Email" written next to a box and knows what to enter.

A screen reader, however, doesn't rely on visual placement. It relies on the HTML. If "Email" isn't actually connected to that input field in the markup, the field may be announced as simply "edit text" or "blank," leaving the screen reader user with no indication of what information it expects.

Placeholder text isn't a substitute either because it disappears as soon as the user starts typing.

The Fix: Associate every form control with a visible

Nearly half of all homepages contain links with no accessible name. The most common examples are icon-only links, such as a search icon, shopping cart, or social media icon. Sighted users recognize these icons immediately, but a screen reader may announce them simply as "link," giving users no indication of what each one does.

The Fix: Give every icon-only link an accessible name using visible text, aria-label, or another appropriate labeling method. This preserves the visual design while allowing screen readers to announce the link's purpose.

About 31% of home pages have buttons with no accessible name, and the share has risen every year since 2021. The usual culprits are icon-only buttons: a hamburger menu, a close "X" on a modal, a play button, or a carousel arrow. A screen reader announces these as just buttons, so users can't tell whether they open a menu, close a dialog, or submit a form.

The Fix: Give every button an accessible name. Use visible text where you can. For icon-only buttons, add aria-label (for example, aria-label="Close dialog") or visually hidden text inside the button. If the icon is an image, provide alt text that describes the action, not the image.

Around 14% of homepages don't specify the page's language. Without it, screen readers have to guess how the text should be pronounced, which can result in words being read with the wrong pronunciation or accent.

The Fix: Set the page's language using the lang attribute on the root element. For example, . It's a one-line change that helps screen readers interpret the entire page correctly.

Many users rely on a keyboard instead of a mouse to navigate a website. If a menu only opens on hover, a custom dropdown only responds to clicks, or a button can't receive keyboard focus, those controls become unusable for them.

The Fix: Every interactive element should be reachable with Tab and Shift+Tab and operable with the keys users expect: Enter for links and buttons, Space for buttons and checkboxes, arrow keys inside menus, tabs, and radio groups, and Escape to close dialogs and menus. You can test this by trying to navigate the entire page using only the keyboard.

Developers sometimes remove the browser's default focus outline to improve the visual design but don't replace it with another focus style. As a result, keyboard users can no longer tell which element is currently selected as they move through the page.

The Fix: Never remove a focus outline without providing a clear replacement. Every interactive element should have a visible, high-contrast focus indicator that tells keyboard users where they currently are on the page.

Videos without captions exclude people who are deaf or hard of hearing and make content harder to follow when audio isn't available or practical. Captions also help users understand speech in noisy environments or when the audio quality is poor.

The Fix: Provide accurate captions for every video. If the video contains important spoken information, include a transcript as well. Automatically generated captions are a good starting point, but they should always be reviewed for accuracy.

On mobile, small buttons and links are hard to hit accurately. Users may tap the wrong control, trigger an unintended action, or have to try multiple times before the touch registers. WCAG 2.2 Level AA sets a minimum target size of 24x24 CSS pixels, with 44x44 CSS pixels recommended (WCAG AAA and Apple's own guidance).

The Fix: Give every tappable element enough size and padding to be reliably tappable, even if the visible icon inside it remains small. Aim for 44x44 CSS pixels, and never go below 24x24.

Run a scanner across a page, and it catches a good chunk of what's wrong. Missing alt attributes, contrast ratios below the required threshold, a form field with no label in the code. Automated scanners catch these immediately.

According to most industry estimates, automated tools catch about 30 to 40 percent of accessibility issues. That's worth running. It also means most of what actually breaks a page isn't something a scanner can see at all.

Take alt text, for instance. A scanner can confirm an image has an alt attribute. It can't tell you if that attribute says anything useful. "Image description here" and an actual description of the photo both pass the same check because the tool only confirms the field isn't empty.

Take another example of a custom div button with role="button". A scanner sees the role and perceives it as a button. It has no way of knowing that nobody added the keyboard handling that makes the button actually work, because that's not something a static scan can test. You'd only catch it by unplugging your mouse and tabbing through the page yourself.

Reading order works the same way. A page can pass every automated check and still present its content in an order that makes no sense once you strip away the layout and just listen to it, top to bottom.

None of this means automated tools aren't worth using. It means they're a baseline, not a final check. Treating a clean scan as proof that a page works is exactly how these errors keep making it to production in the first place.

Most of the errors covered here aren't difficult to fix on their own. The harder part is catching them before they enter your codebase. The best time to find these problems is while you're designing, building, and reviewing a feature, not right before a release.

Automated testing should be part of that process. It catches common issues quickly, right as they're introduced, but it isn't a substitute for manual testing. A clean scan only tells you that no automatically detectable issues were found.

That's where platforms like TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) come in. TestMu AI's Accessibility Testing Suite is built around that split. Its axe-core-powered scanner can run on every build in your CI/CD pipeline, on a schedule to catch issues introduced by content or third-party updates, and inside your IDE through its MCP server. For the checks automation can't cover, you can test manually with real screen readers, including NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack, and with keyboard navigation, so a person can confirm what users actually hear and can reach.

If your team writes code with AI coding agents, you can bring those checks into the same workflow with TestMu AI's accessibility agent skill. It's an instruction pack from TestMu AI's open-source agent-skills repository that teaches agents like Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, or Gemini CLI how to add WCAG scanning to an existing Selenium, Playwright, or Cypress suite. You tell the agent which pages to scan, and it wires the checks into your framework and runs them on the TestMu AI cloud, with each scan's issues and WCAG mappings in your Accessibility dashboard. A passing scan still isn't the whole job, which is why the manual checks below matter.

Before shipping, spend a few minutes using the page yourself. Navigate using only the keyboard and verify that the focus indicator remains visible. If your site includes forms, menus, or dialogs, ensure they work without a mouse. For critical user journeys, testing with a screen reader will surface issues no automated tool can flag.

Finally, if the same issue keeps recurring, update your design system, component library, or review process to prevent it from happening again. Preventing a bug at the root is always easier than fixing it repeatedly.

Every error in this piece affects a real person trying to use your site. Low contrast text means someone with low vision can't read what you've written. A missing form label means someone using a screen reader can't fill out the form at all. These aren't rare situations; they happen constantly, on ordinary pages, to people who are simply trying to use your product.

That's what accessibility actually comes down to. It is not just a standard to meet, but the same usability you already care about, extended to people who navigate a page using assistive technologies.

KFC has announced a collaboration with Marvel Studios ahead of Avengers: Doomsday, introducing a limited-time menu inspired by Doctor Doom.

The fast-food chain is teaming up with Marvel for the first time, bringing a range of themed burgers, wings, fries, drinks, and collectibles to restaurants from November 9.

Although it will be available in the UK, through January 2027, the United States will miss out.

The new menu features several items inspired by the Marvel villain, including the Doom Burger, which combines KFC’s Original Recipe chicken with lettuce, pickles, cheese, Doom Cola sauce, and Smoky Green Mayo inside a black sesame bun.

The Doom Cola sauce is described as a sweet, sticky cola glaze with smoky BBQ notes, while the green mayo and Doom Dust seasoning add more unusual flavors to the lineup.

Other menu items include Doom Dripped Wings coated in the cola sauce, Doom Loaded Fries topped with both sauces, and a Doom Bucket featuring chicken, dipping sauces, and Doom Dust.

There’s also a Doom Supreme Fizz, featuring sparkling lemonade, green apple or kiwi syrup, and boba pearls, alongside Masked Mozza Melts served with the themed sauces.

However, some items won’t be available in some countries, with KFC saying it will vary between markets.

The collaboration also introduces five collectible Colonel Sanders figurines, each dressed in costumes inspired by Avengers: Doomsday characters. These will be available with qualifying menu purchases in select markets while supplies last.

#10557. Claude Code Hooks: Enforce Project Conventions with Gates and Linting

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Claude Code hooks solve a problem that every developer running agentic coding sessions eventually hits: the AI drifts from project conventions, and soft instructions in the prompt cannot prevent it. This article walks through two working hooks — a pre-write gate and a post-edit lint pipeline — that enforce conventions deterministically.

Claude Code hooks solve a problem that every developer running agentic coding sessions eventually hits: the AI drifts from project conventions, and soft instructions in the prompt cannot prevent it. A popular r/Frontend post captured this precisely. The developer reported that Claude Code wrote roughly 1,000 lines of code for a simple helper function that already existed in a project dependency. The prompt stated the project conventions. Claude ignored them anyway. The result was duplicated logic, bloated output, and wasted review time.

The root cause is structural, not incidental. Prompt-based instructions are probabilistic. They work well in short sessions, but as the context window fills during extended agentic loops, earlier instructions degrade in influence. Tool outputs, file contents, and intermediate reasoning bury the initial convention reminders. A long enough session means the agent effectively forgets what it was told. Any enforcement mechanism that relies solely on prompt text will exhibit this degradation pattern.

Claude Code hooks offer an alternative enforcement mechanism: shell scripts that bind to lifecycle events inside the agent loop. These scripts use exit codes to enforce rules. Exit 0 means proceed. Exit 2 blocks the action, and the script's stderr is surfaced to Claude as feedback. Any other non-zero exit code is a non-blocking error. This is deterministic. No matter how full the context window gets, an exit code of 2 stops the action every time.

No matter how full the context window gets, an exit code of 2 stops the action every time.

By the end of this article, you will have two working hooks: a pre-write gate that forces Claude to verify whether an implementation already exists before writing new code, and a post-edit lint and format pipeline that runs Prettier and ESLint on every changed file. Together, these hooks catch duplicated or unnecessary code before it lands and enforce style rules automatically.

Prerequisites: Claude Code installed and functional; a Node.js project with Prettier and ESLint already configured; jq installed (brew install jq / apt install jq); Prettier and ESLint must be installed as local node_modules dependencies (not relied upon via npx remote fetch); and basic familiarity with Bash scripting.

Hooks operate on an event-driven model. They fire at specific points in Claude Code's agent loop, intercepting actions before or after they occur. Four lifecycle events are relevant:

PreToolUse fires before any tool call executes. This is the interception point for blocking actions. For file-write gating, the tool names to match are Write, Edit, and MultiEdit. You can also match against Bash for command-level gating.

After a tool call completes, PostToolUse runs. This is the point for validation: linters, formatters, or test suites check the result of an edit. Because the tool has already executed, an exit code of 2 from a PostToolUse hook does not block the original action. Instead, it surfaces the script's stderr as feedback to Claude, which can then issue a follow-up edit to correct the issues.

When the user submits a new prompt, UserPromptSubmit fires. This is useful for resetting state between conversational turns.

Notification fires when Claude sends a notification. Non-zero exit codes from Notification hooks do not block any action. (The documentation does not specify any exit-code effect for this event type.) This makes it useful only for logging or side effects.

The contract is simple. When a hook script exits with code 0, the action proceeds normally. Exit code 2 is the blocking signal. For PreToolUse, exit 2 blocks the tool call and the script's stderr is fed to Claude as feedback. For PostToolUse, the tool has already completed, but exit 2 surfaces the script's stderr to Claude, which can take corrective action. The stderr content becomes part of the agent's reasoning context, which is what makes hooks corrective rather than merely restrictive. Any other non-zero exit code counts as a non-blocking error, not a block.

Configure hooks in the hooks object within .claude/settings.json for project-level scope or ~/.claude/settings.json for user-level scope. Each entry is keyed by event name and contains an array of matcher groups. Each group pairs an optional matcher (a pattern matching specific tool names) with a hooks array of one or more handlers, and each handler declares a type (command for a shell command) plus the command to execute.

This skeleton shows the structural pattern. The matcher field accepts pipe-delimited tool names. When a PreToolUse event fires for a Write tool call, Claude Code checks whether any hook entry matches, then executes the command, piping a JSON payload to its stdin containing the tool name and parameters.

The following configuration wires together all three lifecycle events. The PreToolUse entry fires before Write, Edit, or MultiEdit tool calls and blocks the first write attempt per prompt, printing a checklist for Claude to verify before proceeding. The PostToolUse entry fires after those same tool calls complete and runs Prettier (auto-fix) then ESLint (check) on the changed file. If ESLint finds issues, it exits 2 and prints them to stderr, surfacing the lint errors as feedback for Claude to self-correct. The UserPromptSubmit entry resets the pre-write gate so it re-arms on every new user prompt. No matcher is needed for UserPromptSubmit because this event has no associated tool. The reset is delegated to a dedicated script to ensure $PPID is evaluated consistently.

Important: Before relying on the UserPromptSubmit reset, verify that $PPID expands to the same value in this context as it does inside the hook scripts. You can add a temporary diagnostic command — echo "PPID=$PPID" >> /tmp/hook-ppid.log — to both reset-gate.sh and pre-write-gate.sh and compare the logged values. If they differ, the gate reset will not function correctly.

All three lifecycle events work together as a system: UserPromptSubmit resets state, PreToolUse enforces the gate, and PostToolUse validates output.

On the first file-write attempt after each new user prompt, the hook exits with code 2 and prints a checklist to stderr, which Claude Code feeds to Claude as the reason for the block. The checklist asks Claude to verify three things before writing new code: Does an implementation already exist in the project? Is there a standard-library equivalent? Is there a well-maintained dependency that handles this? This directly addresses the r/Frontend scenario where Claude wrote 1,000 lines duplicating existing functionality.

After Claude acknowledges the checklist (by seeing the stderr feedback, adjusting its plan, and attempting the write again), subsequent writes within the same prompt pass through. The gate opens for the duration of that conversational turn and re-arms when the user submits a new prompt.

The stateful pattern uses a temp file to track whether the gate has been opened. The file path follows the pattern /tmp/claude-hook-gate-$PPID. When the file exists, the gate is open and writes proceed. When it does not exist, the gate is closed and writes are blocked.

The UserPromptSubmit hook entry in settings.json handles the reset by running scripts/reset-gate.sh, which deletes this temp file, so every new user prompt re-arms the gate automatically.

Note on shared systems: The temp file path is predictable and based on a process ID, which can be a symlink attack surface on multi-user systems. On shared machines, consider using mktemp -d to create a session-specific directory and store the gate file there, or ensure /tmp permissions are appropriately restricted.

Each hook invocation spawns a new child process, so $PID (or $$) changes on every run. $PPID refers to the parent of the hook script. In the expected case, this is the Claude Code session process, which ties the gate state to the session rather than to the ephemeral script invocation.

However, this assumption should be verified in your environment. If Claude Code launches hooks through an intermediate shell (e.g., sh -c "bash scripts/..."), $PPID may point to that intermediate shell rather than the Claude Code session, and the value may change between invocations. Before relying on this mechanism, add a diagnostic hook that logs echo "PPID=$PPID" >> /tmp/hook-debug.log and confirm that the value is stable across multiple hook calls within a single session. If it varies, replace $PPID with a fixed session identifier.

This script reads the JSON payload from stdin, extracts the tool name and file path with jq in a single invocation (avoiding double-fork and potential echo mangling), checks for the gate file, and either allows or blocks the action. On the first blocked attempt, it prints the checklist and creates the gate file so the immediate retry succeeds. The UserPromptSubmit hook runs scripts/reset-gate.sh to delete the gate file and re-arm everything for the next prompt.

Note that set -uo pipefail is used rather than set -euo pipefail. The -e flag is deliberately omitted because it would cause the script to exit immediately on any non-zero subcommand return, potentially before reaching the touch or exit 2 lines. This would cause the gate to silently pass through instead of blocking, defeating the entire mechanism.

MultiEdit payload caveat: This script assumes the hook payload contains a single .tool_input.file_path key. The MultiEdit tool may pass an array of edits with a different payload structure. Before deploying, verify the actual payload schema by adding printf '%s' "$INPUT" >> /tmp/hook-payload.log before the jq line, triggering a MultiEdit operation, and inspecting the log. Adjust the jq extraction accordingly.

This script is called by the UserPromptSubmit hook to reset the pre-write gate for the current session. Using a dedicated script ensures $PPID is evaluated in the same way as in pre-write-gate.sh.

Verifying the hook works before relying on it in a live session takes three terminal commands. Pipe sample JSON into the script, check the exit code, then observe the behavior change after the gate opens.

The first run should print the checklist and report exit code 2. The second run, with the gate file now present, should exit silently with code 0. Deleting the gate file simulates what the UserPromptSubmit hook does automatically during a real session.

Note that $$ is used here instead of $PPID because these commands run directly in the terminal rather than as child processes of Claude Code. This means the PID used for the gate file will differ from production. These manual tests verify the script's logic (block-then-allow behavior), but they do not verify that $PPID is stable in the actual Claude Code environment. Use the diagnostic hook described in the PPID section above to confirm production behavior.

Claude has already written the file by the time this hook runs. Prettier auto-fixes formatting, then ESLint checks for lint violations. If ESLint reports issues, the hook exits 2 and prints the errors to stderr, surfacing them as agent feedback; Claude can then issue a follow-up edit to fix them. PostToolUse hooks cannot prevent a write; they can only trigger corrective action after it. If both tools pass, the hook exits silently with code 0.

Here is what that looks like in practice: Claude writes code, the hook formats it and checks it, and if something fails, Claude immediately sees what went wrong and retries. Prettier's step is non-blocking (it writes fixes in place), while the linting step surfaces errors for Claude to act on.

Claude writes code, the hook formats it and checks it, and if something fails, Claude immediately sees what went wrong and retries.

The script canonicalizes the file path using realpath and verifies that it falls within the project root directory. This prevents path traversal attacks where a crafted path like /tmp/../etc/passwd could bypass simple prefix checks. PROJECT_ROOT derives from the script's own location ($(dirname "$0")/..), which also ensures ESLint and Prettier configs are discoverable.

Prettier runs with --write to fix formatting in place; its exit code is deliberately ignored with || true because formatting fixes do not block the pipeline. The command -v check ensures both Prettier and ESLint exist locally before attempting to run them. ESLint runs with --max-warnings 0 to treat warnings as errors, enforcing a strict zero-warning policy. The timeout 30 wrapper prevents ESLint from hanging indefinitely on large or problematic files.

ESLint exit codes are handled distinctly: exit code 1 indicates lint violations (actionable by Claude), exit code 2 indicates a configuration or fatal error (requires developer attention, not a code fix), and exit code 124 indicates a timeout. This distinction prevents Claude from endlessly retrying lint fixes when the actual problem is a broken ESLint configuration. In each failure branch the hook itself exits 2 and writes to stderr, the combination Claude Code surfaces to Claude as feedback.

Both tools are invoked via ./node_modules/.bin/ rather than npx to guarantee that locally installed versions are used. Using npx without --no-install can cause it to silently download packages at runtime if they are not found in local node_modules, introducing network latency, non-determinism, and unexpected cost during hook execution.

Files outside the project root, such as /tmp scratch files that Claude sometimes creates during multi-step operations, are skipped by the realpath canonicalization and project-root check. This is more robust than a simple prefix check against /tmp/* or /var/*, because it also catches path traversal patterns like /tmp/../etc/passwd and handles symlinks correctly.

Missing Prettier or ESLint binaries are handled gracefully. Both steps check for the binary with command -v before running. If ESLint cannot find a config file, it reports a fatal error (exit code 2), and that error flows through stdout to Claude with an explicit "configuration error" label, making it clear that the fix needed is not a code change. This is preferable to silently swallowing the failure.

Binary files and non-JS/TS files are handled by the extension filter in the case statement. The hook exits with code 0 for any unmatched extension, letting the write proceed without interference.

Layer the two: use CLAUDE.md for the "why" behind conventions, and hooks for the "must." CLAUDE.md explains that the team prefers existing utilities over new implementations, while the pre-write gate hook enforces that preference. CLAUDE.md describes the formatting standard; the post-edit hook runs the formatter. Neither mechanism replaces the other.

Hooks run synchronously. While a hook executes, the agent is blocked. Aim for under one second per hook invocation. Prettier and ESLint on a single file meet this target on typical developer hardware with local node_modules. Scripts exceeding two to three seconds will noticeably stall the agent loop. Running a full test suite as a hook would not be appropriate.

Hook input payloads follow a JSON structure that may evolve across Claude Code versions. grep or sed parsing is brittle and breaks on structural changes. jq provides safe, schema-aware extraction and handles missing fields gracefully with the // empty fallback pattern used in the scripts above.

When setting up hooks for the first time, appending output to a log file (>> /tmp/claude-hooks.log) helps diagnose issues with path extraction, exit codes, and unexpected tool names. Remove or disable logging once you have confirmed correct behavior over several sessions, to avoid filling disk space during long runs.

Commit the scripts/ directory and .claude/settings.json to the repository. Every team member gets the same guardrails without manual setup. Hooks become part of the project's development infrastructure, not a personal customization.

Commit the scripts/ directory and .claude/settings.json to the repository. Every team member gets the same guardrails without manual setup.

The two-hook setup built in this article addresses both sides of convention drift: the pre-write gate catches duplicated code before it happens, and the post-edit pipeline enforces formatting and lint rules on every change. The pattern extends to security scanning, test runners, or any file-level validation that runs in under a few seconds.

#10556. MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment. This allows autonomous vehicles to detect objects in their path and respond quickly. However, conventional lidar sensors are often large and costly, and many rely on moving components that can wear out over time. These limitations make the systems difficult to use in a wider range of settings.

MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts. Their advance centers on a new silicon-photonics chip, a type of semiconductor device that controls light instead of electrical signals.

Existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view. As a result, they struggle to scan areas located toward the edges of a scene. Previous attempts to expand this viewing range have often introduced extra noise and reduced measurement accuracy.

The MIT team addressed those problems by creating an array of integrated antennas that greatly limits unwanted crosstalk, which occurs when neighboring antennas interfere with one another. The design allows the chip to scan across a broader field of view while producing less noise than other silicon-photonics-based methods.

The advance could support the development of more capable lidar sensors for challenging uses, including autonomous vehicle navigation, aerial mapping, and the monitoring of construction sites.

"The functionality we demonstrated in this work solves a fundamental problem for integrated optical-phased-array technology, enabling future lidar sensors that can achieve significantly higher performance than we could demonstrate previously," says Jelena Notaros, the Robert J. Shillman Career Development Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) at MIT, a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and senior author of a paper on this innovation.

The study also includes lead author and EECS graduate student Henry Crawford-Eng, along with EECS graduate students Andres Garcia Coleto, Benjamin M. Mazur, Daniel M. DeSantis, and Tal Sneh. The findings were published recently in Nature Communications.

Many traditional lidar systems use a large rotating unit to direct light pulses across a scene. When the light strikes nearby objects, it reflects back toward the sensor. The returning signals provide the information needed to reconstruct a detailed map of the environment.

Silicon-photonics-based lidar works differently. Rather than rotating a mechanical device, it scans a beam of light electronically in several directions with a system known as an integrated optical phased array (OPA).

At the heart of an OPA is a group of integrated antennas. Each antenna contains tiny, regularly spaced variations along its length. These features, known as corrugations, cause light from an input source to scatter upward and out of the photonic chip.

Researchers can control the direction of the outgoing beam by changing the phase of the light sent to each antenna. Adjusting these phases changes the angle at which the array releases light, making it possible to steer the beam without moving any physical components.

Placing the antennas close together creates a serious obstacle. Neighboring antennas can couple with one another, scrambling the light they produce. Engineers have traditionally prevented this interference by increasing the distance between antennas, but wider spacing creates a different set of problems.

When antennas are too far apart, the array produces several copies of the same beam at different angles. The primary beam can only be moved a limited distance before it becomes difficult to distinguish from these additional copies.

"This limits our field of view, so the autonomous vehicle now only knows what is in front of it for a certain angular range," Garcia Coleto explains.

The unwanted beam copies, called grating lobes, can confuse the sensor and generate false detections. They also consume energy that could otherwise be directed into the main beam.

To overcome this tradeoff, the MIT researchers developed antennas with reduced crosstalk that can be positioned close together without strongly coupling.

In a conventional OPA, every antenna has an identical structure and uses the same pattern of corrugations. When these matching antennas are placed close together, they interact very strongly.

The MIT team instead created a repeating set of three antennas with distinct shapes. They changed the width of the antennas as well as the size and placement of the corrugations. Because the antennas have different geometries, each one also has a different propagation coefficient, which describes how light moves through the structure.

"Because the antennas have very different propagation coefficients, when we put them close together, essentially each antenna doesn't 'see' the antenna next to it. Therefore, it won't couple with its neighbor," Garcia Coleto says.

Making Different Antennas Behave the Same Way

Reducing the coupling was only part of the challenge. Although the antennas needed different propagation coefficients, they still had to release light in the same consistent manner.

The team designed the antennas around three essential requirements.

Each antenna had to emit the same amount of light. Every antenna also needed to release its beam at the same angle when receiving the same wavelength. Finally, the angle of emission had to change evenly across the entire array as the beam was steered.

"We have this challenge where we require the antennas to have different geometries to reduce the crosstalk, but we need to simultaneously design the antennas to have the same emission characteristics. While it is possible to engineer this, it is extremely difficult because, typically, when antennas are designed with different geometries, they tend to behave differently," Crawford-Eng says.

The researchers began by developing the basic electromagnetic theory describing how radiative modes couple. They then used this theoretical framework to guide the design and computer simulation of the antennas.

Based on those calculations, the team manufactured an OPA containing the reduced-crosstalk antennas. The antennas were placed much closer together than those in a conventional system, and the completed device was then tested experimentally.

Interference Falls From About 100 Percent to 1 Percent

Under the conditions of the experiment, a typical OPA would have produced coupling of approximately 100 percent. The MIT design lowered that coupling to about 1 percent while still generating one clean and precise beam.

The system accurately steered the beam across a broad field of view without producing any grating lobes. This combination of wide scanning, low interference, and strong beam quality addresses one of the central obstacles facing integrated lidar technology.

The researchers now plan to refine the method so the system can cover an even broader viewing range. They are also studying another possible approach to wide field-of-view performance that emerged while they were developing the underlying theory.

"This work addresses a longstanding challenge in integrated optical phased arrays: simultaneously achieving both a wide field of view, which requires dense antenna spacing, and high beam quality, which requires low crosstalk between neighboring antennas. The authors solve this problem with an elegant antenna design. Their innovation is an important step forward for chip-scale, solid-state beam-steering technology," says Joyce Poon, professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Toronto and director of the Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics, who was not involved with this work.

The Semiconductor Research Corporation, the National Science Foundation, an MIT MathWorks Fellowship, the U.S. Department of War, and the MIT Rolf G. Locher Endowed Fellowship supported the research, in part.

Some of the work was carried out using MIT.nano facilities.

#10554. Delivery driver goes viral throwing coffee at customer after delivering it to her

A delivery driver has been put on blast in a viral TikTok after being confronted by a customer as he was seemingly trying to steal a coffee that he had just delivered.

When delivery drivers drop off parcels, food, or anything else you’ve ordered online, they typically have to snap a photo to prove that it has been delivered. However, there have been cases where orders are stolen from people’s porches too.

In the case of Karmen Karma, the TikToker put a delivery driver called Darian on blast after he appeared to be trying to steal her coffee order on November 3. “Your coffee is right here, I don’t want your $4 coffee,” the driver said before throwing the cup at the TikToker.

“He delivered coffee to my front door, took a photo, and then went running back to his car with my coffee,” Karmen explained. “Tried to drive off fast but got stuck in a cul-de-sac, so on his way back down my street he decided to do this with my two small children present next to me. Also, tell Darian my coffee was $19.70.”

A number of commenters urged Karmen to provide proof to the delivery service as a way to get the driver punished in some way.

She did just that a few hours later, showing footage from her doorbell of Darian dropping the coffee off and snapping a photo of the delivery.

In that video, the driver can be seen speeding off too with the TikToker also in view, recording him doing so. Karmen added that she had tipped 33% of the cost of the order too.

Some viewers argued that there is “more to the story,” while others are completely on the TikToker’s side.

#10552. Winnie-the-Pooh turned into anime girl for new psychological horror game

A new psychological horror Steam game has transformed Winnie-the-Pooh and his companions into anime girls, putting a unique spin on Christopher Robin’s adventures through the Hundred Acre Wood.

When you think of Winnie-the-Pooh, your mind probably conjures up images of the cute, cuddly bear with a crippling addiction to honey. However, in a move not too dissimilar to Umamusume turning real-life racehorses into anime girl idols, a horror visual novel has transformed Pooh and his pals into waifus (words I’m still struggling to come to terms with).

Yes, Piglet, Eeyore, Rabbit, and co. have all been given an anime girl makeover, and according to the Steam Store page, the visual novel has been tagged as having psychological horror and dating sim elements.

Winnie-the-Pooh: Honey Distortion is an upcoming point-and-click mystery visual novel that has been inspired by A. A. Milne’s stories. Players take on the role of Christopher Robin as they explore the Hundred Acre Wood, unravel mysteries, and make decisions that can lead to different endings.

As shown in the screenshots, Honey Distortion has transformed every character into an anime girl. Winnie-the-Pooh retains the character’s signature red top, but now comes with some added short shorts, while Rabbit is shown wearing a bunny girl outfit.

Meanwhile, Piglet is shown sporting a textured black hairstyle with pink streaks and a matching pink sweater. She’s also shown holding a handgun in one scene, threatening to blow Christopher Robin’s head off (I guess this is where the horror elements come in?).
