Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

LLM structured output remains one of the most persistent pain points in production systems. This article walks through native JSON schema mode, function calling, Zod runtime validation, retry logic with error feedback, and a concrete provider comparison to guide architectural decisions.

LLM structured output remains one of the most persistent pain points in production systems. Developers building on top of large language models routinely encounter inconsistent response structures, missing fields, hallucinated keys, and malformed JSON that breaks downstream logic. A single unexpected null where an array was expected can cascade through an application and take down an entire pipeline. The core issue: LLM outputs are, by default, untyped free text masquerading as structured data.

A single unexpected null where an array was expected can cascade through an application and take down an entire pipeline.

By the end of this article, readers will have a typed, provider-agnostic validation layer with bounded retries that works across OpenAI, Google Gemini, Anthropic, and self-hosted vLLM endpoints. The approach covers native JSON schema mode, function calling, Zod runtime validation, retry logic with error feedback, and a concrete provider comparison to guide architectural decisions.

This article assumes the following environment and package versions:

Two levels of structured output support differ in what they guarantee. JSON mode, available in providers like OpenAI and Gemini, guarantees that the model emits syntactically valid JSON. It does not guarantee any particular shape. The model might return {"foo": 42} when the application expected {"sentiment": "positive", "rating": 5}. Valid JSON is not the same as correct JSON.

Schema-constrained mode goes further. It enforces a declared JSON Schema at the token-generation level: the provider guides token decoding to produce output conforming to a specific structure. OpenAI supports this through the response_format parameter with type json_schema. Google Gemini offers it via generationConfig.responseSchema. vLLM provides schema-constrained decoding through its guided_json parameter. The strictness and subset of JSON Schema supported varies across providers, but the core mechanism is the same: constrain token sampling so only schema-valid sequences are generated.

Function calling (also referred to as tool calling) provides an alternative path to structured output. When a tool is defined with an input_schema, the provider forces the model to emit arguments matching the declared schema. This is Anthropic's primary structured output mechanism for Claude, which does not offer a dedicated response_format JSON schema mode. Instead, developers define a tool whose input schema matches the desired output structure, and the model returns the structured data inside a tool_use content block.

Use function calling when the application also needs to route actions based on the model's decision. Use response_format schema when the goal is purely typed data extraction. Both mechanisms benefit from the validation layer described below.

TypeScript's type system operates entirely at compile time. It erases all type information at runtime, which means a JSON.parse call returns any regardless of what interface was declared. Zod fills this gap by providing runtime type safety: it validates that a parsed object actually conforms to the expected shape, with rich error messages that pinpoint exactly which field failed and why. When an LLM returns "rating": "five" instead of "rating": 5, Zod reports the exact path, expected type, and received value. This level of detail is essential for debugging malformed LLM responses.

The zod-to-json-schema library converts a Zod schema into a standard JSON Schema object, enabling a single schema definition to drive both runtime validation and provider-level schema constraints.

This ProductReviewSchema becomes the single source of truth. The same Zod object validates LLM responses at runtime, generates the JSON Schema sent to providers, and infers the TypeScript type used throughout the application. There is no separate interface to keep in sync.

Note: Each provider code block below depends on ProductReviewSchema, ProductReview, and productReviewJsonSchema defined in the "Building a Reusable Schema" section above. These blocks are not standalone — copy the schema setup code first or structure your project as a single file.

OpenAI's response_format parameter with type json_schema provides token-level schema enforcement. The JSON Schema generated from Zod is passed directly into the API call.

When strict: true is set, OpenAI requires that the schema include additionalProperties: false and that all fields appear in the required array. Zod excludes .optional() fields from required by default; restructure them using .nullable() or a union to satisfy strict mode. Verify the JSON Schema output before sending it to the API for any schema that uses optional fields. The returned content is a JSON string that can be passed to JSON.parse and then validated with Zod.

The same JSON Schema works with Google Gemini's generationConfig.responseSchema, demonstrating the portability of the Zod-driven approach.

Gemini's schema support has notable subset limitations. It does not support $ref for schema references, and its handling of complex oneOf constructs is limited. The $refStrategy: "none" option passed to zodToJsonSchema earlier inlines all references, which avoids the $ref problem. For schemas involving discriminated unions, test against Gemini specifically to confirm support.

Anthropic's Claude models do not expose a response_format JSON schema mode. Structured output is achieved by defining a tool whose input_schema matches the target JSON Schema. The API call includes a tool definition with the ProductReview JSON Schema as its input schema, and the model returns the structured data inside a tool_use content block within the response.

The tool_use block's input field holds the structured object, not the top-level response content. Extract that specific block rather than attempting to JSON.parse the entire response body. The same Zod schema validates the extracted object identically.

vLLM supports schema-constrained decoding through its guided_json parameter, which accepts a JSON Schema object and constrains the model's token generation accordingly. When using the OpenAI SDK against a vLLM endpoint, pass the schema via extra_body:

This works with any model served through vLLM's OpenAI-compatible API endpoint. It avoids per-token billing and keeps data on-premises, making it well-suited for self-hosted deployments where provider-level schema enforcement is desired without vendor lock-in.

Azure OpenAI mirrors the OpenAI API's response_format contract. The same code that targets OpenAI's API works with Azure OpenAI by swapping the base URL and using Azure-specific authentication. Note that Azure OpenAI structured output support depends on the deployed model version and the API version header; not all deployments support json_schema. No schema format changes are required once a compatible deployment is confirmed.

Even with schema-constrained generation, responses still fail validation. A provider might not support strict mode for a particular schema feature. The model might truncate long responses, producing incomplete JSON. Function calling can return partial arguments when the model's context window is exhausted. For these reasons, the architecture follows a three-step flow: send request, parse and validate with Zod, and on failure, retry with the validation error injected into the prompt so the model can self-correct. A hard upper bound on retry attempts prevents infinite loops and runaway API costs.

The function is generic over T, which is inferred from the Zod schema. The fetchResponse callback abstracts away the provider entirely, accepting an optional feedback string that gets injected into the prompt on retry attempts. Parse errors and Zod validation errors are both handled, with feedback constructed from structured Zod issues rather than raw error text. The buildFeedback function caps the number of issues and truncates the message length to prevent overly long or adversarial content from being re-injected into the prompt. The StructuredOutputError thrown on final failure carries the last set of Zod issues for observability and logging.

Note that each retry incurs an additional API call with associated token cost and latency. The maxRetries parameter controls the number of retry attempts after the initial call, so maxRetries: 2 results in up to 3 total API calls.

The returned value carries the full ProductReview type. No type assertion or manual casting is needed. The same pattern applies to Gemini, Anthropic, or any other provider by swapping the callback implementation.

Gemini supports both responseSchema (schema-constrained mode, row 2) and function calling. These are distinct mechanisms with different schema subset limitations. The table above lists Gemini under schema-constrained mode, which is the mechanism demonstrated in this article.

For production systems, combining response_format JSON Schema with the Zod validation wrapper provides the strongest guarantees. The provider-level constraint eliminates most malformed responses at the source, while the Zod layer catches edge cases and provides type safety that persists regardless of which provider is in use. The retry mechanism acts as a safety net that fires infrequently when both layers are active, keeping costs and latency low.

Your Zod validation error says pros.0.details.subRating: Expected number, received string, three levels deep in a nested object the model half-hallucinated. Schemas beyond 3 levels of nesting increase token usage and raise failure rates during constrained generation. Flatten object hierarchies where possible; doing so reduces truncation probability and gives Zod simpler error paths to report on validation failure.

Never use open-loop retries with LLM APIs. Two to three retries (three to four total API calls) is a practical default when provider-level schema constraints are not active. With schema-constrained generation enabled, a single retry handles the most common failure mode: truncated output from long responses. Log every failure with the full Zod issue set for observability so your team can identify schemas that consistently cause problems.

Never use open-loop retries with LLM APIs. Two to three retries (three to four total API calls) is a practical default when provider-level schema constraints are not active.

The JSON Schema acts as a contract between the application and the LLM provider. When it changes, re-test against each provider. A field added to the Zod schema that Gemini cannot express, or a constraint that triggers an OpenAI strict mode rejection, will only surface at runtime. You will only catch these failures before production if you validate schema changes against each provider as part of your CI or deployment process.

Forget to set additionalProperties: false on an OpenAI strict mode call? The API rejects the schema outright, with an error message that does not always point to the root cause. OpenAI strict mode also requires every field in the required array. Gemini does not support $ref or complex oneOf constructs, making inlined, flat schemas the safer choice. Anthropic's tool use returns the structured object inside a tool_use content block. Attempting to JSON.parse the entire API response rather than extracting the specific block is a common source of bugs.

The pattern presented here forms a three-layer defense. Provider-level schema constraints catch malformed output at generation time. Zod runtime validation catches anything the provider misses. Bounded retry with error feedback gives the model a chance to self-correct. The Zod schema is the single source of truth powering all three layers, eliminating the synchronization burden of maintaining separate type definitions, JSON Schemas, and validation logic.

The Zod schema is the single source of truth powering all three layers, eliminating the synchronization burden of maintaining separate type definitions, JSON Schemas, and validation logic.

Adding the validateLLMResponse wrapper to existing LLM calls adds zero latency to calls that validate on the first attempt. It requires no changes to the initial prompt or provider configuration; the retry mechanism appends a correction prompt only on subsequent attempts. As more providers adopt strict JSON schema mode, the retry layer fires less frequently, but the Zod validation boundary still catches the edge cases that slip through.

#10525. Humanoid robots fail supermarket jobs after “slacking off” and having ‘bad attitude’

Robots were put to the test in a supermarket in China, but two actually failed to complete their tasks, and one needed to have more “enthusiasm.”

If you believed sci-fi movies back in the day, humans should have been replaced by robots at this point. As it is, though, engineers are still playing catch-up and trying to develop increasingly life-like humanoids.

Some have already rolled out across the United States and China, mainly focused on companionship and doing some menial at-home tasks. There are some, though, that are working in stores too.

In China, those supermarket working bots have been put to the test: trying to complete a 24-hour shift. However, as TechSpot pointed out, two of them actually failed to complete their tasks.

The test, which was focused on Agibot’s G2 robots, was run by the company itself and advertised as ‘Robots Never Clock Out.’ The bots worked around the clock on tasks across four different periods of the day.

While four of the six robots were able to complete almost 2000 tasks that were required of them, two didn’t and were not promoted to “official employees” as a result. One of these was a cleaning bot that had to deviate its path due to a trash can.

The other bot was assigned to checking stock levels on shelves, but “lacked initiative” and couldn’t keep up with the pace of the work. As per ITHome, this bot was seen to be “slacking off,” and the robot’s “on-duty enthusiasm” was found lacking too.

Robots Never Clock Out | AGIBOT G2’s 24-Hour Convenience Store Challenge Six AGIBOT G2 take on a 24-hour shift as convenience store trainees. From rush-hour crowds to late-night solo duty and the morning breakfast sprint, can they keep up with nonstop customers and…

These two bots will remain in an “observation” group with the hopes that they will follow the other four in becoming full-time employees in the future.

As noted, robots have been popping up in stores anyway, with Japanese convenience stores blending AI tech and robotics to tackle labor shortages and streamline shopping.

#10522. IBM quantum computer solves classically intractable problem in 15 minutes

Scientists used a new error correction strategy to encode 70 logical qubits and tackle a problem considered classically intractable.

The quantum computation was completed in about 15 minutes, while leading classical computing methods would require an impractical amount of time to perform the same task.

IBM and researchers at the University of Chicago have announced a quantum computing demonstration that meets key criteria for quantum advantage. The experiment performed a calculation beyond the practical reach of leading classical simulation techniques while also providing evidence that the quantum computer produced a reliable result.

In a new paper, "Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity," the researchers describe how they achieved both goals using a newly designed form of encoded quantum circuit. The work represents one of the largest demonstrations of logical quantum computing reported so far.

The circuits and experimental results have also been made publicly available through the Quantum Advantage Tracker.

Why Quantum Results Are So Difficult to Verify

Researchers have long used a benchmark called random circuit sampling (RCS) to explore whether quantum computers can outperform conventional machines.

In simplified terms, RCS challenges a quantum computer to generate patterns that become so complicated that a classical computer cannot efficiently reproduce them. That makes the benchmark useful for testing the limits of classical simulation.

But it also creates a major problem. Once the quantum calculation becomes too difficult for a classical computer to reproduce, verifying that the quantum machine actually produced the correct result becomes increasingly difficult as well. Eventually, checking the answer can itself become infeasible unless researchers make strong assumptions about how the quantum computer behaves internally.

The IBM and University of Chicago team approached this verification problem by developing a more structured alternative to RCS.

The researchers showed that their method preserves the same computational hardness criteria associated with RCS, meaning the problem remains extremely difficult for classical computers. At the same time, the added structure allows errors to be detected during the quantum computation.

"Verification remains one of the biggest challenges in firmly establishing experimental quantum advantage," said Bill Fefferman, Associate Professor at the University of Chicago. "This experiment develops techniques to better characterize the fidelity of hard quantum states under noise, increasing confidence that the quantum computer is solving a computationally hard problem."

Soumik Ghosh, PhD student in Fefferman's group at the University of Chicago, added, "Beyond strengthening experimental validation, advances in verification have the potential to unlock practical applications for the next generation of quantum computers."

The experiment also included one of the world's largest-known demonstrations of quantum error correction.

The researchers operated 70 logical qubits. Unlike individual physical qubits, logical qubits are encoded in a way that helps protect quantum information from errors and noise.

Using those logical qubits, the team carried out 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical "T gates," two measures that reflect the complexity of the quantum circuit.

The encoded design significantly improved reliability. Effective logical error rates were 10 times lower than the underlying physical error rates, allowing the circuit to maintain unusually high fidelity even while performing a large number of quantum operations.

IBM Says Quantum Advantage Has Entered a New Stage

"We are now firmly in the quantum advantage era," said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow. "We have demonstrated a quantum computation beyond the practical reach of classical computers that establishes, with statistical confidence, a lower bound on how faithfully it was executed. This milestone gives scientists, developers, and businesses a new foundation for trusting quantum computers as they scale to problems far beyond what we can achieve classically."

The researchers found that many leading classical simulation methods would face prohibitive runtimes when attempting the same task.

The IBM quantum computer, by comparison, completed the computation in approximately 15 minutes.

A Step Toward Larger, More Trustworthy Quantum Computers

Speed alone is not enough for quantum computing to become useful at larger scales. Researchers also need ways to suppress errors and establish confidence that a quantum system produced a valid result.

This experiment advances both goals at once by combining large-scale logical quantum computing with a method for evaluating the reliability of a calculation that is already beyond practical classical simulation.

Error correction and trustworthy verification are considered essential for scaling quantum computers toward more difficult problems, making the new demonstration an important step toward that goal.

#10520. React useEffect Cleanup Patterns for Timers, Listeners, and Fetch Races

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Code examples require React 18+. StrictMode double-invocation behavior was introduced in React 18.

Missed cleanup functions in React useEffect are among the most common sources of memory leaks, stale-state bugs, and race conditions. Typical beginner tutorials demonstrate the happy path: fetch data, set state, render. They rarely address what happens when a component unmounts mid-flight, when a dependency changes faster than an async operation resolves, or when event listeners silently pile up across re-renders. This article provides a unified mental model for useEffect cleanup across three categories (timers, listeners, and fetch races), a reference table mapping setup to cleanup to pitfall, and a copy-paste PR review checklist that development teams can adopt immediately.

The mental model is simple: React runs the setup function when the component mounts, runs the cleanup function when the component unmounts, and on every dependency change, runs cleanup for the previous render's effect before running setup for the current render's effect. This cleanup-then-setup cycle on dependency change is the part most developers either overlook or misunderstand. It means that every effect invocation is paired with a corresponding teardown, and React guarantees that ordering. The setup function acquires resources; the cleanup return releases them. The dependency array declares which values, when changed, trigger that cycle again.

React 18's StrictMode intentionally runs each component's effect twice in development by simulating an unmount and remount: setup → cleanup → setup. Your setup function executes twice on the initial render in development. This double invocation exists specifically to surface missing cleanup logic. If a component registers an event listener in setup but never removes it in cleanup, StrictMode will produce two listeners after the simulated remount, making the bug immediately visible during development. As documented in the React docs on StrictMode (https://react.dev/reference/react/StrictMode), this behavior only occurs in development mode and does not affect production builds. However, the bugs it exposes are entirely real. A component that behaves incorrectly under StrictMode's double-mount has a latent cleanup bug that will manifest in production whenever the component remounts due to navigation, conditional rendering, or parent re-renders.

A component that behaves incorrectly under StrictMode's double-mount has a latent cleanup bug that will manifest in production whenever the component remounts due to navigation, conditional rendering, or parent re-renders.

When a setInterval starts inside a useEffect that depends on a prop or state value, every time that dependency changes, React re-runs the effect. Without cleanup, the previous interval continues running. A second interval starts. Then a third. The observable symptom depends on what the interval does: a counter increments N times per tick (where N is the number of orphaned intervals), a polling callback fires multiple times per tick, or a UI animation speeds up erratically. Each orphaned interval holds a closure over stale state, compounding the problem. Under StrictMode's double-mount in development, this bug surfaces immediately as two intervals running from the very first render.

The correct pattern creates the interval in setup and clears it in cleanup. When the dependency changes, React clears the old interval before starting a new one with the updated value. This guarantees exactly one active interval at any point in time.

The same principle applies to setTimeout. Replace setInterval with setTimeout and clearInterval with clearTimeout. Store the timer ID returned by the scheduling function, then clear it in the cleanup return.

Adding an event listener to window, document, or any DOM node outside the component's own render tree requires manual cleanup. Without a matching removeEventListener in the cleanup return, every re-render (or StrictMode double-mount) attaches an additional handler. The handlers accumulate. A resize listener that updates state will trigger setState multiple times per resize event, once for each orphaned listener. This degrades performance and can cause subtle state corruption when multiple handlers race to update the same state variable.

The critical detail is that removeEventListener must receive the exact same function reference passed to addEventListener. An inline arrow function created inside the effect body produces a new reference on every invocation, so calling removeEventListener with a different inline arrow does nothing. The listener is never removed. Declare the handler as a named function (or a variable holding the function) inside the effect, then pass that same variable to both addEventListener and removeEventListener.

The critical detail is that removeEventListener must receive the exact same function reference passed to addEventListener.

If the handler depends on a prop or state value and is defined outside the effect (for example, with useCallback), that handler must appear in the dependency array. When the reference changes, React cleans up the old listener and attaches the new one. Note that re-adding the listener on each dependency change is correct behavior: the old handler (with stale closure) is removed and the new handler (with fresh values) is attached.

Consider a search component where the user types quickly. Each keystroke triggers a new fetch. The request for "rea" might take 300ms while the request for "react" takes 50ms. The "react" response arrives first, and the UI shows the correct results. Then the "rea" response arrives, and because nothing prevented it from calling setState, it overwrites the UI with stale, incorrect results. This is a classic race condition. The slower response wins not because it is more recent, but because it resolves later. Without cancellation, there is no mechanism to tell the browser to discard an in-flight request whose results are no longer relevant.

The modern solution is AbortController. Each effect invocation creates a new controller instance. The controller's signal property is passed to fetch as an option. When the cleanup function runs (because the dependency changed or the component unmounted), it calls controller.abort(), which cancels the in-flight request. The fetch promise rejects with an AbortError. Browsers generally attempt to cancel the underlying network request as well, though the behavior varies by engine (see the Fetch spec on AbortSignal and MDN's browser compatibility tables). This guarantees that only the most recent request can successfully set state.

Calling abort() rejects the promise. This is normal, not an error condition. The catch block must distinguish AbortError from genuine network failures. Without this guard, the UI would flash an error for every intentional cancellation, or the rejection would trigger error-logging infrastructure. The standard check inspects the error's name property: if it equals 'AbortError', the catch block returns early without updating state or surfacing an error.

Note that the effect function itself is not async. An inner async function is declared and called immediately. This matters because useEffect expects its return value to be either undefined or a cleanup function. React ignores a returned promise and never registers a cleanup function from it.

The following table captures the universal pattern across the most common side effects in React applications. Each row shows the same structure: acquire a resource in setup, release it in cleanup, and understand the specific failure mode when cleanup is missing.

WebSocket and Firebase patterns appear here for reference; see MDN's WebSocket API docs and Firebase documentation for full implementation details.

The pattern is always the same: acquire resource, release resource, declare dependencies honestly. If setup creates something, cleanup destroys it. If setup connects, cleanup disconnects. Memorize this symmetry and every new side effect becomes a direct application of the same principle.

This checklist is designed to be dropped directly into a team's contributing guidelines or used as a mental walkthrough during code review. Every question targets a specific category of cleanup bug.

A PR that passes all seven checks covers the most frequently reported categories of cleanup-related bugs before they reach production.

The react-hooks/exhaustive-deps ESLint rule exists to catch missing dependencies that cause stale closures. Disabling the rule hides the bug instead of fixing it. The effect closes over a stale value and never re-runs in response to that value changing, producing a stale closure that is difficult to reproduce and debug. When the rule flags a dependency, add it. If that causes unwanted re-runs, restructure the effect: extract logic, split into multiple effects, or stabilize references with useCallback or useMemo. Suppression should be a last resort, always paired with a comment explaining why the omission is intentional and safe.

Marking the effect callback as async is a common trap. An async function implicitly returns a promise. React expects the return value to be either undefined or a synchronous cleanup function. React ignores a returned promise and never registers a cleanup function, so nothing runs on unmount or dependency change. The fix is always the same: define an inner async function inside the effect and invoke it immediately, keeping the outer effect function synchronous so that the return statement provides a proper cleanup function.

React ignores a returned promise and never registers a cleanup function, so nothing runs on unmount or dependency change.

#10516. Ampere PMU Profiler: A Guide to Microarchitecture Profiling

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The Ampere® PMU Profiler (APP) is a Python-based tool designed to provide deep insight into the microarchitectural behavior of applications running on Ampere CPUs (e.g., Ampere® Altra® and AmpereOne®). Unlike standard profilers that identify where time is spent (for example, which functions consume CPU time), the PMU Profiler explains why time is being spent by measuring low-level hardware events associated with the CPU pipeline and execution behavior.

A key outcome of APP is that it enables performance engineers to move from coarse symptoms to actionable causes. For example, while application-level profiling can show an expensive code path, APP can help identify whether the expense stems from inefficient instruction fetching, data cache misses, or other microarchitectural factors that are difficult or impossible to isolate using application-level tools alone. The document outlines a top-down performance analysis methodology and positions APP as an essential final step for expert-level tuning, particularly on Ampere platforms, where you must understand hardware-level bottlenecks and then apply targeted code optimizations.

APP is intended to complement system-level analysis rather than replace it. System-level profilers are useful for identifying high-level bottlenecks such as resource saturation or contention, but APP is focused on microarchitecture-level analysis by collecting hardware events. This makes APP especially valuable after system bottlenecks have been eliminated or ruled out, leaving "microarchitecture inefficiency" as the remaining likely cause of slowdowns.

The Ampere PMU Profiler uses the Linux perf utility with validated PMUs and metrics on Ampere CPUs. Its purpose is to capture microarchitectural performance indicators through hardware event measurement. In practice, this means APP collects events measured by perf stat that relate to the CPU pipeline and execution mechanisms, allowing engineers to determine not only what is slow, but the underlying microarchitectural reason.

A central distinction between APP and application profiling tools is the level of visibility. Tools that sample stack traces (or count function invocations) typically answer: "Which functions are active during the slow period?" APP answers a more hardware-specific question: "Which microarchitectural mechanisms are consuming cycles, and what stalls or inefficiencies are present?"

The APP workflow assumes that developers can form a hypothesis about where the bottleneck likely originates, such as a particular loop or data access pattern, and then rely on PMU event measurements to confirm or refute those hypotheses at the microarchitectural level.

Performance problems are frequently multi-layered. Even after system-level bottlenecks are addressed (for example, ensuring that the CPU is not idling due to I/O, ensuring there is sufficient memory, and verifying resource utilization), some workloads still perform poorly because the CPU spends cycles in inefficient pipeline states.

APP helps solve this class of problems by measuring hardware-level behavior. For example, APP can identify microarchitectural bottlenecks such as:

This capability is important because microarchitectural causes often do not map cleanly to application symptoms. Code can appear "hot" in a profiler, but the reason it is slow might be due to how it interacts with cache hierarchies, how it causes translation or fetch inefficiencies, or how the processor recovers from pipeline disruptions. Those details are what PMU-based measurement aims to expose.

APP also links investigation to unlocking the full performance potential of the hardware. By understanding CPU-level bottlenecks, engineers can choose targeted optimizations that application-level tools alone cannot determine with confidence. This ultimately leads to more efficient software and better utilization of Ampere hardware for competitive workloads.

Performance tuning is a process of systematic investigation, moving from a broad, system-wide view down to the specific interactions between code and hardware.

Performance optimization is as much art as it is science. The APEX framework uses tools and methodologies to add structure and rigor to the process and can bridge the gap between creative intuition and empirical fact.

We propose applying the APEX (Adaptive Profiling and Execution) methodology to enable root cause analysis for solving performance problems. Follow the funnel above from top to bottom to effectively use the procedure.

The methodology recommends starting with assessing platform health as a first step to ensure that the platform used for performance analysis is set up well. An unhealthy platform may mislead the performance analysis.

Consider capturing initial performance metrics before tuning any system or application settings. This establishes a clear understanding of the current workload and identifies key scalability knobs. We recommend using Ampere's PerfKit Benchmarker (APB), which supports many open-source applications, to create a reliable baseline for further analysis and tuning.

Next is to assess system performance and any hardware or system bottlenecks while the code runs — this is where the Ampere System Profiler (ASP) is useful to eliminate any system or resource bottlenecks. ASP can also be used to right-size the instance shape and ensure that the compute resources are efficiently consumed by the workload.

One method which may be used is to leverage APB's automated benchmarking framework to start and stop ASP's collectors during the run phase of a given APB benchmark. This ensures that the profile is collected while critical code paths are executed and a clear profile report is generated.

Once system and resource bottlenecks are eliminated, if the performance issue persists and points to CPU cycles not being used efficiently, we propose going to the next step in the pyramid and using the Ampere PMU Profiler to root-cause the issue further.

Finally, system benchmarking should be done after all bottlenecks are resolved or analyzed to effectively measure the system's performance for the workload.

Following this systematic APEX methodology ensures that we eliminate possible issues as part of a structured process to efficiently conduct root cause analysis.

At the microarchitecture level, performance is shaped by how the CPU pipeline handles instruction delivery, execution, and memory access. APP leverages PMU measurements to identify pipeline behavior and stall sources.

APP emphasizes the performance significance of the memory hierarchy. As data access moves from registers to L1 cache, then L2 cache, then L3 cache, and finally DRAM, access becomes exponentially slower. Because of this, cache misses are a primary cause of performance loss. This provides a conceptual foundation for many APP investigations: if a workload touches large working sets or accesses data in a non-contiguous pattern, it may trigger cache misses that increase effective latency and reduce throughput.

APP can be used at the microarchitecture level to understand where stalls might be in the pipeline. The APP role is to collect hardware events related to pipeline stall behavior and to use those events to characterize the workload's execution profile. This capability matters because pipeline stalls and inefficiencies can dominate runtime even when application-level profiling points to a "hot" function without explaining the root cause.

APP is structured around answering questions that cannot be fully resolved with application-level profiling alone. Based on the described APP workflow and report interpretation strategy, APP can help you answer:

APP enables PMU hardware event measurement to provide microarchitecture-level performance insight on Ampere CPUs. It is designed to answer the "why" behind performance problems by identifying microarchitectural causes such as inefficient instruction fetching and data cache misses, which are difficult to detect through application-level profiling alone.

The APP workflow is top-down and hypothesis-driven: form a hypothesis from the hot function, measure with APP profiles, then analyze using the APP HTML report with TDA sunburst charts to characterize where cycles are being spent (instruction retirement, frontend bound, backend bound). APP is most valuable when system-level bottlenecks have been characterized or ruled out and microarchitecture-level explanation is required for expert tuning.

#10515. A “quantum bath” puts quantum entanglement on autopilot

Future quantum computers may depend on the ability to connect widely separated modules through distributed entanglement. Until now, creating this kind of connection has generally required active control and repeated measurements. Physicists at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) have now demonstrated a fully autonomous alternative based on a "quantum bath" made from correlated particles of light.

Published in Physical Review X, the experiment provides the first demonstration of a prediction proposed more than 20 years ago. The approach could eventually offer a new foundation for practical quantum technologies.

Entanglement is one of the defining phenomena of quantum physics. It allows particles or systems to share correlations that cannot be explained by classical physics. Creating distributed entanglement between physically separated qubits (quantum bits) could be important for building larger quantum computers and future quantum networks.

Previous attempts to entangle distant qubits have generally followed one of two strategies. One method sends a single, actively controlled photon from one qubit to another. Another has each qubit emit a photon, with the two photons then matched in an effort to generate entanglement.

The second approach was recognized by the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. However, it still depends on repeated measurements and post-selection, and even then, the process does not always successfully produce entanglement.

PhD student Alejandro Andrés-Juanes and professor Johannes Fink at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) worked with international collaborators to develop a different solution. Their system uses a quantum bath that automatically brings distant qubits into synchronization. In a prototype device, the researchers used a shared source of correlated light particles to entangle two separated qubits, experimentally realizing an idea that had remained theoretical for more than two decades.

Quantum entanglement can take several forms. Continuous-variable entangled states can be produced efficiently and are therefore relatively accessible. They can be compared with a pendulum, whose position and momentum change continuously.

Many useful quantum technologies, however, depend on "discrete-variable" systems. These involve 'all-or-nothing' forms of entanglement that stationary qubits can use. The challenge for the ISTA team was finding a way to connect these readily available continuous forms of entanglement with the discrete forms needed for practical applications.

"In this work, we aimed to overcome this mismatch between the readily available and the practically useful forms of entanglement," says Andrés-Juanes. "By stabilizing the entangled states remotely, our approach is fully autonomous and requires no active control or measurement."

A Quantum Bath Powered by Correlated Light

Maintaining both entanglement and quantum coherence is one of the major difficulties facing quantum computing.

The researchers addressed that problem by making the qubits' surrounding environment itself responsible for producing and stabilizing entanglement.

"In our method, the quantum bath -- meaning the qubits' environment -- is the source of entanglement. It creates a new ground state through a continuous stream of correlated photons," says Fink. "This way, the entangled qubit state is stabilized, even beyond the qubits' own 'lifetime', and remains always available as a resource for further quantum processing. This makes the approach conceptually significant."

Because the entangled state remains available, researchers can access it whenever it is needed. That differs from temporary entanglement, which has to be used during the brief period when it exists.

To couple the qubits with the entangled photon source, the researchers relied on microwave photons. These low-energy light particles are especially useful for manipulating quantum information and are already central to leading superconducting-qubit technology.

Optical photons serve a different role and are commonly used in optics and atomic physics. They may also become important for carrying quantum information between distant quantum computers through fiber optics, an area that the Fink group at ISTA is also investigating.

The researchers needed to confirm that the two qubits were actually synchronized inside the quantum bath. To do that, they used quantum tomography, a technique that reconstructs a quantum system by examining many different 'slices' of its behavior.

"Qubits can be in a superposition of states, but all these states collapse when we measure them, leaving us with a 0 or 1 state," says Andrés-Juanes.

Quantum tomography allowed the researchers to perform measurements lasting only 20-80 nanoseconds and use those observations to investigate the qubits' underlying states. A nanosecond is one billionth of a second.

A 20-Year Prediction Becomes an Experiment

By successfully entangling two isolated qubits through a quantum bath, the ISTA researchers created a proof-of-concept laboratory prototype for the long-standing theoretical proposal.

"We present a relatively simple method that could be scaled up to synchronize multiple distant qubits," says Andrés-Juanes.

The new approach is promising, but it is not yet as efficient as methods that actively control qubit states. "Our method currently transfers about 10% of the bath's available entanglement."

The researchers suggest that one reason the idea took more than two decades to demonstrate is that the original theory was developed under idealized conditions that are difficult to reproduce experimentally.

"Our experiments helped us reveal several factors that may have prevented scientists from designing a functional quantum bath using a single source of correlated photons for distributed entanglement," says Fink.

The prototype developed at ISTA could provide new opportunities for quantum-optics experiments. It may also contribute to efforts to expand quantum processors and ultimately move them closer to fault-tolerant operation.

#10514. The 13 scariest, spookiest video games you should play this Halloween

The nights are drawing in, which can only mean one thing: more bed. But also the impending frights and sights of All Hallow's Eve. Yes, the season of good fear is upon us again, summoning visions of cardboard box robot costumes and other, more devilish things.

And in the spirit of it all, we've crowded around the ouija board to spirit up a list of our horror game favourites - playable on PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 1 & 2, and VR - that might just sate your macabre appetites this Halloween. Some are scary, some are grim, others offer milder - but no less spooky - chills. We'll be doing a smattering of other spooky stuff as the week goes on, but if you're looking for more recommendations, we did a different horror list last year. And if you've your own favourites, please do share them below!

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

Where better to start then with Resident Evil, one of the granddaddies of survival horror gaming? And Resident Evil Requiem is, as much as anything, a celebration of the series as it turns 30. If Resident Evil is a series of two halves - one part campy action, one part genuine scares - Requiem is the perfect tribute, and when it leans heavily into horror in its sublime opening hours, it's genuinely terrifying. New protagonist Grace Ashcroft is the perfect accompaniment as she leads these first-person segments, roaming a wonderfully atmospheric Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Centre and dealing with some very human zombies who, disturbingly, don't yet seem to realise they're dead. Then comes series stalwart Leon S. Kennedy, roundhouse kicking and quipping to ease the tension in intermittent third-person interludes before it's back into the scares. Eventually, the horror gives way to heavier action, but then go on the party hats for a final stretch of glorious fan-service that feels entirely deserved. It's not only a great Resi game, it's one of the best games this year.

Silent Hill, another grandaddy of the survival horror genre, has always been the moodier of the two big series, trading Resident Evil's B-movie thrills for quieter, more ambient psychological scares. And it's the same story with this year's Silent Hill Townfall, which - continuing the trend established by last year's marvellous Japan-set Silent Hill F - shifts the fog-shrouded action again, this time to a small Scottish island blighted by tragedy. Developer Screen Burn, known for the acclaimed likes of Stories Untold and Observation, takes some big swings here, trading the series' classic third-person perspective for a more intimate first-person one, and shifting the focus from erratic gunplay to stealth. It also tells an unexpectedly gritty and very British tale as it jumps between multiple protagonists. The result is an effective, affecting, and relentlessly suffocating piece of horror. It's not perfect, proving perhaps a bit too relentless, but few series remain this exciting, and so willing to reinvent themselves, after nearly three decades.

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

What Little Nightmares originator Tarsier Studios did next. Having stepped away from the horror series that made its name a few years back, Tarsier returned earlier this year with a fresh macabre offering that, on paper at least, doesn't sound like much of a departure at all. Much like Little Nightmares, Reanimal follows the adventure of two lovable, spindly-limbed moppets - here, Boy and Girl - lost in a hellish, hostile world players traverse by scrambling over platforms, solving light puzzles, and fleeing horrifying entities during the big crescendo moments. What sets it apart, however, is the sumptuous cinematic flair of presentation and a much darker mood: in Reanimal, Little Nightmares' Burton-esque whimsy gives way to a bleaker, more vicious - and undoubtedly more violent - vision that's often genuinely disturbing. That darkness is somewhat alleviated by the comfort of two-player co-op, but however you choose to play, Tarsier's latest is a treat. A game of phenomenal mood and artistry, as striking as it is enigmatic, and a wonderfully grim accompaniment for Halloween.

If the name sounds familiar but the game does not, that might be because developer David Szymanski's Iron Lung was turned into a movie earlier this year by none other than YouTuber Markiplier. And even if you've seen the film adaptation, the original game is worth checking out; it's a masterclass in lo-fi horror that's quite unlike anything else. Early on, Iron Lung seals you into a squalid submersible and plunges you into a blood ocean on a distant alien world. Your goal is to chart its labyrinthine depths - an unknowable expanse of suffocating darkness and silence - searching for several points of interest. The problem? No windows. Instead, you're forced to rely on the tiny, murky image of the world outside beamed onto the submersible's TV screen; the darkness so overbearing, all you can see are the glimpses of strangeness caught in your floodlights. As such, movement becomes a game of blind micro-bursts and cautious rotations, as you sporadically consult your map. That's stressful enough, but Iron Lung plays some clever tricks; its stellar sound design increasingly suggesting something terrible lurks in the darkness. Slowly, the tension reaches suffocating, unbearable heights, and you'll frankly be glad it only takes 45-minutes or so to complete.

Ghost Town's biggest roadblock is the fact it's a VR-exclusive game. But if you've got the means to check it out, it's a gem. Ghost Town is the work of Fireproof Games, and it shares some similarities with the studio's earlier, acclaimed The Room series - particularly in its love of tactile puzzle boxes and contraptions. But Ghost Town is far more ambitious, building a propulsive urban fantasy adventure around its core puzzling, and plunging players into a brilliantly evocative recreation of 1983 London as protagonist and ghost hunter Edith Penrose hunts for her missing brother. As the grimy streets of the capital make way for the craggy seclusion of the North Sea, and, eventually, strange realms beyond, it's wonderfully spooky stuff - full of great writing, captivating world-building, endearing characters, fantastic puzzles, and some magnificently imaginative set-pieces - there's a bit with a lighthouse trapped in time thanks to a troubled spirit that's a real highlight. This one's for you if you've ever suspected dark arts were occurring on the London Underground.

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

It's 1879 and you, private investigator Declan Ward, have been summoned to a remote, rain-lashed corner of western Ireland in search of a young woman named Evelyn Deane. It's a journey that brings you to the titular Blake Manor, now a grand hotel, where the turnips - historically accurate jack-o'-lanterns, if you were wondering - are out in force. We are, you see, three days from All Hallow's Eve, and the hotel is bustling with guests: spiritualists, mentalists, naysayers, and more; here to witness the Grand Séance and a never-before-seen attempt to commune with the dead. All, perhaps, also know something about Evelyn Dean's whereabouts. Soon enough, the detective work begins, and you 'll start sniffing around empty rooms and tantalising corners, searching for discarded notes, newspaper clippings, and other useful clues. You'll also want to interrogate the guests as they move around the house according to their hourly schedule. But every action nudges the clock on further, meaning you'll need to spend your time wisely as awful calamity approaches. Soon new secrets, new mysteries, begin to emerge, and as the clockwork rhythms of day make way for the nightmarish hallucinations of night, is anyone safe?

A tribute to a Doom modder's childhood friend, replicating the family home they used to play together in. As Myhouse.wad creator Veddge explained when he first shared the acclaimed level on the DoomWorld forums back in 2023, an unfinished, work-in-progress version of the house was found on a floppy disc gifted to him inside a box of his dead friend's belongings. A journal included in the download file explains more about the mod's somewhat difficult creation - an endeavour Veddge chose to undertake to honour his friend's memory. But the effort was undoubtedly worth it - as is the slight faff of getting Myhouse.wad to run if you're new to Doom things - and it serves as a simple but touching tribute to friendship across its ten minutes of nostalgic 90s FPS playtime. Only... what's that looking through the window on the ground floor? And was that door in the hallway always there?

Really, you could pluck any Rusty Lake game out of the 18 or so released across the series' ten years of existence, and you'd be in for a grimly macabre treat. But Servant of the Lake is developer Rusty Lake's latest offering, taking players back to 1839, where they've been hired to serve the troubled Vanderboom family across an increasingly strange three-day reunion. Servant of the Lake isn't quite as ambitious as some of the series' other games, such as 2022's excellent co-op mysteryThe Past Within. But what it lacks in structural and narrative experimentation, it makes up for in puzzles, serving up an enjoyably refined take on the series' deceptively clever mix of casual point-and-click adventuring, room-escape-style puzzling, and fascinatingly fragmented, centuries-spanning narrative. And oh yes, it's weird, as its bucolic vistas and gentle bird song gradually give way to blood and butchery, and the comforting logic of reality dims. Sure, it's more darkly amusing than outright disturbing, but Rusty Lake still calls for fresh meat this Halloween.

Probably not one for the faint of heart, Horses gained infamy after being banned by Steam and then Epic Games last year. It all unfolds across two weeks on a farm where humans are kept, masked and naked, in filthy captivity - a grim sight that goes completely unacknowledged for a surprisingly long time as you perform your daily tasks of gardening, woodchopping, and so on to satisfy the farmer's demands. Soon enough, though, Horses charges full-tilt into the grotesque. But while it'll probably make you gasp, and definitely make you squirm; its shocks are comparatively tame. Instead, writer and director Andrea Lucco Borlera's gleefully odd first-person narrative horror - developed in conjunction with Saturnalia studio Santa Ragione - gains its power from its wholly unique ambience, where surreal, slapstick comedy collides with arthouse experimentalism to create a thoroughly destabilising mood. All this, and it has something meaningful to say - not bad for £4.

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

As a game, Hellraiser Revival is wobbly at best, particularly in its opening hours where its wonky gunplay and undercooked stealth never quite coalesce. That means its real-world bits - which include a lengthy stay in a dildo-strewn BDSM club - have a tendency to drag. But when the Labyrinth intermittently calls, developer Sabre Interactive pulls out all the stops. As Hellraiser Revival protagonist Aiden enters this confounding realm - an Escher-esque, non-Euclidean nightmare of piercing chains and endless, impossibly configured stone that serves as home to the Cenobites and their demonic deity Leviathan - the dull, uneven combat gives way to puzzles, platforming, and wonderfully orchestrated pursuit sequences. And it makes the whole thing worthwhile. Slowly, as the line between the Labyrinth and the real-world blurs - and as Saber starts to have more fun with its combat tools - it gets considerably more engaging. Revival and its endless tableaus of horrifically rended flesh are definitely, absolutely not for the squeamish, but Hellraiser fans - and anyone looking for a bit of body horror nastiness - should get a kick out of this one.

Platforms: Meta Quest, PC, PS5, PSVR2, Xbox Series X/S, Switch

Back in 2023, Vertigo Games released a genuinely brilliant remake of developer Trilobytes' seminal 90s CD-ROM adventure, The 7th Guest, for VR. I loved it, and spent many happy hours roaming evil toymaker Henry Stauf's wonderfully eerie mansion, reimagined in new-fangled, fully explorable 3D. Its puzzle made some clever use of VR's 1:1 movement capabilities, and its cast - bringing to life the ill-fated guests of Stauf's macabre soiree - were a blast, hitting exactly the right level of camp and presented using some kind of volumetric witchcraft, letting you walk around their apparitions despite being live-action and FMV. It's great, spooky fun for puzzle fans - even if you're not familiar with the original - but its VR requirements meant it couldn't be enjoyed by all. Well, earlier this year, Vertigo released a non-VR version for Xbox, PS5, and PC. And while it loses a little in translation to flatscreens and standard controls, it's still an enjoyable way to enjoy a cult-classic.

Well, it's solitaire, isn't it? Only, that's not entirely true. Forbidden Solitaire is a clever bit of found media horror, inviting players to explore the titular CD-ROM game - an imagined relic of the short-lived 90s multimedia boom in which the games industry convinced itself the future was lurid colour palettes, awkward pre-rendered polygons, and juddery grainy FMV. Developer Night Signal Entertainment and Grey Alien Games capture the era perfectly as you begin to investigate the enigmatic game, which - as your sister quickly informs you over DM during the game's 2019-set narrative framing device - was embroiled in controversy on release, not least because of its disturbing links to gruesome unexplained deaths. Forbidden Solitaire's fictional history is told across police records, press clippings, 90s local news reports, grisly photos, and even a pitch-perfect VHS recording of a cheesy true-crime-style mystery show. But the majority of your time is spent playing Forbidden Solitaire itself, lost in a ghoulish labyrinth said to grant immortality to those that can reach the end. But of course all is not as it seems. Forbidden Solitaire is a wonderfully creepy haunted media yarn, and - wholly unexpectedly - plays a damn good game of solitaire too.

For a while, it looked like Routine might not make it. First announced in 2012, it vanished into the kind of development hell that rarely results in anything good. But Routine isn't just good, it's great; a cracking first-person sci-fi horror that's got a particularly old-school vibe. Routine's tale of ancient influences and rogue AI takes place on a retro-futuristic lunar resort where the lo-fi 80s tech lends proceedings a disorientatingly anachronistic flavour. Here, adverts for VHS recorders flash up on chunky CRT screens as you ride the sleek transportation train, and the mall, with its futuristic pre-fab curves, meets an explosion of neon and plastic palms. Routine is refreshingly unforthcoming about what to do and where to go; giving you a loose objective, your C.A.T. device - a wonderfully tactile gadget that's half maintenance gun, half PDA - then just sending you off to explore. Unfortunately, the resort is kaput; full of flickering lights and ominous shadows. Still worse are the Terminator-like security bots, always primed to give chase when they spy you - their relentless footsteps reaching a horrifying crescendo behind you. It's a game of claustrophobic stealth and panicked pursuits - and that's just for starters. You're about to have a very bad shift.

#10512. Alabama high school offering $180K to coach struggling football team

An Alabama high school is offering up to $180,000 a year for a new football coach, nearly three times what the state’s average teacher earns.

Dothan High School is looking for someone to turn its struggling football program into a championship contender, and the school district is prepared to pay big money to make it happen.

According to an official job posting published October 28, Dothan City Schools is offering between $150,000 and $180,000 annually for its next head football coach, depending on experience.

For comparison, the average Alabama teacher earns $62,659 annually, according to figures reported by AL.com in February 2026. Starting salaries for first-year teachers were just $47,600 during the 2025-26 school year.

That means the school’s highest advertised coaching salary is approximately 2.9 times the statewide teacher average and nearly four times the starting pay for a new educator.

The job description makes it clear that the district expects results for that money. Applicants must have a proven record of winning football games, making playoff appearances and developing championship-caliber teams.

The position is also a full-time, 12-month role, with the district offering additional salary supplements to attract offensive and defensive coordinators.

Dothan’s search comes after former head coach Jed Kennedy resigned in September following a 2-3 start to the season. Kennedy finished his tenure with a 29-19 record, while the Wolves ended their 2026 regular season at 3-7.

The district hopes to have its new coach in place by late February 2027, according to Yahoo Sports.

College offers to pay students’ tuition if they can watch a full football game

Rivals starts charging high school athletes $500 for scouting evaluations and ranking consideration

High school football coach fired after “one in a million” kick hits player in groin

The unusually high coaching salary highlights the money surrounding high school football, where expectations can be enormous.

Just weeks earlier, a high school football coach was fired after his team took a 63-0 lead in a game that was ultimately called off at halftime.

For Dothan, the message is clear: The district is prepared to spend big to build a winning football program. Whether that investment delivers a championship remains to be seen.

#10511. AI fan wikis riddled with errors are muddying the waters of an already contested part of games culture

"These tools have made it very easy for bad actors to crowd out good information..."

Recently, I was writing a piece about Nighthawks and wanted to remind myself of some basic information about the companion characters. As I have a thousand times before, I put the question into Google and clicked the first result: the Nighthawks Wiki.

Of course, wikis aren't necessarily reliable, especially fan-run projects that might not have enough engaged individuals to immediately spot and fix errors. But the "Nighthawks Wiki" that I landed on immediately and obviously had deeper issues. Firstly, it wasn't a wiki at all. Rather than being editable by anybody, this website only invited "corrections" by email. Secondly, it was full of false information that didn't seem likely to have been added by fans getting their facts slightly wrong, like listing companions and skills that don't exist. It also regularly included unrelated information about the 1981 movie and the Edward Hopper painting, both of the same name, and listed them in its "sources" even when they had no relevance to the page in question.

I don't like to accuse anybody of using generative AI, because its hallmarks are difficult to pin down and are often misattributed to the LLM rather than the human writers it rips off – ask any of us how much we enjoy the em-dash, for example. But, interest piqued by the rate and intensity of apparently made up facts, I managed to trace the domain name to a website building service called Spaceship, which also offers an "AI Website builder." (I emailed the address on the "wiki" for comment, but the message bounced.)

A quick search turned up many more similar sites, some of which were actually editable as wikis and others which only called themselves by that name. They typically targeted indie games without gigantic playerbases – the sort of game that people might seek out help with and not find a thriving community ready to provide it.

It's a problem that Tim Bender, CEO for publishing company Hooded Horse, knows well. Unlike most publishers, Hooded Horse creates wikis for their own games, working with fans to make sure they're well-populated with useful information. But lately the company has had to "play whack-a-mole" with AI-generated sites competing for the search results and providing inaccurate information. One of these, for example, appeared for their game Corsair Cove, but was actually part of a more than 20 game scattershot collection operated by a site called GameDB, which the creator admitted to using generative AI to make. "[Generative AI] enables a run of basically commercial enterprises to mass produce and try to flood the search engine results of games to soak up their traffic," says Bender. Attempts to reach GameDB for comment via their public contact email resulted in an error, stating "the remote server is misconfigured".

And the combination of elbowing out legitimate wikis and being full of incorrect information ends up with a lot of frustrated players. "The whole purpose of putting out a wiki is so when [players] search for help, they end up at a site that helps them. And instead we continually hear from players who stumbled up on these things and got confused and are wondering what's going on," says Bender.

That collection of genAI wikis includes one for the 100-player FPS Wardogs; one of at least five that FlamingMojo, a member of the Independent Game Wiki Network, saw appear in the days after the game's release in September. And he says that the frustration the genAI-created sites causes players also impacts those who are trying to do the legitimate work of creating and maintaining these volunteer-led resources: "It's hurt our reputation, as players have been misinformed but we haven't created or updated the relevant page yet so they bounce off [wikis] entirely."

Fanwikis are already a contested part of games culture. Hosting sites like Fandom dominate the space, and have themselves introduced AI features that had to be rolled back due to their inaccuracies and unpopularity. Many groups have decided to leave these hosts, but those who go independent often struggle to show up in Google's search rankings underneath the competition from the umbrella sites.

Whether on a hosting site or independent, fans rarely make any money from the effort they put into their wikis. Either they sacrifice any ad revenue to the bigger platforms, or they pay for their own hosting, which is rarely covered by ads or donations. FlamingMojo, for example, pays for the Dune: Awakening Community Wiki out of his own pocket and doesn't run any ads on it.

But counterintuitively, the low profitability of these kinds of sites only leads to worse outcomes when generative-AI versions are concerned. "There's not that much ad revenue, but there's going to be a little bit and that's all it takes," says Bender. "Because the barrier is so low, why not just spew out a mountain of it and flood the search results?"

It's also possible the generative-AI sites are sometimes aiming for outcomes beyond a little ad revenue. "Some of them, you don't know what data they're collecting," says Bender. In at least one case, a generative-AI site was pointing users to download additional software that offers a paid subscription. The software had been reviewed poorly online and opening the website caused my malware software to kick in and warn me it had been flagged as "potentially unsafe." (None of the sites I attempted to contact for comment responded to my emails.)

Independent wikis also now shoulder a double burden, as generative AI scrapers send huge amounts of traffic their way, potentially affecting site stability. Publicly available internal data from the Dune: Awakening Community Wiki shows 7m requests in a 30 day period from AI crawlers. (5m of these come from Meta alone. While FlamingMojo is able to tame other scrapers using files that direct them to real pages rather than brute-force trying every link, he's found that Meta simply "hammers every page multiple times per second" with no care for "any sensible ratelimits.") These scraping waves hit smaller wikis particularly hard, as their maintainers aren't necessarily expecting huge amounts of traffic and don't have the compute capacity to handle huge spikes in visitors.

"Independent gaming wikis are in a difficult place," says FlamingMojo. As well as competition for SEO, both from corporate sites and now genAI, he says server costs have increased between three- and ten-fold, again due to the impact of genAI. Building a group of people who want to volunteer their time and energy to keep a resource updated isn't easy, although the Dune: Awakening Community Wiki has found success through gamifying contributions, in affiliation with the developer giving out in-game rewards.

And, Bender points out, all of this is happening within a much wider context of genAI's impact on the availability of information. "In a more fundamental way … these tools have made it very easy for bad actors to flood things and crowd out good information which people put dedicated time into. This is just one example of a much broader struggle that, honestly, whatever frustration I feel for this on my end, I'm sure you [journalists] feel at a thousand times that."

But it's possible that, by being one part of the wider issue, fanwiki culture could also hold a sliver of the bigger solution. "The way we survive the AI pollution is with community," says FlamingMojo. "Many people chipping in a small bit, and feeling a sense of shared ownership."

#10509. YouTuber WILDCAT says YouTubers are “underrated” compared to streaming stars

YouTuber WILDCAT believes that YouTubers as a whole are “underrated” compared to streamers, given that you don’t really see YouTube content outside of the platform.

For years, if you wanted to be a content creator on the internet, having a successful YouTube channel was your best bet. Now, there are plenty of other routes to take, including becoming a livestreamer across Twitch, Kick, TikTok, and beyond.

YouTube is still the go-to for a lot of creators, but streaming dominates the zeitgeist a little more, seeing as clips of different streamers are everywhere.

That is one of the reasons why WILDCAT believes YouTubers are “underrated” compared to streamers.

Speaking to Dexerto, the Vanoss Gaming crew member said: “Outside of MrBeast and a handful of like the biggest ones, I feel like there is such a focus on streamers, whether it be Twitch, Kick, IRL, these people that keep going viral on Twitter and TikTok because their random clips are blowing up all the time.”The gaming creator noted that YouTube has done a “really good job” at “encapsulating” content on the platform – be it long-form videos, Shorts, or streams. “There’s no reason to really pull that stuff outside of the platform,” he added.

“I just think YouTubers in general are underrated at the moment. There are some people pulling crazy numbers doing crazy things.”

WILDCAT pointed to “lawnmowing channels” that people have “never heard of” getting “five million views” on videos as another example as well.

In the past, creators like Disguised Toast have said that solely being focused on YouTube is “harder” than streaming, as the latter has become more mainstream over the years.

#10508. Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster

Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings. The longer a quantum operation takes to complete, the more time there is for those errors to build up. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now developed a method that can perform a broad range of advanced quantum operations more than a thousand times faster. The advance tackles a major obstacle in the field and could help move quantum computing closer to becoming fault-tolerant.

Quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics. Before that can happen, however, these machines need to become much more dependable.

A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects. Electrical noise, cosmic radiation, and overheating can all introduce errors while information is being processed.

Traditional computers can experience errors too, but decades of development have produced reliable error correction methods that can quickly detect and repair them. Quantum systems are much harder to protect because the information they use is extraordinarily delicate.

"The fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, known as qubits, are so sensitive that even the smallest disturbance can cause the quantum state to deviate from the target, resulting in the loss of information. If too many errors accumulate before they can be corrected, the computation can fail," says Lei Du, researcher in Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, and lead author of the theoretical study published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

A Different Way to Protect Quantum Information

To make quantum computing more resilient and eventually fault-tolerant, researchers are investigating new ways to shield quantum information from errors. One promising strategy uses so-called bosonic quantum codes*.

Instead of assigning quantum information to individual qubits, this approach stores it in microwave fields inside superconducting circuits.

"Rather than storing quantum information in individual qubits, bosonic codes encode information in the microwave fields found within superconducting circuits. This approach has been shown to provide stronger protection against certain types of errors," explains Tangyou Huang, researcher in Quantum Technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Quantum Operations More Than 1,000 Times Faster

Working with bosonic quantum codes is not simple. Creating and controlling the required quantum states has traditionally involved guiding a quantum system through thousands of repeated driving cycles.

That process can take considerable time, and every additional cycle creates another opportunity for outside disturbances to interfere with the calculation. In quantum computing, speed is therefore closely tied to reliability.

Chalmers researchers Lei Du and Tangyou Huang have now proposed a different strategy. Rather than constructing the desired quantum states one small piece at a time, their method can perform a wide variety of operations much faster.

"Our method shows that a diverse range of quantum operations on bosonic states can be completed within a single driving cycle, rather than the several thousand cycles that have been required previously. This makes the operations both faster and more efficient, while reducing the risk that disturbances will corrupt the information before the process is finished. It represents an important step towards fault-tolerant quantum computers," says Lei Du.

The new approach is built around Quantum lattice gates, a recently proposed universal set of quantum gates developed by the same research team.

These gates act somewhat like shortcuts. Instead of requiring a long sequence of repeated control steps, they can allow the intended quantum operation to be completed in just one driving cycle. That could make the process faster, simpler, and less vulnerable to errors.

"You can think of it like building a large Lego castle. Instead of assembling it brick by brick and risking mistakes along the way, quantum lattice gates act like pre-built Lego modules that can be connected quickly and efficiently," says Tangyou Huang.

Designed for Superconducting Quantum Computers

The technique is especially well suited to superconducting quantum computers, which are among the most prominent technologies being developed in the international push toward large-scale quantum computing.

Chalmers University of Technology is also using superconducting technology as it develops a 100-qubit quantum computer.

"A key advantage of our approach is that it can be implemented using existing superconducting quantum circuit platforms. We are already discussing possible experimental realizations with colleagues at Chalmers, and we hope to see a demonstration of the method in the near future," says Tangyou Huang.

The researchers say the work addresses a central problem facing the field: efficiently producing and controlling quantum states that are capable of helping correct errors.

"Our results address one of the major bottlenecks in the field: how to quickly and reliably create and control the error-correcting quantum states that could play an important role in future quantum computers," says Lei Du.

More About Bosonic Codes, Quantum Lattice Gates and Floquet Control

*Bosonic quantum codes store quantum information in the states of, for example, microwave or optical resonators rather than in individual qubits. They are considered a promising tool for quantum error correction because they can provide built-in protection against certain types of errors.

Quantum operations are needed to process that stored information. Quantum lattice gates are a recently proposed collection of basic building blocks that can be used to control bosonic quantum states. By combining and designing these gates, researchers can carry out a wide range of more complicated quantum operations.

One method for implementing these operations is known as Floquet control, which uses periodic control signals to drive a quantum system. Earlier Floquet-based techniques have generally depended on slower processes involving many repeated driving cycles. The approach developed at Chalmers can instead perform quantum lattice gates directly in a single driving cycle, making some operations more than a thousand times faster.

The scientific paper "Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates" has been published in Physical Review Letters. The authors are Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo. The researchers are affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and Tianjin University in China.

The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT), and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

Materials provided by Chalmers University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
