#10492. Brazil football match sets record with 51 red cards after massive brawl involving chairs & stretchers

A football match in Brazil descended into absolute chaos after a massive brawl involving players, coaches, and even ball boys resulted in a staggering 51 red cards, with police later called to the stadium.

The incident occurred on November 1 during an Under-20 championship semifinal between Uberlândia and Mamoré at the Parque do Sabiá Stadium in Minas Gerais.

Mamoré was leading 3-1 deep into stoppage time when a goal celebration sparked a confrontation that quickly spiraled out of control.

According to Brazilian outlet O Tempo, Mamoré player Davi Fernandes Bittencourt made provocative gestures and shouted insults toward the opposing bench.

Uberlândia’s goalkeeping coach, Paulo Sérgio Dias dos Santos, then reportedly stormed onto the field and pushed Bittencourt, triggering an all-out brawl that looked more like something out of a hockey game than a football match.

Players and coaching staff began exchanging punches and kicks, with footage showing chairs and even stretchers being thrown during the violence.

The referee’s report also claimed that six ball boys joined the fighting, attacking players and staff with punches, kicks, and thrown objects.

Referee Fernando Patrick Drosghic Modesto ultimately abandoned the match, recording 48 additional dismissals in his official report because the chaos prevented him from showing the cards on the field.

As ge.globo reported, three players had already been sent off before the brawl, bringing the final total to 51.

Of those dismissed, 43 were players and eight were members of the coaching staffs.

“Upset” man warned by police after kicking 9-year-old player during football game

Soccer match goes viral after loose ball flies into traffic and causes crash

Richard Lewis: Gaules’ actions lead to harassment and it needs to stop

The trouble didn’t end on the pitch, either.

Military police were called after the match following reports of vandalism in the visiting team’s locker room.

Officers discovered approximately 14 damaged doors, along with broken sinks, toilets, showers, electrical installations, and furniture. Two hot tubs were also reportedly damaged. No arrests were made.

Remarkably, the match had already been suspended for around 40 minutes earlier in the second half after Uberlândia officials confronted the referee over another dismissal. The official subsequently reported receiving threats.

The 51 dismissals comfortably surpass the previous Guinness World Record of 36 red cards, set in 2011 during an Argentine fifth-division match between Atlético Claypole and Victoriano Arenas.

A post shared by TMC Esporte (@tmcesporte)

However, Guinness has not yet officially updated its record to recognize the Brazilian incident.

It’s also not the first time football has produced bizarre scenes this year. In March, masked fans sabotaged a VAR monitor during a German match, while streamer IShowSpeed was forced to leave an Algerian football game after spectators began throwing objects at him.

Uberlândia and Mamoré are scheduled to meet again on November 8, although the unprecedented number of dismissals could create major complications for both teams.

#10491. Designing Maintainable CSS Architecture: A Practical Guide to Scalable Stylesheets

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

CSS is easy to write when a website contains only a handful of components. As an application grows, however, stylesheets can become difficult to manage. A change intended for one button may affect several unrelated components; repeated declarations accumulate, and developers begin adding increasingly specific selectors to override earlier rules.

These problems are rarely caused by CSS itself. They often result from unclear styling conventions, poorly defined component boundaries, and a lack of consistent decisions about how styles should be organized.

A maintainable CSS architecture provides a predictable structure for writing, extending, and debugging styles. It does not require a particular framework or a complicated build process. Instead, it relies on clear naming, controlled scope, reusable design tokens, and an understanding of the CSS cascade.

This guide explores practical techniques for creating CSS that remains understandable as a website grows.

A CSS architecture defines how developers organize styles and how different parts of a stylesheet interact.

Without shared conventions, one developer might use deeply nested selectors, another might rely on element IDs, and a third might repeatedly override existing rules. Each approach may work in isolation, but the combined stylesheet becomes harder to reason about.

These selectors repeat the same styling intent while depending on different structural paths. Changes to the HTML can also break the relationship between the selector and its target.

A simpler approach is to give the component a meaningful class:

The shorter selector communicates the styling intent directly and is easier to reuse.

The objective is not to make every selector as short as possible. It is to ensure that selectors express a clear relationship between a component and its presentation.

A growing interface often uses the same colors, spacing values, border radii, and typography rules across multiple components.

Repeating these values throughout a stylesheet makes future changes unnecessarily difficult. CSS custom properties provide a central place for shared design decisions.

If the primary brand color changes, developers can update the token instead of searching through multiple component rules.

Tokens are also useful for implementing themes:

This example changes selected design values for a dark theme. A complete theme should also consider text contrast, interactive states, shadows, and other visual properties rather than changing only three variables.

For smaller websites, a few custom properties may be enough. Larger design systems may benefit from clearly defined token categories for colors, typography, spacing, and component-specific values.

CSS class names should help developers understand which component a rule belongs to and what the rule represents.

One established approach is BEM, which stands for Block, Element, Modifier.

The corresponding classes communicate different roles:

article-card__title identifies an element within that component.

article-card__link--featured Represents a variation of the link.

This convention can make class names more predictable, especially when several developers work on the same project.

However, BEM is a naming convention, not a requirement. Other approaches can work equally well when they are applied consistently. The important consideration is that class names remain understandable and do not depend excessively on the component's current position in the document.

CSS specificity determines how competing selectors are prioritized, alongside factors such as origin, importance, cascade layers, and source order.

Problems arise when developers repeatedly increase specificity to override earlier rules.

The second selector is more specific, which makes later changes harder to manage.

A more maintainable approach is to keep component rules focused:

A modifier class now expresses the intended variation explicitly.

For larger projects, cascade layers can establish a predictable order between groups of styles:

This example declares the intended order of the layers. Normal declarations in later layers take precedence over competing normal declarations in earlier layers, subject to the CSS cascade rules.

Cascade layers can reduce the need for increasingly specific selectors, but developers should understand how layered and unlayered styles interact before introducing them into an existing project.

A maintainable stylesheet structure should help developers find the relevant rules without searching through an enormous file.

For example, a component-oriented project might use this organization:

reset.css normalizes selected browser defaults.

layout.css manages larger page structures.

components/ contains component-specific rules.

utilities.css provides small, reusable helper classes.

This structure is an example rather than a universal template. A small static website may be easier to maintain with one or two stylesheets, while a larger application may benefit from a modular system.

The decision should reflect the project's complexity, team size, build tooling, and expected lifespan.

Splitting CSS into many files without clear responsibilities can create more overhead rather than less.

Responsive styling becomes difficult to maintain when media queries are scattered throughout the codebase without a consistent strategy.

Developers can simplify responsive rules by using flexible layout primitives where possible and reserving media queries for meaningful changes in presentation.

This layout automatically adjusts the number of columns according to the available space.

For typography, a fluid value can reduce the need for multiple font-size breakpoints:

The clamp() function keeps the font size between a minimum and a maximum while allowing it to scale fluidly in between.

These techniques do not eliminate media queries. Navigation patterns, page composition, and other design decisions may still require explicit breakpoints.

A useful architecture distinguishes between properties that can adapt naturally and changes that require a deliberate layout transition.

Interactive components often have several visual states, including hover, focus, active, disabled, and invalid.

If each state is implemented differently across the application, the interface can become inconsistent.

A shared button component can establish predictable behavior:

This example gives the component a consistent baseline and defines visible focus and disabled states.

Developers should still check contrast and keyboard behavior, and ensure that disabled styling is paired with actual disabled functionality where appropriate.

A reusable component should not merely look consistent. It should also behave predictably across the application.

Reusable CSS can reduce duplication, but creating an abstraction for every repeated declaration can make the code harder to understand.

Suppose two components share only a small amount of spacing. Creating a complicated class hierarchy to reuse those few declarations may not provide meaningful value.

On the other hand, a repeated button pattern used across dozens of pages is a strong candidate for a shared component style.

Does this pattern appear in multiple places?

Does it represent a meaningful design concept?

Would a shared rule make future changes easier?

Can the abstraction be understood without tracing several unrelated stylesheets?

If the answers suggest that reuse will improve clarity, a shared rule or component is likely worthwhile.

Otherwise, a straightforward local declaration may be the better choice.

A stylesheet can become difficult to maintain even when its original architecture is sound. New features, temporary overrides, and inconsistent contributions can gradually undermine the conventions.

Automated tools can help enforce standards. Stylelint, for example, can identify certain syntax problems and enforce configurable style rules.

Consistent formatting and naming conventions.

Visual regression tests for important page layouts.

Browser testing at representative viewport sizes.

Accessibility checks for focus visibility and color contrast.

Unused CSS should be removed carefully. A class that appears unused in a static search may be generated dynamically by JavaScript or applied through a content management system.

Similarly, visual regression tests should be interpreted in context because font rendering and browser differences can produce legitimate variations.

The purpose of these practices is to catch unintended changes before they become difficult-to-diagnose production problems.

Maintainable CSS architecture depends on clarity and consistency, not the number of tools or files a project uses. Design tokens centralize shared values, meaningful class names improve readability, controlled specificity reduces conflicts, and sensible stylesheet organization makes components easier to maintain.

Responsive layout primitives and reusable interaction states further reduce duplication, while automated checks help prevent conventions from deteriorating as a project grows.

The most effective architecture is one that fits the actual needs of the website and its developers. By establishing a small set of clear rules and applying them consistently, teams can create stylesheets that remain flexible, understandable, and easier to extend over time.

#10490. Mouthwashing is finally on consoles and Xbox Game Pass, and it's a Halloween must for horror fans

A mutilated man stares at you, his single piercing eye following as you move around the room. His filthy bandages hide a ruined face, raw lips circling disturbingly perfect teeth, and his moans echo through the halls. But that eye: it knows something you don't. At least not yet.

Developed by Wrong Organ, Mouthwashing rightly earned a lot of praise when it was released in 2024; it's an extraordinary first-person horror adventure game placing you among the five-strong crew of the Tulpar, a commercial space freighter part-way through its year-long mission to carry its unknown cargo across the stars. Moments into its dramatic opening scene - "0 days before the crash", we're told - things go dramatically awry, establishing a dire tone and a baseline of dread that only builds from there.

Mouthwashing isn't a game laden with jumpscares; instead it is a masterfully crafted discomfort simulator, conjuring unease through its claustrophobic environmental design, strong audio work, disorientating structure and pacing, and a lo-fi visual style that creates spaces for your imagination to fill.

Slowly, for instance, the Tulpar's already gloomy corridors constrict, shrunk by the crew's increasingly desperate use of repair foam; this continuous degradation of the space around you mirroring the minds of its characters, as circumstances grow increasingly dire. For as enjoyable as Mouthwashing's light puzzling is, you're really here for its unexpectedly impactful story.

This is an intelligent game that trusts its audience, and that's most obvious in its breathless, non-chronological narrative. It's a story that doesn't stay still, that offers no moment to breathe. Scenes transition into each other with a digital datamoshing effect, almost as if you're watching system files recovered long after the fact. And each transition often signals a different, disorientating kind of switch, as it's not always clear when - or even who - you are now.

I don't want to spoil much, but there's a surprising amount of subtlety to the way characters are portrayed and gradually evolve. One crew member, for instance, sleeps near a statue of the shipping company's cartoon mascot, which emits voice lines whenever someone draws near. The reason why isn't spelled out to you, but on a second playthrough, this small act of self-preservation becomes clear. And Mouthwashing only grows more rewarding with each subsequent return as you start to notice this attention to detail more and more.

Speaking of characters, one is particularly deplorable; a truly detestable creature up there with Shepherd from the original Modern Warfare trilogy and perhaps even Eric Sparrow if you're a Tony Hawk's Underground fan. Their narcissist journey, culminating in a spiral of delusion that really made my skin crawl, exemplifies what makes Mouthwashing work so well.

Its horror stems from the psychological disintegration of the Tulpar's crew, and the way the resulting violence unfolds. Violence is sparse and unglorified here, but you're often an active participant, much of the nastiest actions occurring when you're in direct control. It absolutely made me wince a few times.

And then comes the closer; one of the most moving monologues I've heard in a video game. It's a final message - not only to a member of the crew, but to you the player - on taking responsibility. By this point, what's done is done, leaving one - perhaps futile - final decision to make. One last chance for a kind of salvation. For me, it's a message that hit home.

Mouthwashing is powerful stuff, then; a different sort of horror this Halloween. It's an easy recommendation, and has been wowing PC players for a while. As of today, though, it's finally available for consoles - PS4, PS5, Switch, and Xbox Series X/S to be exact - and is out on Game Pass too. Additionally, there's currently 40 percent off on Steam.

#10488. The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics

A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to new ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.

In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.

The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem

The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.

Familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.

In 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.

"What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," says lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena."

Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure

To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.

When laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.

Chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.

"We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials."

Light Responds to Direction and Polarization

The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.

When the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This showed that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a new type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.

"These results open a new direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity."

From Abstract Mathematics to New Optical Physics

The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.

More broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover new ways to control and study light.

Materials provided by Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10486. Dragon Ball Z composer elected Texas Attorney General

A former Dragon Ball Z composer has been elected Texas Attorney General, marking an unlikely career transformation from creating music for Goku and Vegeta to becoming the state’s top lawyer.

Democrat Nathan Johnson defeated Republican Mayes Middleton in the November 3 election, marking the first time in 32 years that a Democrat has been elected Texas Attorney General, with Dan Morales being the last to win the office in 1994.

Johnson, who has served in the Texas Senate since 2019, will take office in January 2027, replacing outgoing Attorney General Ken Paxton.

While his election is a major political upset, anime fans might recognize Johnson’s name from an entirely different career.

Before entering politics, Johnson worked as a composer for Funimation’s English dub of Dragon Ball Z, providing music for the first 67 episodes of the 2005 Ultimate Uncut edition.

He also contributed music to five Dragon Ball Z movies, including Broly: Second Coming, Fusion Reborn, and Wrath of the Dragon.

In a 2012 interview with The Dao of Dragon Ball, Johnson revealed that he had never watched the anime before being hired and initially struggled to connect with its characters and story.

However, he eventually developed an appreciation for the series, particularly through Gohan, whose relationship with his father resonated with Johnson as a parent.

His connection to Dragon Ball Z even became part of his political identity when he first ran for the Texas Senate in 2018.

Speaking to The Dao of Dragon Ball following that election victory, Johnson revealed that younger voters were surprised to discover his anime background.

“Along the way some of them found out about my music background, and specifically about Dragon Ball Z, and they got really excited about it,” he explained.

#10485. Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 review

It's easy to dislike Call of Duty. Aside from the annual cycle of development, marketing, and controversy that has defined the series identity for the past 22 years, the series has become an integral part of how video games prop up the military-industrial complex. Whilst some of the stories - especially 2025's Black Ops 7 - have deteriorated into the realms of science-fiction absurdity, many of the narratives you'll find in the Modern Warfare splinter of the series are more grounded in reality. When you're playing as semi-fictional UK and US troopers, taking part in illegal operations in foreign territory, wantonly executing people over differences in ideology, Call of Duty can feel gross: paper-thin propaganda designed to glorify war and reinforce lines between 'them' and 'us'.

But Modern Warfare 4 shies away from this. A little. The bar is low, granted, but there is a slightly more humanitarian slant to the game this year - aping 2009's No Russian, there are a few missions that plant you into the shoes of the 'enemy', and ask you to make moral choices that, I won't lie, I was rather shocked to see manifest in a CoD game. In 2019, developer Infinity Ward asked what would happen if there was a terrorist attack on the streets of London. In 2022, the studio ponders what happens when a co-ordinated international military operation goes awry on a Mexican oil rig. In 2023, we go to Lower Manhattan as the Russian army stages an attack on the New York Stock Exchange. So, in moving our lens and making us play as a North Korean militiaman, I was genuinely surprised to learn that - if you refuse your orders - you are summarily shot, leaving the rest of the mission to play out in front of your lifeless corpse. There is no 'game over' state for not complying: the horrors carried out by the ruthless regime carry on even in the face of your dereliction of duty. It might be using baby speak, by literary standards, but here I think Call of Duty is trying to make a point.

And it doesn't fall on ears unwilling to listen, either. Just this week, a South Korean politician urged the country's president to play Modern Warfare 4, so striking is its depiction of a theorised North Korean assault on the nation (which makes the dev's inclusion of real disaster footage an even more regrettable gaffe. Whilst it's important to remember that a country's population is not its leadership, the news has been full of North Korean threats and bluster for many years now. And in Modern Warfare 4, Infinity Ward wanted to tell a story "ripped from the headlines". The result is a slightly more 'reactive' setup, where a militarised nation responds to an invasion rather than instigates one, which in turn gives a sense of urgency and speculation that is more agreeable than, say, another shadowy skirmish in the Middle East, or an insurgency into some proxy state secretly controlled by Russia (don't hold your breath).

As we flip back and forth between ex-SAS hard bastard, John Price (who we've been following since 2007) and a ragtag bunch of conscribed South Korean soldiers and US Marine allies that find themselves in the middle of a brutal, casualty-heavy North Korean invasion, we get to see Call of Duty campaign design at its finest. There's a rousing John Wick-inspired shootout in a club that evolves into a parkour dash across Manhattan rooftops. There's a cinematic and genuinely impressive shooting gallery-like encounter in a trainyard that evokes classic arcade lightgun design. There's an expansive open world area that toys with stealth and sniping, there's a car chase through the streets of Paris, and there's a beachhead assault that ties it all together nicely.

Beyond even those, the standout mission is Stranded, which sees the South Korean team deep in enemy territory, fighting for their lives. This introduces crafting for a few missions - something that could feel tacked-on and rote, but is actually deployed like a lever by Infinity Ward to wedge open just how important each of the various tools at your disposal are. Want a thermal scope? Then you're going to prioritise that over more munitions. Want explosives? Then your basic arms will suffer. It serves to emphasise just how well every aspect of Modern Warfare's toolkit complements every other piece, resulting in this rich, deep, interlocking marvel that makes older Call of Duty games look rudimentary in comparison.

This is complemented by setpieces like Traffic, where you engage on a breakneck chase through the streets of Paris in a romp sure to cost the Parisian treasury millions in collateral damage. Here, you get to see the breadth and depth of the enemy AI that Infinity Ward has crafted - which no doubt went hand-in-hand with the new DMZ mode, more on that later - as we witness just how complex the studio's engine can get: destruction, cover mechanics, and so many different kinds of visual effect all rush on-screen at once. It's overwhelming, it's intimidating, it's electrifying. It's peak Call of Duty.

Between these standout missions, there are moments where you're asked to consider what it's like for the pawns on the board - the other soldiers, the unnamed, those whose strings are being pulled by forces they don't understand. It's a bit Fisher-Price, a bit A-Level, a 'War is Bad' pin badge worn on a jacket from an Army Surplus store, but hey: I'd rather this than a completely unobserved 'ooh-rah!' story about the US army coming to the rescue again.

The downside of the campaign comes more from its setup and pacing than its content, then. Price's story wraps up without applause, really - I won't ruin the specifics here, but his actions and what he does to quash the machinations of a very oddly-implemented Mads Mikkelsen are sort of left in the dark to rot, as the desperate resistance of our South Korean recruits takes the spotlight. Again, I think Call of Duty might be trying to say something here: that the morally ambiguous and collateral damage-accumulating actions of one desperate operative that actually saved the world don't get to breathe in the daylight; instead, the 'courageous' defense of privates on the frontline should be lauded. War is messy, no-one is in the right, everyone loses except for the multinationals putting the hardware in the hands of the humans. Is that what I'm supposed to come out of this thinking?

Whatever the emotional impact is, you can't argue with the physical one: this is a tight, eight-hour campaign with moments up there with Modern Warfare's best. It stops before it ever risks getting overlong, it's got plenty of new ideas to throw at you and - played on the hardest mode - it's a tight puzzle box of encounter design that's just as obsessed with detail as it is with Michael Bay-esque spectacle. It's a far cry from whatever the hell was going on in Black Ops 7 last year.

Reeling from the fact I think I nearly felt something during a Call of Duty campaign, I needed to boot up the multiplayer - a mode which has by now been refined into its near-perfect form, an ultra-fast, turbo-injected mosh pit of quick scopes, slide cancels, and kill corridors. Map design is great - of course it is, it's Infinity Ward - and the gunplay is good as it ever has been in the Modern Warfare games. Since 2019, when Infinity Ward went to great expense to rebuild its engine, the Call of Duty experience has been luxurious. The sound design alone is worthy of applause, every clack of a bolt-action lever, every shell casing falling to the floor, every fizz of thermite boring through your cover… it's immediately identifiable and extremely important. To play Modern Warfare 4 without a decent set of headphones or a good surround sound setup is to intentionally handicap yourself.

There are a few qualms, as ever: some respawn mechanics are vexing (especially on quicker, gnarlier maps - this week's addition of Shipment is a hilariously bad example of this), and some of the weapon balancing has yet to be totally calmed down, in part owing to a last-minute change to weapon damage that extends the time-to-kill beyond Infinity Ward's usual fare. Whilst this means there's a bit of chaos for early adopters like myself, it actually speaks to the level of nuance Infinity Ward has to play with: I'd love to see the backend of Modern Warfare 4, with all its knobs and dials, seeing how the studio tweaks and balances guns to keep up with what players are doing. The slightly lower time-to-kill is actually a fascinating experiment in figuring out what Modern Warfare is beyond its selection of guns - and I'd happily take a bit of weird balancing a deeper, more intricate damage system.

Speaking of, the customisation system also works nicely here. With the right attachments, some guns are elevated from 'useful' to 'essential'. The ISO Nightshade SMG seems a bit busted right now, and I keep getting chewed up by suspiciously powerful one-two taps of the Type 73 LMG. I'm a born sharpshooter, and the Oris 8.6 is an early favourite for popping heads across the map, especially dressed up with a 2.1x scope with thermal imagine. The overall economy of guns and range-versus-power feels a bit off as it stands - and is quite literally being addressed as I type - but I'm playing multiplayer in launch week, so there's always going to be some friction.

Then there's Kill Block: an experimental and dynamic rotating multiplayer map and mode concept. It's absurd in its pitch: by using a selection of 'slabs', it can form 500+ unique combinations of map, meaning no match plays out quite like the last. Maps in Call of Duty are (in)famously defined by their sight lines; if you stand here, you can shoot someone there. If you camp this corner, you'll rack up kills. If you snipe on this lane, you'll collect greenhorn scalps a-plenty. Kill Block turns all that on its head, forcing players to be more reactive, and engage more with the systems on offer in Modern Warfare 4, rather than rely on instincts baked in from two-plus decades of CoD. With the promise of more modular elements to come - from fan-favourite maps like Crash, for instance - I can see this mode and setup becoming yet another staple in the ever-expanding Call of Duty canon. This is how you breathe life into the more competitive-focused modes that often fail to shine alongside respawn-focused experiences like Team Deathmatch.

I have to praise the complexity and wizardry Infinity Ward has displayed with how the guns handle; each attachment is meaningful, most guns feel unique, and the feedback you get from firing any armament is exquisite. It has all the production value of a dedicated military sim, but in action it's readable and almost arcade-like in its simplicity. No one does it like Infinity Ward, and even though this feels like an iteration on the last three Modern Warfare games, I won't knock the developers down for staying in their lane and developing a formula that works.

And that brings us to DMZ. Initially, I was cynical. 'This is Call of Duty chasing the bag', I thought. 'This is trend-chasing gone awry'. But Infinity Ward is not afraid of change, and I shouldn't be either. The extraction shooter trend shows no signs of abating, and with even Call of Duty managing to make it work within the specific arcade-cum-sim setup of its engine, I need to accept that. I don't think it's a stretch to say DMZ could be a standalone game - packed with enough to go toe-to-toe with the likes of Marathon or Arc Raiders.

Simplified controls, motion sensor functionality, deadzone/trigger customisation, vibration/trigger effects, reduce tinnitus sound, audio focus (PS5 only), mono audio options, HUD customisation, motion blur/DoF customisation, colour filters, camera movement reduction options, aim assist, aiming sensitivity, movement/sprint assists, FoV sliders.

The Hajin city map, smartly repurposed from the campaign, is expansive and packed with nuance, and the tasks you're given within the city limits are quick and painless - more than I can say of Marathon. You can easily and somewhat permanently get cash that persists even if you die, you can sacrifice max health to 'revive' from a down-but-not-out state, and you get XP for doing just about anything. The result is an extraction shooter experience that feels more casual and agreeable to the average FPS enjoyer; this isn't a 'lifestyle game' like other extraction shooters. Even if it does have its own pseudo-stealth system, for some reason.

In many ways, DMZ emulates what Activision did with Warzone: a wrangling of a complicated formula that makes sense within the uber-specific Call of Duty ecosystem. It's a great interpretation of the PvPvE formula that's been slowly but surely evolving over the past decade or so, and I think this is where DMZ finds its niche: Arc Raiders has become more about the PvE side of things (at least in my experience) and Marathon and Tarkov go hard on the PvP. DMZ somehow treads the line between both and, as time goes on and Infinity Ward monitors the mode and how people engage with it, I imagine its niche will only become more distinct compared to its genre stable-mates. We're already seeing some changes bleed into the game, and it's not even been out a week - it bodes well for the future.

Modern Warfare 4 represents the highest tide for Call of Duty in seven years. Infinity Ward needed to pull off a balancing act I don't envy; injecting just enough nostalgia into a series propped up with so many conventions and expectations there's barely room for anything new, alongside enough innovation and intrigue to keep people interested. Beyond that, after several weaker years in a row, Black Ops 7 in particular caused enough reputation damage that even the most loyal CoD fanatics started to see through the series' aging veneer. And so, even if the campaign occasionally struggles under the weight of legacy, and the multiplayer is happy to keep rolling on the same wheels Modern Warfare has been using for four games now, Infinity Ward has succeeded - after four years away from the helm - in saving Call of Duty. Modern Warfare 4 is a course correction sorely needed, and deftly deployed.

A copy of the game was provided for this review by Activision Blizzard.

#10484. MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

Researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a new approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

"We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

Chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller

Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

The team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

The physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

To solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

"The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates new capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How says.

Teaching a Tiny Robot to Plan Difficult Maneuvers

The first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

Although this method requires substantial computing power, it can plan difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

Repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each new flip under the proper conditions.

"If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How says.

The researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate quickly enough for real-time flight.

A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

"The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

Experiments showed that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

"This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up new opportunities for multimodal locomotion," says Hsiao.

The team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a new position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

"This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen says.

One major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

The team also plans to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

"For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a new control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," says Chen.

This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

#10482. Modern HTML Forms: Building Accessible, Secure, and User-Friendly Experiences

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Forms are among the most important components of modern websites. They allow users to register accounts, submit contact requests, search for information, complete purchases, and interact with web applications.

Despite their apparent simplicity, forms can introduce significant usability and development challenges. Poorly labeled fields, unclear validation messages, inaccessible controls, and unreliable submission behavior can prevent users from completing even basic tasks.

Modern HTML provides many built-in features that help developers create more reliable forms with less JavaScript. When combined with semantic markup, thoughtful CSS, and carefully designed validation, these features can improve both usability and maintainability.

This article explores practical techniques for building modern web forms that are accessible, responsive, and easier to maintain.

A well-structured form begins with the correct HTML elements. Native controls provide built-in browser behavior and communicate their purpose to assistive technologies.

Each control has an explicitly associated label. The name attributes identify the fields when form data is submitted, while autocomplete helps browsers recognize common information types.

The required attribute indicates that a field must be completed before a normal browser submission can proceed.

These native features reduce the need for custom code and provide a more consistent starting point across browsers.

HTML provides several input types designed for specific kinds of information.

For example, type="email" enables browser validation for email-shaped input, while type="tel" identifies a telephone number field and can prompt mobile browsers to display a suitable keyboard.

Selecting appropriate input types improves the user experience, especially on mobile devices.

However, native validation has limits. An email input does not establish that an address exists or belongs to the person entering it. Similarly, a URL input does not guarantee that a submitted address is safe to access.

Client-side validation should therefore be treated as a usability feature, not as a substitute for server-side validation.

Browser controls can look different across platforms. A small set of reusable CSS rules can make a form feel more consistent while preserving native functionality.

The box-sizing: border-box declaration makes width calculations more predictable because padding and borders are included in the declared width.

Using font: inherit helps form controls remain consistent with the surrounding typography.

The visible focus outline is equally important. Keyboard users need to identify which control currently receives focus, so removing browser outlines without an accessible replacement should be avoided.

HTML can handle many common validation requirements without a custom script.

For example, a username field can use length constraints:

A numeric field can define a suitable range:

These attributes help the browser identify certain invalid values before submission.

Developers should choose constraints based on actual application requirements. For example, a quantity field may require a positive integer, while a measurement field might legitimately accept decimals.

Custom JavaScript validation is useful when rules depend on other fields, remote data, or business logic. For basic requirements, native HTML validation is often simpler and easier to maintain.

A useful validation message explains what went wrong and how the user can correct it.

For more complex forms, developers may need to provide custom feedback:

JavaScript can use the browser's constraint validation API to identify invalid input:

This example prevents submission when the email field is invalid and displays a more specific message.

For production forms, validation should be coordinated across all relevant fields. Errors should remain associated with their controls, be communicated accessibly, and not rely on color alone.

The server must repeat relevant validation because client-side checks can be bypassed.

Users may accidentally submit a form multiple times by clicking a button repeatedly or interacting with a slow interface.

For an asynchronous form, the submit button can be disabled while a request is in progress.

This is an illustrative example and assumes that the form has an appropriate action URL and that the server accepts the submitted fields.

A real application should provide accessible inline status messages instead of relying on alert(). It should also consider authentication, server-side error responses, network timeouts, and whether retrying a request could create duplicate records.

For operations that must not be repeated, server-side idempotency controls may be necessary. Disabling a button alone cannot guarantee that a request is processed only once.

Forms frequently collect personal or business information, so security must be part of their design.

Validate all submitted data on the server.

Apply appropriate authorization checks to sensitive operations.

Use CSRF protection where required by the application's authentication architecture.

Escape or safely render user-provided content to reduce injection risks.

Avoid placing passwords, tokens, or sensitive personal information in URLs.

Apply appropriate rate limits to public-facing endpoints.

HTML validation helps users correct mistakes, but it does not establish trust in submitted data.

For example, a hidden input containing a user's role must never be treated as authoritative proof of that role. A malicious client can change the value before submission.

Security decisions belong on the server, where the application can verify permissions and enforce its rules.

Forms should remain usable on mobile devices without forcing users to zoom, scroll horizontally, or interact with cramped controls.

A responsive form container can use flexible sizing:

The min() function limits the container width while allowing it to adapt to smaller viewports. Logical properties such as margin-inline also make the layout more adaptable to different writing directions.

Developers should test forms at narrow widths and with browser zoom enabled. Long labels, validation messages, and translated content should be allowed to wrap naturally.

It is also worth checking that touch targets are comfortable to use and that the form does not depend on hover effects to communicate important information.

A form that works when every field contains valid data may still fail under realistic conditions.

Submitting the form with required fields empty.

Navigating every control using a keyboard.

Checking focus indicators and error announcements.

Testing on mobile-sized screens and at increased zoom.

Simulating server errors and network interruptions.

Verifying that the server rejects invalid or unauthorized requests.

Confirming that successful submissions provide clear feedback.

Automated browser tests can cover common validation and submission scenarios. Manual testing remains valuable for checking whether error messages are understandable and whether the form feels usable to people with different accessibility needs.

The most reliable forms are designed to handle failure clearly, not just to demonstrate a successful submission.

Modern HTML provides a strong foundation for building accessible and maintainable forms. Semantic elements, appropriate input types, native validation, and reusable CSS can reduce unnecessary JavaScript while improving the user experience.

When custom validation or asynchronous submission is required, developers should add it carefully and preserve clear feedback, keyboard support, and server-side security controls.

A well-designed form does more than collect information. It guides users through a task, helps them recover from mistakes, and communicates what happens next. By treating usability, accessibility, and security as connected parts of the same design process, developers can build forms that are more reliable and easier to maintain.

#10481. Dave & Buster’s changes its name to Doom & Buster’s with new Marvel games and drinks

Dave & Buster’s is temporarily changing its name to Doom & Buster’s as part of a nationwide takeover celebrating the upcoming release of Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Doomsday.

The arcade and entertainment chain announced the promotion on November 4, revealing plans to transform its locations with Marvel-themed games, exclusive merchandise, collectible prizes, and a new lineup of cocktails and mocktails.

The promotion begins rolling out this week before the full takeover launches on November 16. It will run through January 31, 2027, giving fans a chance to experience the themed attractions before and after Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters on December 18.

As part of the promotion, participating Dave & Buster’s locations will feature dedicated Doomsday Zones, complete with themed entrances, Marvel games, signage, and interactive experiences.

Several attractions begin rolling out November 4, including MARVEL Cosmic Invasion, a four-player beat ’em up that lets players select two Marvel superheroes and switch between their abilities during combat.

Avengers: Roller Race & Battle is another four-player experience that challenges guests to race against each other while defeating a villain.

Other attractions featured in the takeover include:

The promotion also introduces limited-time Avengers-inspired cotton candy flavors, themed merchandise, and collectible Power Cards featuring characters such as Thor, Doctor Doom, and Yelena.

Alongside the new games, Doom & Buster’s is introducing five limited-time beverages, including three alcoholic options and two mocktails.

The cocktail lineup features Doomsday’s Dominion, made with Smirnoff vodka, melon liqueur, pineapple, lemon-lime soda, and a Black Magic sidecar.

The Multiversal Mule combines vodka, blue orange liqueur, dragon fruit, and ginger beer, complete with edible shimmer and an LED glow cube.

Burger King reveals wild Avengers: Doomsday menu with green Whopper, chicken and Sprite

KFC reveals Avengers: Doomsday menu with black burgers, green mayo and ‘Doom Dust’

Dunkin assembles Avengers: Doomsday menu featuring Doctor Doom and X-Men

Guests can also order the Fantastic Flight, which includes four miniature cocktails featuring different flavors inspired by Marvel superheroes.

For those looking for alcohol-free options, Panther’s Potion combines cherry, ginger beer, and citrus sour with a blue shimmer sidecar, while Captain Punch features blue raspberry, coconut, pineapple, and lemon-lime soda.

All five beverages will be available from November 16 through January 31.

The promotion also includes a new event called DOOMHOUR, which gives D&B Rewards members the opportunity to earn double tickets on green-swipe games during randomly selected one-hour periods.

Members will receive a notification through the D&B Rewards app 24 hours before the next DOOMHOUR, followed by another notification revealing the exact time on the day of the event.

“When one of the biggest movies of the year is coming, you don’t put up a poster. You bend the knee,” said Jeremy Tucker, Chief Marketing Officer at Dave & Buster’s.

“We gave Doom our name. We gave him the floor. We gave him the bar. Doom & Buster’s is a world fans can only walk into with us, and it’s built for the thing we do better than anyone: bringing people together to play, compete, and be part of the action.”

Dave & Buster’s isn’t the only chain celebrating the upcoming Marvel movie. KFC also announced an Avengers: Doomsday collaboration featuring black burgers, green mayo, themed drinks, and collectible figurines. However, while the KFC promotion will launch in more than 100 countries beginning November 9, it won’t be available in the US.

#10480. 8-bit horror Tenebris Somnia mixes weird live-action horror with a retro 2D adventure to impressive and unsettling effect

I've been captivated by the idea of wrong-footing an audience ever since playing Faith: The Unholy Trinity. That game presents like an 8-bit horror, then proceeds to bend the rules of what an 8-bit game can do - or perhaps what you remember they could do - in order to surprise and scare you. Tenebris Somnia is very similar. Indeed, it's executive produced by the developer of Faith, Airdorf Games, so the connection runs even deeper. Tenebris Somnia utilises the same retro aesthetic with its grinding chiptune music, its pixelated graphics, and old-school presentation. But the difference is it takes the rule-bending a step further, essentially welding two very different experiences together: a retro-styled 2D adventure and a full-on live-action film. And it's horrific, in all the right ways.

To begin with, Tenebris Somnia is a slow, plodding, fairly unremarkable affair that plays a bit like a point-and-click adventure. You're a young woman on her way to her former boyfriend's apartment, checking it out because you suspect something has happened there. You move from screen to screen, examining points of interest as you pass them, collecting odds and ends - an empty bottle, a mysterious book - and storing them in your inventory for later. Eventually, there's a locked door, and you'll have to piece together the scattered clues in order to unlock it. And despite the apparent urgency of the situation - the carnage you find in your ex-boyfriend's apartment - the pace is slow; deliberately old-school in its approach. Walk back and forth, examine everything, try "combining" items in your inventory, "use" them on the environment. Did it work? No? Try something else.

But this is where Tenebris Somnia begins to distinguish itself: your busywork is often rewarded with a glossy live-action sequence - clips of real actors in impressive costume and make-up enacting key moments from the unfolding adventure. A person with what appears to be two faces, one inverted, rushes out of the darkness toward you. A strange woman suddenly appears in a lift, offering you a gift. Two waxen figures embrace each other in bed. A giant lady with a hole in her face stretches towards the ceiling. It's captivatingly weird and very well-produced, finished with a level of polish that's impressive in an otherwise lo-fi indie experience such as this. And there's a reason for this: the live-action scenes are made by filmmaker Andrés Borghi, who's worked on a number of films including acclaimed Argentinian horror When Evil Lurks. Borghi has also made games of his own, so there's a natural overlap and understanding there.

It's these live-action sequences that stand Tenebris Somnia apart, that bring another, unusual dimension to it. That pixelated creature rushing toward you in the hallway: it has more substance in your mind now you've seen it up close. That enigmatic lady in a cocktail dress: you know the contours of her face and the strange demonic symbols branded there. You know the world better, more intimately now, and that gives it more impact. These live-action moments also create a kind of propulsive anticipation, knowing that when you do solve a puzzle or unlock that mysterious door, lavish reward and revelation awaits you there.

But I have my doubts about the game overall. Granted, I'm only early on, so perhaps I'm yet to really settle in. But I find its plodding stop-start rhythm works against the suspense and horror. Laboriousness deflates the tension. Frequently revisiting areas robs them of their surprises. And I haven't found much inherent interest in exploring new areas of the game; the writing feels functional to me rather than intriguing, and that's a problem, because in the adventure game sequences it has to do so much of the heavy lifting.

But I remain hopeful. I've watched a little more of Tenebris Somnia than I've managed to play, and the movie-making story at its heart - one focusing on a horror short of your ex's creation - appears to deepen and circle back on itself in interesting ways. Everything you do somehow seems tied to that movie - around deals with devilish entities and the grotesque consequences they bring. That filmic motif repeats again and again. And who knows? Perhaps the live-action sequences represent more than the things our character is experiencing. So there's intrigue there, depth, thought, layers, and, by the looks of it, plenty of imagination to support it.

#10478. What we've been playing - "I've been intrigued by horrible images of live-action sequences for weeks"

A few of the things that have us hooked this week.

Happy Halloween! Are you scared? I am: I'm in a theatre play that opens next week and we're not ready yet. I'm also off to a ghost stories evening at the theatre tonight; I've had a few people there tell me, with faces as straight as a ruler, of their eerie encounters. Actually, one encounter involved me.

I was in a two-hander there, a play with only two people in it, and I got to the changing room one evening to see a concerned look on the face of the other person in the show. "Have you only just got here?" he asked. "Yes," I said in response. And at this, he blanched. He's a gruff sort of fellow with a streetwise sensibility: not a person I would associate with being easily scared. But he was. "I was just talking to you," he said. "You made the curtain move as you walked past." I remember the hairs on my arms and neck standing up, and I haven't been as confident sitting in that dressing room alone since.

But back to games! This, as you know, is our regular feature where we talk about what we've been playing this week. This week, Marie cooks with Death; Connor revisits a game that terrified him as a teenager; and Bertie is a little bit disappointed by a new indie horror.

But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago (it happens). And now onward!

My supernatural farm is coming together very slowly, and I do mean slowly. I'm not in a rush this time - my many restarts of Stardew Valley have taught me to be patient while building or I'll want to wipe everything and start afresh. Also, I do not do scary games in the slightest, so this is my version of a halloween-themed entry, and I am fine with that.

So: my current farm contains a small livestock barn, a vegetable patch, a rather fetching vineyard next to some kegs, and I've just started to renovate the lower level by the beach. What that will be is yet to be decided, but the slow progress isn't bothering me as much as I thought it would. In fact, being unable to race through it is making it more enjoyable.

Also, watching Death learning to cook was not on my 2026 bingo card, but I am adamant a friendship will form from the literal ashes of his creations.

Given we're in the Halloween season and the site has been diving into all things scary, I wanted to pop back and play the game that kicked off a horror revival of sorts when I was almost a teenager: Amnesia!

Like many my age, my first exposure to Amnesia was through YouTube playthroughs back in the Let's Play early years. I didn't actually touch it myself until years later, dipping my toes in the game and swiftly pulling them back out, frightened.

Now I'm older and hardened by adult life, I wanted to give it another go and see how horror games have evolved over time. While they certainly have come a way since 2010, Amnesia holds up! It's well worth playing if you want a blast from the past.

I'm a bit disappointed. I've been intrigued by horrible images of live-action sequences from Tenebris Somnia for weeks, anticipating what I believed would be a terrifying experience. But a couple of hours into the game, I haven't had that. I've written about this at more length in a Tenebris Somnia preview, but suffice to say the adventure game half of Tenebris Somnia lets it down a bit, I think. However, I'm still impressed; I'm impressed by people approaching horror - and games - in these interesting ways.

It also reminds me strongly of Faith: The Unholy Trilogy, which is another, closely related 8-bit horror game that really is terrifying. It's tighter and meaner, and its crazed, hand-drawn MS Paint cinematics are worth seeing up close for yourself.

What a spooky week it's been! After Monday's trawl into some of our favourite scary games, I delved - some 30 years after my original encounter - back into pioneering survival horror Ecstatica, dongs and all. Since then, we've had post-Soviet grimness, minty fresh breath and misery, plus Bertie straddling the line between retro pixel art and retro FMV.

In amongst all that (and a bit of Silver Pines), I've squeaked in some time with The Killing Stone. It's very early days, but I'm already intrigued by its distinctive mix of roguelike deck-builder and first-person narrative horror, especially given the folkloric aspects of it all as you, a Scandinavian witch's apprentice, reckon with previous dealings with the devil.

It's fascinating so far, with an unusual card-based combat system that plays out across a single line, meaning placement matters as you attempt to snuff out your opponent's orb at the far end by battling through - or around - its guards. Each of your units can be augmented with spells and abilities placed strategically, and adjacently, outside of the battlefield, introducing even more possibilities. And I especially love the fact you can play the whole thing in modern or ye olde English, the strong voice cast making fine work of both.

I'm excited to explore more, then, but with Halloween here I've other engagements to see through first. Two annual movie traditions: Trick 'r Treat, and then - as someone old enough to have been scarred by it the first time around - controversial BBC classic Ghostwatch, with Michael Parkinson, Craig Charles, and Sarah Greene. Over three decades later it remains remarkably effective, and that bedroom Pipes reveal still haunts me.

#10477. Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software. Researchers have now demonstrated a new way to reach that level of flexibility using unusual quantum objects known as non-Abelian anyons.

Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons. Their results provide the first experimental demonstration that this approach can support the broad range of operations required for universal quantum computing.

"We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," said Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the new study published in Nature.

A Possible Shortcut Around Costly Quantum Error Correction

The strategy could do more than help create a general-purpose quantum computer. It may also offer a more efficient route toward reliable quantum machines.

Quantum computers are extremely vulnerable to errors, so researchers typically protect information by distributing it across many physical qubits. These error correction methods can preserve data, but they usually do not provide every operation needed to perform universal quantum computation on that protected information.

To fill the gap, engineers often rely on specially prepared resources called "magic states." Producing them usually requires an intensive purification process known as distillation, which can consume a large fraction of a quantum computer's available qubits. The new results suggest that non-Abelian anyons may offer a way around that expensive step.

"Non-Abelian codes are a dark horse in the race to quantum error correction," said Henrik Dreyer, managing director and scientific lead at Quantinuum's Munich office and a co-author of the study. "In this work we show the first universal gate set in a non-Abelian code, which demonstrates that fault-tolerant computations can in principle be done without resorting to magic state distillation or cultivation, which are the most expensive operations in standard quantum error correction codes."

Ordinary qubits encode information using two basic states, along with quantum combinations of those states. Non-Abelian anyons work in a fundamentally different way.

These anyons do not appear as ordinary standalone particles in nature. Instead, scientists create them inside quantum circuits by entangling many conventional qubits into a collective state that behaves as though it were a new type of particle with its own unusual rules.

"The way I think about these codes is they're creating little universes -- alternative universes, but ones that reflect some of the properties of our own," Verresen said.

Each non-Abelian anyon carries an internal state that changes when one anyon is moved around another in a process known as braiding. The sequence of those braiding operations matters (that's what non-Abelian means), allowing information to be encoded and manipulated in ways that are unavailable to ordinary particles.

Because the information is spread across many entangled qubits rather than stored in a single location, it can also be naturally protected from some of the small disturbances that frequently disrupt conventional qubits. Braiding the anyons can also perform computational operations.

In 2024, a research team that included Verresen used a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer to create anyons associated with a symmetry group called D4 -- the rotations and reflections that leave a square unchanged -- demonstrating this form of non-Abelian order on quantum hardware for the first time.

That experiment showed that the unusual particles could be created and manipulated, but braiding them alone was not sufficient to carry out every operation required for universal quantum computing.

"In that work, we didn't demonstrate that those emergent forces were enough to do quantum computation," said Verresen. "That particular universe we created was not powerful enough."

Fusion Unlocks Universal Quantum Operations

For the new study, the researchers switched to another symmetry known as S3 -- the rotations and mirror-image flips that leave an equilateral triangle unchanged -- and created the corresponding anyons on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor using 54 entangled qubits.

The S3 system had the properties needed for universal quantum computation, but only when braiding was combined with another operation called fusion. During fusion, two anyons are brought together and the resulting state is measured.

The underlying concept was proposed theoretically in 2003 by Carlos Mochon, then a student of John Preskill at Caltech. Turning that theoretical idea into an experiment that could actually run on quantum hardware, however, required extensive additional theoretical and experimental work.

The researchers used pairs of anyons to encode "topological qutrits" which store three possible levels of quantum information instead of the two levels used by ordinary qubits.

By combining different braiding and fusion operations, the team demonstrated three key tools: one entangling gate produced through braiding and two different measurements created through fusion. Together, those operations can in principle produce any quantum operation, including operations that braiding alone could not achieve.

Beyond their possible computing applications, these unusual quantum states could also help researchers investigate fundamental aspects of physics.

"It is gratifying to see ideas we have spent our PhD work thinking about realized in the lab, and it has been made possible by remarkable advances in quantum hardware over the past few years," said Anasuya Lyons and Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, graduate students at Harvard University in the group of Ashvin Vishwanath who helped lead the work.

The researchers also demonstrated that non-Abelian anyons could directly produce a magic state using topological operations -- sidestepping the costly distillation process used in most quantum systems.

The experiment did not yet include active error correction. Instead, the researchers focused on testing the individual building blocks of the method and confirming that they could create a magic state consistent with theoretical expectations.

"So far, we've ignored the question of error correction. Here, it's more like a proof of principle," Verresen said.

The next major step will be combining these operations with active error correction. If that can be achieved, non-Abelian anyons could eventually become a practical basis for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Verresen is already working with other PME researchers on new techniques for stabilizing non-Abelian quantum memories.

Materials provided by University of Chicago. Original written by Sarah C.P. Williams. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10475. Wendy’s free RPG rewards players with real food for beating bosses and is 15 hours long

Wendy’s has officially launched its free RPG, and somehow, the fast-food chain has created a game longer than some AAA blockbusters, complete with boss battles that reward players with actual food.

When WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones was first announced, the biggest surprise was that Wendy’s was making a full-blown, Final Fantasy-style RPG.

As it turns out, the company wasn’t messing around.

According to Wendy’s official website, the free-to-play adventure clocks in at approximately 15 hours of gameplay, featuring over 1,000 lines of dialogue.

For comparison, that’s more than double the length of some AAA campaigns such as Wolverine, which can be finished in 13 hours.

That’s an absurd amount of content for a game about a redheaded burger mascot fighting the forces of frozen beef.

Wendy’s has confirmed that players can unlock real-world food offers by defeating five bosses throughout the adventure.

Each boss provides a chance to earn a reward code redeemable through the Wendy’s app, with prizes including free medium fries, a small Frosty, 10-piece chicken nuggets, a breakfast biscuit or croissant, and even a Dave’s Single burger.

There is, however, a catch. Every food reward requires a separate purchase, and codes are available on a first-come, first-served basis while supplies last. Rewards are also restricted to US residents aged 18 and older.

Still, getting a burger for defeating an RPG boss is certainly a more delicious incentive than unlocking another achievement.

As for the game itself, WendyQuest features turn-based combat, puzzles, and five food-themed regions as players attempt to save the kingdom of Savoria from the villainous Dr. Mechborg.

Wendy’s is releasing free Final Fantasy-style RPG on Steam

Wendy’s launches gigantic MEGA burger with 7 patties and it’s 2,614 calories

Wendy’s quietly brings back “banned” 9-patty burger as an eating challenge with special prizes

Players can recruit allies including Frostyna, Sir Chicken, and the Baconator, who apparently wields a bacon sword. Naturally, there’s also a collection of enemies seemingly inspired by McDonald’s, including Golden Archers.

WendyQuest launched on November 4 and is available for free on Steam, iOS, and Android.

Whether it’s actually a good RPG remains to be seen, but at least Wendy’s has figured out how to make grinding bosses feel a little more rewarding.
