#10474. Silver Pines is a great survival horror throwback with an unexpected Metroidvania twist, but it makes me glad the genre's moved on

It's those bloody typewriters all over again. Developer Wych Elm Games' Silver Pines is fantastic in a whole bunch of ways, from its woozy small-town ambience to its mix of taut survival horror and exploratory Metroidvania. But from the very first moment I saw its save system, its please-insert-coin phone box demands, I knew our relationship was going to be a fractious one.

Silver Pines begins, however, in the gloom of a 1950s diner; lights off, windows boarded, as the titular town awaits an oncoming storm. You are private investigator Red Walker, but your jittery demeanour and Valium drawl suggests you're equally oblivious to the whos, whats, and whys of it all. Out in the parking lot, a phone box rings; there's cryptic talk of a missing musician and a motel room. Then, the scene set, it's onward into the heart of the town.

Silver Pines dabbles in neo-noir and psychological horror, but its debt to David Lynch - Twin Peaks in particular - is unmistakable. If the 50s diner opener wasn't enough of a tip-off, it's not long before the town's cast of beautifully rotoscoped oddballs begin making themselves known; enigmatic conversations unfurling in awkward non-sequiters. Then later: as Red passes through a suspicious door, reality seems to bend entirely, taking him to a dingy nightclub bar somewhere out of time. There's no talking giant, but we do get a song.

Twin Peaks' iconography has been borrowed and repackaged so much in the 36 years since its landmark arrival, it's hard to pay it homage without ringing the creative death knell. So it's testament to Silver Pines that, for all its hat-tips, it still manages to find a mood that feels like its own. Granted, its one that exists at the intersection David Lynch and Silent Hill (itself indebted to Twin Peaks) but the town's ambience - a kind of dishevelled melancholy - is an affecting one. Its world, built from layers upon layers of strikingly painterly 2D artwork, is drab and desolate; perpetually dank and lost in artfully controlled shadow. Its sorrowful monstrosities shimmer like a suggestion. And beneath the wind and the rain and the wailing of lost souls lies an ambient synthline so slight the soundscape skirts close to ASMR.

That, though, is entirely fitting for an adventure whose pace is such a languid one; as woozily unfocused as Red seems to be when he first picks up that phone. That's not a criticism though. Silver Pines isn't afraid to create space for its insidious ambience to slither in. There are pockets of staccato violence, absolutely, but between the deliberately stilted gunplay and awkwardly stumbling melee its primary rhythms are exploratory ones.

Which is where the Metroidvania stylings come in. Silver Pines, the town, is a vast, interconnected space: drizzly exteriors lead to gloomy interiors that branch out to new pathways or double back to previously impassable ones (you'll be hearing Red muttering "The door opens from the other side!" in your dreams). Sometimes you'll stumble across a perfectory puzzle, but progress most often requires identifying which part of the map, perhaps a location first seen much earlier, might succumb to new tools: a boxcutter that opens up passageways sealed with plastic; a pistol that can shatter rusty padlocks. And a shout-out to one of my favourite underused Metroidvania mechanics - the ability to photograph points of interest and pin them to your map, serving as reminders for future you.

It all makes for a haltingly ambulatory flow that suits and serves the quieter mood. But truthfully, having hit the five-hour mark, I'm finding the whole thing a bit of a struggle as I grapple with its intentional throwback design. Beneath Silver Pines' sumptuously bleak presentation lies an ancient heart. And while I'm certainly not criticising a deliberately old-school adventure for playing it old-school, it is making me thankful the genre's moved on.

Silver Pines, like most survival horror, builds tension through scarcity and impermanence, offering thrilling glimpses of power only to take them all away again: bullets are limited, melee weapons break, and the resources needed to restore them are equally few. Without all that, your only hope of survival is a stumbling duck-and-weave. But Silver Pines spins a particularly punishing web, tying everything to the finite number of coins left out in the world. Ammo, duct tape, health items, and so on are rare finds on the map, but comparatively plentiful in vending machines. However, coins are also the currency you'll need for phone box saves, meaning every choice you make feels even more perilous; the perpetual threat of a death spiral.

And the truth is, as much as I love survival horror, I've always hated limited saves; not just the push-your-luck stresses they invoke as I'm forced to decide if I dare risk - for instance - my last Resident Evil typewriter ribbon, but the steadily deflating atmosphere when my luck runs out and I've got to do the same section all over again. It's a problem modern survival horror still grapples with, of course, but, by jettisoning the arbitrary restrictions of limited save currency, they're able to manage a more sustained momentum.

And by binding its survival systems so tightly - the threat of weapons failure, the threat of death - under the guise of coins, Silver Pines has made me even more obsessive about my saves, even more cautious about frivolous spending. And it's turned mood into mechanisms. I'm min-max route plotting, enemy tracking, bullet counting, and limiting my box cutter swings - so much energy spent on mental spreadsheet-building I'm no longer immersed in the mystery of the thing. And the open-ended structure does rather exacerbate the issue: its long, slow stretches of nothing followed by unexpected deaths make redoing bits particularly wearying.

Of course, it's not Silver Pines' fault it's igniting my old-school survival horror PTSD. And I'm fully aware there are sickos out there who love this kind of thing; the queasily unshakeable threat of spiralling disaster and the harsh punishment when calculations are off and disaster finally comes. But you know what? I certainly respect Silver Pines, even if we don't always get along. It's a gorgeously woozy exercise in mood, with a fishing line mystery that - for all my grumbles - just keeps pulling me on. Not for nothing is its enigmatic bar known as The Rabbit Hole, and as the search for Eddie Velvet continues, here I am; lost in the warrens again.

#10472. 9 Browser-Based Checks That Make Design-to-Development Handoffs More Reliable

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A design file shows what an interface should look like in a particular state. A browser reveals what happens when the headline doubles in length, a request fails, someone uses a keyboard, or a device struggles to render an animation.

That gap explains many frustrating handoffs. A developer believes the implementation matches the design, while a designer notices behavior that was never discussed. Both can be right about the evidence they have.

A more useful review combines the rendered interface with repeatable browser checks. Each check should produce a small, actionable finding: the conditions, the observed behavior, and the expected result.

The nine checks below use browser tools to turn visual opinions into implementation decisions. Chrome DevTools provides the main examples; tool names and locations can vary between versions.

When a component looks wrong, first identify which rule actually controls it. The value in a stylesheet may be overridden, inherited, or constrained by its parent.

Select the element in DevTools and inspect its computed width, spacing, typography, and box model. Toggle a suspected declaration to see whether it explains the problem. Chrome’s CSS inspection guide covers this workflow.

Suppose a card heading overflows. Reducing its font size might hide the symptom while damaging the visual hierarchy. Instead, investigate whether the text container can shrink:

This is a targeted pattern, not a universal fix. Check the actual layout before applying it.

Record the finding: “At a narrow width, the flex child’s minimum size prevents the heading from wrapping.” Include the selector and the source change needed. Temporary DevTools edits are experiments; commit the fix in the project.

General technical documentation should capture the reasoning behind reusable layout rules. For this card, explain why the text container must be allowed to shrink and which long-content cases should be checked after future changes.

Testing only a desktop and a mobile preset can miss awkward layouts between them. Navigation may wrap at one width, while a toolbar collides at another.

Use Device Mode to resize the viewport gradually. Try long labels, empty content, and a larger number of cards. Watch for clipping, unnecessary horizontal scrolling, and controls that become difficult to reach.

Choose breakpoints based on the point where the content stops working. A device name does not explain why a layout should change.

Record the viewport width in CSS pixels and the content that triggered the failure. “Broken on mobile” is much less actionable than “At 390 CSS pixels, a two-line product name pushes the action button outside its container.”

Device emulation does not reproduce every hardware, operating-system, or browser behavior. Confirm critical flows on real devices and the browsers your audience uses. SitePoint’s cross-browser responsive testing guide provides additional background.

Record the finding: The failing width, the content variant, and the intended reflow behavior.

Browser tool: Accessibility pane and accessibility tree

A control can be visually obvious while exposing an unclear name to assistive technology. This often happens with icon-only buttons.

Inspect the computed role and accessible name using DevTools’ accessibility features. Check that the name describes the action and that the element has appropriate semantics.

If a button already has clear visible text, an extra ARIA label may be unnecessary. Keep visible and accessible naming aligned rather than adding ARIA everywhere.

Then use the keyboard. Can you reach the control, see focus, activate it, and continue through the interface? Inspecting the accessibility tree cannot replace testing the interaction.

SitePoint’s overview of web accessibility principles offers broader context for this review.

Record the finding: The control’s role, accessible name, keyboard behavior, and expected outcome.

Loading states are part of the interface, even when they are absent from the mockup.

Use the Network panel to inspect the requests made by a user action. Check the status, timing, and response. Apply network throttling to observe loading behavior that disappears on a fast connection.

A network error, an HTTP error, and an empty successful response are different conditions. Exercise each through controlled development fixtures or mocks rather than assuming that one failure test covers everything.

Record the finding: The action, request outcome, UI state, and recovery path. A screenshot of a spinner alone does not explain whether the application can recover.

A page may load promptly but become sluggish when a user filters a large list or opens a complex menu.

Record a short session with the Performance panel. Start recording, perform the problem interaction once, and stop. Inspect the period surrounding the delay for scripting, layout, and rendering work.

Keep the investigation narrow. A recording containing several unrelated actions is harder to interpret.

For example, if typing into a filter causes repeated expensive updates, investigate the work triggered by each keystroke before adding an animation to disguise the delay. The appropriate fix might involve reducing rendered content, avoiding repeated calculations, or changing when work runs.

Compare before and after using the same content, browser, and throttling settings. A local trace is diagnostic evidence, not proof of the experience of every user.

SitePoint’s introduction to optimization auditing with Chrome DevTools provides useful background on this investigative approach.

Record the finding: The precise interaction, test conditions, suspected expensive work, and measured effect of the change.

The default appearance is only one version of an interface. Users may prefer reduced motion or a different color scheme.

Chrome’s Rendering panel can emulate relevant CSS media features. Use it to review the component in each supported state.

For example, a decorative notification animation can be disabled for reduced-motion preferences:

The message should still appear and remain understandable. Avoid relying on an animation-end event to perform an essential action if that animation can be disabled.

When reviewing dark mode, inspect borders, focus indicators, disabled controls, charts, and illustrations—not only the background.

Record the finding: The preference being tested, the affected component, and the fallback behavior.

The Coverage panel shows which JavaScript and CSS bytes were used during the recorded session. It can help identify large bundles worth investigating.

However, unused during one session does not mean safe to delete.

A navigation menu, validation error, print layout, or another route may need code that a simple page-load recording never exercises. Start the recording, then perform representative interactions before interpreting the result.

For a component library, ask whether every page receives styles for components it never renders. For JavaScript, investigate whether a large feature can be loaded when it is needed rather than included in the initial bundle.

Confirm any removal or loading change against the supported routes and states. Coverage can suggest a question; it cannot establish the answer by itself.

Record the finding: The route, interactions covered, bundle involved, and evidence needed before changing delivery behavior.

Lighthouse runs automated audits that can highlight performance, accessibility, and other implementation issues.

Run it under consistent conditions and examine individual findings. A score is a summary, not a complete assessment of the product.

An accessibility audit does not prove that a dialog has a sensible focus order or that an error message is understandable. A good performance score does not prove that a complex signed-in workflow remains responsive.

Choose a finding, reproduce it, make a targeted change, and rerun the audit. If results vary, investigate the test environment before concluding that the code improved or regressed.

Designers can help prioritize findings by identifying which affected content or interaction is central to the user’s task. Developers can then connect that priority to the relevant implementation work.

Record the finding: The audit issue, affected user task, proposed fix, and remaining manual checks.

Browser tools: Screenshots, inspected styles, and diagnostic recordings

Browser evidence becomes more useful when another person can reproduce it without attending the original review.

Technical references can include setup guidance, component specifications, and troubleshooting procedures. For a web interface, connect those references to specific browser observations so the documentation describes behavior that the team can verify.

This structure separates observation from proposed implementation. A screenshot can show the clipping, but it does not establish the underlying cause.

Keep documentation beside the component or in a place linked from the relevant issue. Update it when behavior changes, and give examples a clear connection to a build or release.

Record the finding: Enough context for another developer or designer to reproduce, assess, and verify it.

You do not need to run every tool against every component. Match the check to the risk: network inspection for asynchronous flows, keyboard checks for interactive controls, and performance recordings for expensive interactions.

The useful outcome is a shared explanation of how the interface behaves under real conditions. Designers gain evidence about the implemented experience, and developers gain clearer acceptance criteria.

Start with one important flow. Inspect it together, document the failures precisely, and turn the agreed behavior into repeatable checks. That makes the next handoff easier to implement—and easier to review.

#10470. This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy

Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a new optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos quickly and accurately. Unlike conventional systems that typically examine videos one after another using digital hardware, the UCLA technology can analyze 15 or more video streams at the same time.

The key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light. This allows many videos to be evaluated simultaneously during a single optical pass rather than requiring each one to move separately through a conventional digital processing pipeline.

The technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight. The researchers designed the optical AI system to serve as a high-throughput, attack-resilient first layer of defense for screening large amounts of manipulated and AI-generated video.

The Growing Challenge of Deepfake Detection

Rapid improvements in generative AI have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, increasing the need for detection systems that are both accurate and capable of operating at large scale.

Many advanced deepfake detectors depend on enormous amounts of digital computation. A single analysis can require hundreds of billions of floating-point operations, and videos are often processed sequentially. As more content must be checked, both the processing time and energy requirements can rise proportionally.

Digital detection systems face another problem. Attackers can deliberately alter fake videos in subtle ways designed to confuse a detector and make manipulated footage appear authentic.

Professor Aydogan Ozcan and his UCLA team developed a hybrid digital-optical system intended to address both challenges.

A lightweight digital encoder first collects compact information about each video, including spatial, spectral, and temporal features. That information is transformed into a phase pattern and displayed on a programmable spatial light modulator.

The resulting optical wavefront then travels through a free-space-based, passive optical decoder. At the other end, paired optical detectors directly produce an authenticity score for each video.

In effect, the system replaces a computationally demanding digital decoding network with a physical process that can handle many streams in parallel.

Nearly 98% Accuracy Across 15 Videos at Once

In experiments using visible light, the processor examined 15 Celeb-DF videos simultaneously during each optical pass.

It achieved an average detection accuracy of 97.79%, along with a sensitivity of 99.86% and a specificity of 95.72%. Sensitivity measures how successfully the system identifies manipulated videos, making the particularly high sensitivity important for a screening tool designed to keep fake content from slipping through.

The 99.86% sensitivity translated to an average false-negative rate of ~0.14%. In other words, only a very small fraction of manipulated videos were incorrectly classified as authentic.

The researchers also pushed the system further by increasing its capacity to 18 videos in a single optical pass. Even at that level, average detection accuracy remained at 96.13%.

The team found that the processor could also become more capable by increasing the physical depth of its passive optical decoder without substantially increasing energy use or inference latency.

When researchers added two optimized passive diffractive layers while testing more difficult deepfake manipulations, detection accuracy improved by ~6.8%.

These phase-only diffractive layers can be manufactured as passive, static optical structures/surfaces. They perform additional calculations through the diffraction of light, meaning they do not require additional electrical power while the system is performing an inference.

That approach could allow more sophisticated processing without the same energy costs that typically accompany larger digital neural networks.

Testing the System Against Google VEO-3 Videos

The researchers did not limit their experiments to conventional face swapping deepfakes. They also challenged the processor with videos produced using Google's VEO-3 model.

Newer generative AI systems can create footage that lacks many of the obvious artifacts associated with earlier deepfake technology, making them a more difficult target for detectors trained primarily on older forms of manipulation.

With only minimal fine-tuning, the optical processor achieved 94.80% accuracy and 97.61% sensitivity on previously unseen VEO-3 videos during experiments.

The results suggest that the approach could potentially adapt as generative AI technology continues to evolve.

A Deepfake Detector Designed to Be Harder to Fool

The optical system also showed resistance to black-box adversarial attacks and provides inherent protection against white-box attacks.

Part of that security comes from the way the detector physically performs its calculations. Because some of the inference process takes place through diffraction, important parameters of the optical model are effectively embedded within the hardware.

Those parameters can be difficult for an attacker to measure, reproduce, or reverse engineer. That makes reconstructing the detector and designing carefully tailored adversarial changes that can evade it considerably more difficult.

The processor also continued working reliably when videos were affected by image noise, blur, JPEG compression, and experimental misalignments. According to the researchers, those results illustrate how optical computation could provide a more secure and dependable foundation for some artificial intelligence systems.

A First Line of Defense Against Deepfakes

Rather than replacing sophisticated digital detectors entirely, the UCLA processor is designed to work as a highly sensitive first stage of a larger detection system.

Massive volumes of video could initially pass through the parallel optical processor. Content identified as suspicious could then be sent to more computationally demanding digital models for a more detailed final assessment.

Such a system could combine the strengths of both approaches. Optical processing could provide parallel operation, low decoder energy requirements, high sensitivity, resistance to adversarial attacks, and the ability to adapt to newer AI video generators, while conventional digital systems could provide deeper analysis when necessary.

The researchers say this combination could eventually be useful for large-scale content moderation, media authentication, surveillance, and other security-critical AI applications.

The authors of this work are Parnian Ghapandar Kashani and Dr. Shiqi Chen, who contributed equally, and Professor Aydogan Ozcan. The researchers are affiliated with the UCLA Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, the UCLA Bioengineering Department, and the California NanoSystems Institute.

#10469. Pro wrestler who plays evil politician elected mayor of Providence, Rhode Island

A professional wrestler who portrays a corrupt politician in the ring has been elected mayor of Providence, Rhode Island, proving that sometimes the bad guy really does win.

David Morales, a 28-year-old Democrat and state representative, defeated Republican Dave Talan in the November 3 election, securing approximately 81% of the vote compared to his opponent’s 17%.

According to Rhode Island Current, Morales will become the youngest mayor in Providence history when he takes office in January 2027.

However, his political career isn’t the only thing that makes him stand out. Morales also happens to be a three-time wrestling champion who plays an evil politician.

Independent professional wrestler David Morales was elected mayor of Providence, Rhode Island in last night’s midterm elections pic.twitter.com/vFjAIABtlQ

Since 2021, Morales has competed in Rhode Island’s Renegade Wrestling Alliance under the name “The Commissioner,” portraying an arrogant political authority figure who loves getting under the crowd’s skin.

He’s even won the promotion’s Hype Championship three times, and once introduced a fictional rule requiring the champion to carry their title belt everywhere, including the statehouse.

In an October 2025 interview with Ocean State Media, Morales discussed the similarities between his two careers.

“I think there’s a lot of overlap,” he said. “Including showmanship, theater, athleticism, drama and humor.”

Ironically, Morales believes politicians have actually started taking too much inspiration from professional wrestling, warning that copying the exaggerated promos of WWE stars can lead to extremist rhetoric.

His wrestling career even became a talking point during the election campaign.

According to The Boston Globe, political opponents distributed campaign materials featuring Morales in his wrestling attire, accusing him of being “all hype, no results.”

Man wins election after telling voters he’s “unqualified” and has no idea what he’s doing

Seth Rollins’ next fight: Logan Paul, Roman Reigns among options for former champion

WWE Legend Kane reignites Die Hard Christmas movie debate and he’s not backing down

Clearly, voters weren’t particularly bothered by his extracurricular activities.

Morales announced his semi-retirement from wrestling while pursuing the mayor’s office, but hasn’t ruled out stepping back into the ring.

“Never say never in the world of professional wrestling,” he said.

Of course, Morales isn’t the first wrestler to trade the squared circle for public office.

WWE legend Kane, whose real name is Glenn Jacobs, was elected mayor of Knox County, Tennessee, which includes Knoxville, in 2018. He served until 2026 and even found time to reignite the debate over whether Die Hard is a Christmas movie while in office.

Former WWE star Jesse Ventura also famously became governor of Minnesota in 1999.

With Morales now heading to City Hall, Providence residents will have to wait and see whether The Commissioner makes an appearance during his time in office.

#10468. The Mortuary Assistant dev on laying his cancelled Paranormal Activity game to rest, resurrecting it as a Halloween freebie, and a potential return to his biggest game

"[It] makes me feel like it was not all done in vain."

Halloween feels like an especially appropriate time for Playable Archive's arrival. It's a genuinely spooky found-footage affair for one - a cleverly orchestrated 30-or-so minutes of scares from the developer of horror hit The Mortuary Assistant, released this week as a Halloween freebie. But more than that, the unusual tale of its creation is also one of death and resurrection. As its slightly cheeky title implies, Playable Archive (a riff on the legendary Playable Teaser created for Hideo Kojima's cancelled Silent Hill game) is a small slice of developer Brian Clarke's much larger cancelled Paranormal Activity game, making it a fascinating window into 'what could have been'. When I heard the news of its release, my curiosity was piqued, so I spoke with Clarke about this unexpected turn of events, of laying his project to rest, and how its legacy might live on - perhaps even as a new Mortuary Assistant game.

Playable Archive's story begins sometime after the launch of The Mortuary Assistant in 2022, when Clarke was approached by publisher DreadXP to gauge his interest in developing a game set in the universe of the Paranormal Activity movies. "I was like, sure, I'd be down to do that," Clarke tells me over video call, "because I love Paranormal Activity. It's one of my favourite horror films." One thing led to another and Clarke found himself submitting a design and pitch deck to Paramount. And the company clearly liked it; amid a major management shakeup at DreadXP, the "slow process of contracts" began, and the game would eventually be announced as Paranormal Activity: Threshold in November last year.

For Clarke, Paranormal Activity was a good fit for his preferred story-first approach to horror: one less about cinematic scares that seize control of the camera, and more about "passive" chills; moments where something happens which might not be obvious, and which many players might even miss, giving them slightly different experiences they'll have fun sharing. "I think the flavour I like to do," he explains, "is something that feels like you're driving the experience as opposed to me just putting you on rails and showing you."

And the project felt like an opportunity to add depth to a series that so far hasn't delved much further than spooky houses and demonic possession, in a way Clarke particularly enjoys. "I love lore - demonic lore was a big thing in The Mortuary Assistant - [and so] I built a whole demonology for Paranormal Activity, and built out this whole new concept that still tied in with everything from the films," he recalls. "I was really excited to do this deeper thing ... that maybe could be used for other things in the future, other games, films, you know."

The vestiges of Clarke's original pitch and his broader ambitions can still be seen in Playable Archive. His take on Paranormal Activity would follow a couple as they moved into a new home - presented using the movie series' familiar found-footage style - with events gradually taking a supernatural turn. Except, at a key point, the perspective would shift, and we'd learn we're watching this old camcorder footage through the eyes of a detective, investigating the house following the couple's unexplained demise. In the planned full-length version of the game, the action would jump between the two timelines as more tapes are found, and information learned in one time period would help players progress in the other. However, a third perspective would reveal "something has been set in motion outside of these two".

Clarke, who works as a solo developer under his DarkStone Digital label, had already spent around two years developing the Paranormal Activity project before it made its PAX East debut earlier this year. And the feedback to his PAX demo - more or less the exact same slice that's now been tidied up for public release as Playable Archive - was extremely positive. But things were about to take a turn. With Paramount's deadline approaching, it was clear there was still work to do, and Clarke requested a "small extension". Not just to finish the game, but to complete QA, localisation, and porting to get Paranormal Activity ready for a simultaneous release. But Paramount, perhaps eager for a Halloween release this year, said no.

"It was really a stressful time because I had put a lot of pressure on myself for the project and I was pouring a lot of myself into it," Clarke recalls, noting that, for him, quality is everything - "I feel it shows when people play any of my projects". With the likes of additional mo-cap, voice acting, and editing work still to be done in order to complement Paranormal Activity's completed mechanics, he was concerned rushing to meet Paramount's inflexible deadline would leave the second half lacking after investing so much time in the earlier part of the game. "That sort of thing … feels much more damaging to an individual [developer's reputation] than a big old company," he says, and so the idea of putting "something out faster, and very much compromising what the game is going to be" wasn't something Clarke wanted to entertain: "I talked to Dread … and we all kind of agreed that, yeah, if we can't [get Paramount to] budge then we'll just have to kind of end it.

"To Paramount's credit, when … we floated [the idea of ending things] they were okay with that." But notably, Clarke was permitted to keep everything he'd created for the project, which is why it's been possible to trim out the Paranormal Activity branding and release Playable Archive this Halloween. It was current DreadXP director Hunter Bond who first suggested giving the project a public send-off of sorts, according to Clarke, so it could "sort of get its flowers [and] be laid to rest". For Clarke, who was in triple-A games development for 13 years before going independent, game cancellations were far from unfamiliar. And while "it's harder when it's just my work" he felt he'd "accepted that, okay, this one's not done." But it wasn't just him: "It seemed like [the project's cancellation] was probably sitting with various people at Dread" and so the decision was made to let it live on in some small way. "And now that it's out there," says Clarke, "it feels really good to let people actually play it."

Playable Archive packs a surprising amount of tension and some killer scares into its scant 30-45 minutes of playtime, but there wasn't really ever any thought of charging for it. "Just knowing it's not the full game [it was intended to be], "explains Clarke, "I can't bring myself to be like, 'Hey, give me money for that.' It's been four years since The Mortuary Assistant came out [and] I would love to put something out that could bring a little something in, but it's just not the piece for it. And Dread felt the same way."

Playable Archive isn't quite the same experience PAX East attendees had with the Paranormal Activity demo earlier this year, though. As well as scrubbing the branding, Clarke took the opportunity to make a number of adjustments, even adding some new lore. At one point, he considered expanding it still further, incorporating found-footage segments from the larger game. In the end, though, he decided there was "no elegant way" to do it.

"I'd want to be like, no, you need to access this to use the demonic connection, and to open this," he elaborates. "And then if you access this, well, this room's art isn't finished so I'd have to finish that. So it turned into a big old can of worms. Like, if I wanted to do more - which I would have loved to have done - it just would have been a bigger time investment, at which point I might as well be trying to finish the game … So ultimately [we decided] let's just polish up and make this demo the experience so people can at least see where I was going with it and get something out of it. It's better than letting it collect dust in the dark."

But there's that elephant in the room: why not finish what he started and release the full game? The answer, Clark suggests, is a little complicated. There are the technical practicalities for one - "What I created was very much meant to tie into Paranormal Activity and so to go back and adjust all of that would be a tonne of work," Clarke explains - but there's the personal aspect too; of resurrecting a game he'd already put to rest after two years of development, and of potentially being drawn back into rhythm - "inviting an unnatural process to my normal process" - he'd already struggled with the first time around. "There're a lot of factors," says Clarke, "beyond just 'Brian doesn't want to do it because he's sad', right?"

And in the end, Clarke found himself asking a simple question: "Is it better to take the concepts that I really like, that are mine and that I got to keep, and make new stuff with it?" That, ultimately, is what felt "more valuable" to him, and since reaching that decision, he's "come up with like five different game ideas, so I'd much rather chase those."

Clarke admits, though, that he's kept a curious eye on Playable Archive's reception, and says the hugely positive response has been "beautiful" to see. "When this much time passes," he says, "I think it's really common for artists and creatives to have impostor syndrome and so it's nice to be like, 'Okay, I still know what I'm doing to some degree, right?'" But with the positive feedback comes the inevitable calls to finish the game. "And I've got to fight that urge," says Clarke, "[but] I see people play through the whole thing again and I go, 'Man, that was a good story.' Like, I know where I was going with it. I know what I wanted to do with it, and people were kind of starting to understand what I was doing."

But despite that lingering temptation, Clarke seems eager to move on, and is already juggling a number of ideas that draw on both The Mortuary Assistant and Paranormal Activity. "I've realised I've got so much here," he says. "What could I build with these? I don't want to build Playable Archive again because that exists … but can I take elements from this?" According to Clarke, there are "two games in particular" he wants to do, that he thinks will strike a chord with players, and that feature concepts recognisable from Playable Archive. "I'm going to execute them again, but with more focus on those things," he explains, pointing to Playable Archive's Ouija board and different timelines. "Those things will live on. So this whole thing, at this point, makes me feel like it was not all done in vain."

For Clarke, the positive response to Playable Archive is "bittersweet", but it's also "really been motivating. It's really made me be like, alright, it's time to roll up and do this again. After everything happened … I'm out on the other side and I want to make something." As for what that something might be, Clarke says he's "already started" work on a new Mortuary Assistant game, and is also tinkering around with a "little prototype" incorporating some of Playable Archive's mechanics. Both, he says, are proving exciting. "This is the problem with the early part of game development: everything is fun. Everything's grey-box. Nothing's anything. It's just ideas. It's really cool … So I think what I need is to get a few ideas out [and decide] do I want to pursue this or do I want to pursue this other idea? You know, whether it's Mortuary Assistant, or this other prototype, or this other [thing]."

Clarke is, though, acuately aware it's been four years since he last put out a full game. "I desperately want to make something full, get it out there, and have people playing it," he says. "So, I'm certainly motivated to have something out soon."

#10466. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) review

I have a friend who first played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time back in the day, when the game was only just released and he was home from university for Christmas. This is objectively the best of all times to play any video game: not Christmas specifically, but dropped out of the regular world and faced with a few weeks filled with nothing pressing to do whatsoever. Years later, though, my friend told me that the magic of the game didn't just come down to the playing of it, but the way that the playing of it unfolded.

Here's what he meant. He'd play all day, curtains drawn, family ignored, working through dungeons and pelting across Hyrule Field on Epona. Then in the evening he'd call his girlfriend, who was back with her own family for Christmas. She always wanted to know what he'd got up to that day. And not in East Sussex; she wanted to know what he'd got up to in Hyrule.

So as he played he took regular breaks to tell someone else about what he had encountered, and what he had discovered, and what he had yet to overcome. It is my bright delight today to be able to tell you that, around thirty years later, having just revisited the game in Nintendo's new remake, Ocarina of Time is still worth telling people about. It's still an adventure so surprising, so satisfying, so moving that I need to talk about it.

Here's the thing, though. Despite the game being a cast-iron masterpiece, this reaction was something of a surprise to me. Or rather, it was a surprise precisely because the game was a cast-iron masterpiece. In truth, a couple of weeks ago I wasn't really aching to head back to Ocarina of Time after all these years. I kind of dreaded having to slog through an echoing, once-great game and summon a thousand words of measured reverence afterwards.

Thankfully I had forgotten two things. The first is that I am an idiot, which means that I had failed to realise that any chance to replay a Zelda should be leapt at. And secondly, it turns out that I'd forgotten exactly what kind of masterpiece Ocarina of Time is. And along with that last point - and we'll get to this properly in a bit - I hadn't realised that there's a secret ingredient to this specific remake that has proved absolutely essential to its greatness, and that has nothing at all to do with the code running on the Switch 2.

Let's deal with remake duties here. This is more or less the game that people played back in 1998. The beats of the adventure, with Link travelling between different eras of Hyrule in order to defeat Ganon, remain the same. You still start in Kokiri Forest and you still ride Epona over the fence at Lon Lon Ranch in one of the great heart-racing, skin-prickling moments in all of art. If you're stuck in a dungeon, you can almost always use an existing guide from the N64 game to work your way through it. The game world is still broken up into little chunks that fade out and in as you move between them. And each game still begins with that unskippably evocative intro that has Link and Epona dashing over a misty hill with the moon behind them, Zelda meets Susan Cooper.

Changes though? For one thing the whole game's been updated with modern graphics, and has ditched any and all fixed cameras for a modern system of movement on one thumbstick and camera on the other. One example: Hyrule Castle Town, in my memory at least, always had a central camera and you would pivot about its streets as if you were a horse on a circus merry-go-round.

Now it's pure Frozen territory, cobbled paths racing off in every direction and you can explore them with the camera rushing behind you. The game's spaces feel less like elaborate machines that you were a mechanical part of, and more like video game spaces. Yes, from the way I've phrased that I now see that something of a trade-off has taken place here. I loved that sense you got in early 3D games that the whole thing was a clever practical trick that was forever almost about to collapse in on itself, but anyway! The new Ocarina is a game you can show kids who weren't alive in 1998 and they will feel at home more quickly.

Sometimes the graphical update is really wonderful. The route to Zora's Domain, which I barely remember in the original Ocarina, is now a lovely scramble over cliffs and arcing crags. A bold smattering of 1990s Nickelodeon colours and glossy textures, meanwhile, makes Jabu Jabu's Belly a cross between a pre-millennium rave and a modern soft play.

My favourite locations of all, however, are two of the mid-game dungeons. The Water Temple is now a drowned Art Nouveau palace that you could easily imagine Captain Nemo knocking around in. And the Forest Temple, which is my absolute favourite Zelda dungeon of all time, is a parquet-floored murder mansion that's been overtaken by trees. Dark wood-panelled corridors and weird bits of church sticking out of the foliage. It's the kind of place you'd hear a weird crime podcast about.

Trade-offs, however. My wife, a huge fan of the original game, would wander in and out as I played, and often felt the game she remembered was a little more characterful in its visuals. The moment you fight Dark Link, for example, has lost a little of its glitchy liminality, although the staging, with an old tree in the middle of a vast smoky room, is still wonderfully strange. Towards the end of the game, with the trip into Gerudo territory, you could also occasionally be forgiven for wondering if you'd stepped into one of a dozen third-person Unreal games in development at the moment. It's pleasant to look at, but it sometimes doesn't look specifically like Zelda anymore.

All that, and some strange character models that inevitably I learned to love, don't really matter very much, however. Not least because a handful of clever tweaks elsewhere mean that Ocarina now races along at an astonishing clip. And all this with a careful paring back of intrusions from Navi the fairy and the owl, who were both there in the original game to help move you along swiftly in the first place.

These tweaks are all pretty great. Link now has a jump button, which removes the original game's contextual jumps from the equation, and makes the thundering jump attack even more pleasing to pull off. Even better, in a loan from the 3DS remake of Ocarina, you can swap out usable items using a trigger mini-menu, and you can change boots and whatever you had on your head with some of the directional face buttons.

This doesn't sound like much, but it's quietly transformative in the way that the best updates are. Take the Water Temple. This is the stuff of memes in terms of difficulty and the patience required in navigating an environment that can be flooded up to three different levels. But now, as on the 3DS, you can enjoy it without having to slip into the menu every few steps to add your iron boots or remove them.

And this in turn means that a dungeon I had been really dreading turned out to be a dungeon that revealed itself via experimentation. I would change the water level and see what options I now had, think about the relationship between spaces I could reach and spaces I could not, all without needing to muddle about in menus and interrupt the flow of things. Flow is the word in fact: a simple UI and item-management tweak has given a legendary Zelda dungeon its perfect pace and sense of revelation.

Alongside tweaks like that which I noticed - oh, it's easier to equip the Hookshot - are no doubt hundreds of little things I didn't notice. I suspect there's a lot more gentle direction prompting built into places like the Water Temple, while elsewhere, in the Forest Temple, for example, I suspected that some of the backtracking had been removed. Individual item placements have been changed around perhaps, and there are generous tweaks like a wallet that holds more rupees from the off. For me at least, all of these tweaks had several things in common: they improved the game without removing or altering anything that was particularly meaningful about the original, and, also, I struggled to confidently spot them.

I did try to spot them for a while. And I measured up what I was playing against my memory, which is always wonky in the first place. Hyrule Field feels smaller now, but it's still thrilling to race across. I remember Epona entering the game sooner, or maybe I just remember the idea of a horse in a Zelda game being a huge, attention-holding deal. I thought a favourite boss involving oil paintings came much later, but again, I had just shifted it to the third act because of its original impact on me.

But this gives way over time to the most important thing about Ocarina of Time, I think, and the reason why this remake has such an emotional impact on people like me. This isn't just another Zelda with an ingenious overworld. It's a Zelda game that's even more preoccupied with time than ever before. And this is because time unfolds within the game, via a central mechanic that takes Hyrule seven years into the future, transforming Link from a child to an adult - and then allows you to go back again.

To play a game like this, a game that is about this stuff, after a period of almost thirty years away, gives your imagination and memory a kind of IMAX treatment. I realised that not only is this a game about the passage of time and the way that the world looks different when you're young to when you're a bit older - I had never really realised that adult Link goes through variations of the same dungeons that young Link went through, but now they're all just a bit harder and more consequential - it's also the kind of game that a lot of players have knowingly or unknowingly measured parts of their lives by.

This time, when I reached the first Fairy Fountain, for example, I remembered that my wife had walked down the aisle to this music - about half the registry office recognised the tune with a shiver of laughter, incidentally. Then there's the Water Temple, which has become cultural shorthand for a challenge that is really not screwing around. How many awful things had I faced in life by first conjuring the spirit of Link about to enter this place.

Players can change camera rotation speed and toggle motion-control aiming. Targeting can be controlled by holding a button or toggling a button, Ocarina can be controlled by the mic or by buttons, controller vibration can be switched on or off.

There's that first arrival in Hyrule Field, which is both a promise of everything that games were about to become in 1998 and that fleeting moment in childhood where the boundaries suddenly change. This game doesn't just send me back into my memories, then. It puts me back in conversation with all the people I have known who have ever loved it. I play it now and think I'm talking to my friend who played it at university, or my wife who loved it long before we met.

Was it always this good? Were the dungeons always so complex and challenging, but also so playful, so coherent? Were the bosses always driven by interesting ideas and drama and humour rather than difficulty? Was the world always so rich with minor characters who linger in the mind - the accordion player in the windmill, the gravedigger who has his own tour he'd really like you to try out? It's impossible for me to say at this point. This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday. If you're new to Zelda and you're coming to this game fresh, you're going to love it. Someone, somewhere, is about to play a game so special for the first time that they need to call up their friend and tell them all about it. But if you're returning to this game? Well, somehow you'll find that you're still coming to it fresh.

My dad always said that you should read Don Quixote three times in your life, and I only recently realised that he meant that the book changes because you change. So. When I got to the Deku Tree back at the start of Ocarina a few weeks ago, and I completed the dungeon and watched the impossible vision of the Deku Tree dying of weariness? I remembered that the first time I'd been here, almost thirty years ago, I couldn't help but identify with Link, freshly gifted a sword and shield, one dungeon down, ready for whatever came next. This time, I think, I was closer to identifying with the Deku Tree.

And here's the important part: this wasn't a depressing thought. It just meant that I had taken the long route to reach this point, and this astonishing game had taken the long route too. And yet we arrived at this point together, and together we were transformed. And that's really why any of this video game stuff matters.

A copy of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was provided for this review by Nintendo.

#10465. Next.js ISR Transient Errors: Prevent notFound from Caching 404s

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Prerequisites: This article targets Next.js 14 (App Router). For Next.js 15+, see the params awaiting note in each code snippet. Requires Node.js 18.18+. Fetch caching defaults changed in Next.js 15; the ISR throw-to-preserve behavior described here is consistent across 13.4 through 14.x. Run the local simulation test described in the Testing section to confirm behavior on your target version.

A single transient database or CMS outage during Next.js ISR background revalidation can silently replace a perfectly valid cached page with a persistent 404. This is not a theoretical risk. Developers using Next.js ISR with notFound() have reported this exact failure mode, where a temporary infrastructure hiccup causes SEO damage and user-facing downtime that persists long after the underlying service recovers. The root cause is a common error-handling pattern that conflates "the data source is unreachable" with "this record does not exist." This article presents a concrete architectural fix that separates those two states, prevents Next.js from ever caching an error-driven 404, and provides an on-demand revalidation recovery strategy.

In the Next.js App Router, Incremental Static Regeneration operates on a stale-while-revalidate lifecycle. When you set a revalidate interval on a page, the first request generates and caches it. Subsequent requests within that window serve the cached version. Once the interval expires, the next request still receives the stale page, but Next.js triggers a background revalidation. This background render re-executes the page's data-fetching logic and, if successful, replaces the cached output with the fresh render.

The critical detail: the background revalidation replaces whatever is in the cache. If that render produces a 404 response, Next.js caches the 404 and overwrites the previously valid page.

The scenario, reported on Stack Overflow, follows a pattern that exists in countless Next.js codebases. A data-fetching helper wraps a CMS or database call in a try-catch block that returns null on any error, whether that error is a network timeout, a 500 from the upstream API, or a genuine "record not found" response. The page component then checks for null and calls notFound().

During a transient outage, the ISR background render hits the data-fetching error path, receives null, triggers notFound(), and the resulting 404 response is cached. The previously valid, fully rendered page is gone. When the infrastructure recovers seconds or minutes later, the damage is already done. The 404 persists until the next revalidation cycle, and if the timing is unlucky, users and search engine crawlers see a 404 for up to one full revalidation interval (60 seconds in this example, but potentially hours in production configs).

A single transient database or CMS outage during Next.js ISR background revalidation can silently replace a perfectly valid cached page with a persistent 404.

Here is the flawed pattern as it typically appears:

The getPost function treats a CMS outage identically to a missing blog post. Both return null. Both trigger notFound(). Both get cached as 404s.

When a Server Component calls notFound(), it returns a response with a 404 HTTP status code. Under ISR with a configured revalidate interval, Next.js treats this 404 as a valid cacheable response. From the framework's perspective, the page rendered successfully and produced a definitive answer: this resource does not exist. Next.js has no mechanism to distinguish between "this record genuinely doesn't exist in the database" and "an infrastructure error prevented the application from fetching it."

A successful background revalidation, including one that results in a 404, overwrites the existing cached page entirely. Next.js provides no built-in rollback mechanism when the page component returns a valid response (including a 404) without throwing an unhandled exception. If the revalidation completes without throwing, Next.js considers it successful and replaces the cache entry. An unhandled exception is the mechanism that prevents this overwrite -- the distinction the refactored code exploits. This is by design for the happy path but destructive when error handling collapses infrastructure failures into the same code path as legitimate missing records.

This fix hinges on a single architectural insight: when a data helper throws an unhandled exception, Next.js treats the background revalidation as failed and retains the previously cached page. This behavior is consistent with reported Next.js ISR behavior (see the Next.js ISR documentation and related community reports); run the local simulation test described in the Testing section to confirm on your deployment version. The distinction between throwing and returning null directly controls whether ISR preserves or destroys the cache.

The third and fourth rows are the critical behavioral change. By throwing on infrastructure errors, the revalidation is treated as a failure, and the stale cache survives.

The refactored data helper introduces a custom error class for infrastructure failures and only returns null when the upstream API explicitly confirms the record does not exist (a 404 response status). Network errors, timeouts, 500-level responses, and connection failures all throw, preventing ISR from caching the failure state.

Both files reside in the lib/ directory at the project root (i.e., lib/errors.ts and lib/data.ts).

Note on fetch caching: In some Next.js versions, fetch in Server Components defaults to force-cache, meaning the fetch itself may serve a cached response during ISR revalidation -- masking infrastructure failures. The refactored helper above uses { cache: 'no-store' } to ensure data is fetched live during each revalidation. If your data must be fetched live during each revalidation, add { cache: 'no-store' } or { next: { revalidate: 0 } } to your fetch call.

Only the fetch call itself sits inside the try-catch, handling network-level failures. HTTP error responses (non-404) are handled by explicit status checking after the response arrives. Only a 404 from the CMS returns null, signaling a genuinely missing record. A content-type check before JSON parsing prevents silent SyntaxError exceptions when the CMS returns an HTML error page.

The page component stays simple. It calls notFound() only when getPost returns null, meaning the CMS confirmed the record does not exist. Infrastructure errors thrown by the helper are not caught here. They propagate upward, causing the ISR background revalidation to fail gracefully and preserving the existing cache.

By throwing on infrastructure errors, the revalidation is treated as a failure, and the stale cache survives.

Path alias note: The @/lib/data import requires a paths alias configured in your tsconfig.json (e.g., "@/*": ["./*"]). This is set up automatically by create-next-app but must be added manually if not already present in existing projects.

For direct visits (not background revalidation), an uncaught error would show the default Next.js error page. Adding an error.tsx boundary in the route segment catches errors from Server Components in the same route segment during direct page renders. It does not intercept errors during ISR background revalidation -- those are handled server-side and the user continues to see the stale cached page.

If a 404 was cached before implementing this fix, or due to an edge case where the fix was not yet deployed, on-demand revalidation provides a manual or automated recovery mechanism. Next.js exposes revalidatePath() and revalidateTag() for this purpose. revalidatePath() purges and regenerates the cache for a specific URL path. revalidateTag() invalidates all cache entries associated with a given fetch tag, useful for bulk invalidation across related pages.

A route handler that accepts a path or slug, validates an authentication secret, and calls revalidatePath() gives teams a deployable recovery tool.

Environment variable: Set REVALIDATION_SECRET in your .env.local file. Use a long, random string (e.g., 32+ characters generated with openssl rand -base64 32).

Wire this route to a CMS publish webhook so every content update purges the affected path. It also works as an admin dashboard button for manual recovery after an outage. For post-outage scenarios, teams can iterate over a list of affected slugs and trigger revalidation for each, effectively warming the cache with fresh, valid data once the infrastructure has recovered.

Cost consideration: Calling revalidatePath() for many slugs simultaneously triggers a full server-side render for each one. Revalidating 10,000 paths at once means 10,000 concurrent renders -- batch in groups of 50-100 with a delay between batches to avoid spiking compute and CDN costs.

ISR only operates in production mode. Do not use next dev -- ISR is inactive in development mode and all pages are rendered on every request without caching. Tests will not reflect production caching behavior.

To test locally, run next build followed by next start. With the application running, visit a blog post page to populate the cache. Then temporarily modify the data helper to force a throw simulating an infrastructure failure by adding the following line at the top of the try block in getPost, guarded to prevent accidental production deployment:

Set FORCE_FETCH_ERROR=true in your .env.local file before rebuilding. After adding the simulated throw, you must rebuild (next build && next start) since code changes require a rebuild to take effect.

Wait for the revalidation interval to expire (60 seconds with the example configuration), trigger a request, and verify that the cached page survives. The previously rendered content should still be served.

To confirm the legitimate 404 path works, modify the data helper to return null for a specific slug and verify that notFound() produces the expected 404 page.

Check the terminal logs where next start is running. A failed background revalidation will produce error output indicating the thrown exception. Refresh the page in the browser. The stale cached version should still be served, confirming that the cache was not replaced with a 404.

Throw on transient failures so ISR retains the previously valid cached page. This is the single most important behavioral distinction in the entire pattern.

Yes. In the Pages Router, getStaticProps returning notFound: true during ISR revalidation has the same effect: the 404 is cached, replacing the previous page. The same principle applies. Throwing an error from getStaticProps causes the revalidation to fail and preserves the stale cache. Run the local simulation test described in the Testing section against your target version to confirm; see the Next.js Pages Router ISR documentation for authoritative behavior.

No stale cache exists to fall back on. The user sees an error page (or the error.tsx boundary). The page remains uncached until a successful render completes. This is an inherent limitation: the "preserve stale cache" strategy only works when a valid cache entry already exists.

No. Next.js does not support conditional revalidation intervals based on response type. The revalidate value applies uniformly. To retry sooner after a failure, use on-demand revalidation via revalidatePath() or revalidateTag(), triggered either manually or through automated health checks that detect recovery.

#10464. This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough

Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a new kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.

The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.

Why Quantum Computers Struggle With Errors

Quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot. Many current systems use superconducting circuits, but these are highly sensitive to electromagnetic noise and stray electrical charges - similar to the static electricity that can make hair cling to a balloon.

Even very small disturbances can disrupt the fragile quantum information stored in a qubit. As more qubits are added, controlling those errors becomes increasingly difficult, making scalability one of the central challenges in quantum computing.

In a study published in npj Quantum Information, researchers from Surrey's Quantum Sciences Group describe a different approach built around superfluid helium-3 - an unusual form of liquid helium that can flow without friction.

Their proposed device, called the Superfluid Helium Oscillator Quantum (SHOQ) device, would use charge-neutral superfluid helium. Because the helium carries no electric charge, the design could be naturally protected from certain types of electromagnetic noise.

A Qubit With Much Lower Predicted Error Rates

According to the researchers, this is the first reported design for a qubit based on a superfluid. Their calculations suggest the SHOQ device could have error rates about 100 times lower than conventional superconducting qubits.

Dr. Priya Sharma, Daphne Jackson Fellow in Hybrid Quantum Systems at the University of Surrey's School of Mathematics and Physics, and lead author of the study, said:

"We are not the first to think about the individual components behind this idea, but what we have done for the first time is bring them together in a microfluidic device and work out the specific details that could enable the device to function as a qubit.

"The maths tells us that it should work. We have taken what we already know about superfluid helium and quantum technologies and turned that into an educated design, with the parameters and specifications needed to build one. The next step is to make a prototype and put those predictions to the test."

Rather than replacing existing quantum computing hardware, the researchers say the SHOQ device could potentially be integrated with superconducting quantum technology.

That could allow different types of qubits to perform different jobs within the same system, depending on their strengths.

One longer-term possibility is to use the SHOQ device as a form of quantum memory. In that setup, a superfluid based qubit could store quantum information while other hardware carries out calculations.

Dr. Eran Ginossar, Associate Professor at the University of Surrey's Department of Physics and Advanced Technology Institute, and co-author of the study, said:

"We don't necessarily need one type of qubit to do everything. Combining different quantum technologies could allow us to take advantage of the strengths of each.

"Superfluid helium gives us a fundamentally different type of quantum hardware to explore. If the predicted performance can be demonstrated experimentally, it could eventually work alongside existing superconducting technologies as part of a larger quantum system."

The team now plans to build a prototype to find out whether the predicted performance can be reproduced in a real device. That effort is being supported by an IAA Commercialisation Fellowship awarded to Dr. Priya Sharma.

The SHOQ device would need to operate at extremely low temperatures, but researchers have already reached the necessary conditions in previous experiments involving superfluid helium-3.

The project was led by the University of Surrey in collaboration with Professor Jens Koch at Northwestern University in the United States. Koch was one of the researchers involved in developing the transmon - a superconducting qubit design that is now widely used in quantum computing.

Materials provided by University of Surrey. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Fitness influencer Goob’s apparent arrest sent social media into a frenzy after Joey Swoll posted footage of him being taken into custody, but Suffolk County police now say the entire scene was staged to promote a charity food giveaway.

Goob, whose real name is John Dorsey, is known for creating fitness content and elaborate holiday charity promotions. His latest Instagram reel told viewers to “Please watch until the end” while tagging the Suffolk County Police Department, HummusFit and GymKatie.

Joey Swoll, another prominent fitness influencer, initially presented the footage as a serious incident. His original Instagram post showed Dorsey apparently being escorted by police and was captioned, “Welcome to the show John.”

“I’m not gonna say what it is that he did, because I don’t have all the facts yet,” Swoll said. He then told his friend to “do better.”

Despite the growing speculation, Dorsey insisted, “It’s not a skit.”

The story changed after a Suffolk County Police Department spokesperson told TMZ that Dorsey was never actually arrested.

“It was part of filming social media posts advertising a charity food giveaway that is taking place later this month,” the spokesperson said.

Swoll later posted a follow-up reel captioned “UPDATE! 😳😳😳 @goob_u2,” while Goob’s own follow-up video asked viewers to watch until the end.
